15 September 2026 — Matching moments are exactly the ordinary-NS annihilator data

R09 complete formalization · binary functional-unary system · constant moment unrestricted

Exact statement and source scope

On an \(m\)-row, \(N\)-column board with \(N\ge1\), let \(\mathcal F^{\mathrm{fun}}_{m,N}\) be the existing ordinary polynomial system containing Booleanity, distinct-cell same-row and same-column exclusions, and \(\rho_i-1\), where \(\rho_i=\sum_jX_{ij}\). For every \(B\ge0\), a linear functional on the actual subspace \(\mathcal P_{\le B}\) annihilates \(\mathcal I_B(\mathcal F^{\mathrm{fun}}_{m,N})\) if and only if it is the linear extension of matching moments \(z_T\), \(|T|\le B\), satisfying exactly

\[ \sum_{j\notin\operatorname{col}(T)}z_{T\cup\{(i,j)\}}=z_T, \qquad |T|<B,\quad i\notin\operatorname{row}(T). \]

Its value on an ordinary monomial is the moment of its squarefree support if that support is a matching, and zero otherwise. Every assigned matching moment is recovered by evaluation on its matching monomial. In particular the value on one is \(z_\varnothing\), with neither normalization nor positivity nor multiplicativity assumed. This verifies the entire indexed completeness audit, including the converse construction and bounded-domain statement.

Reusable normal form and ordinary-degree proof

Let \(\mathcal A\) consist of Booleanity and all explicitly supplied distinct-cell row/column collision equations. The checked encoding identity is \(\mathcal F^{\mathrm{fun}}_{m,N}=\mathcal A\cup\{\rho_i-1:i\}\); it rearranges the original generators, rather than replacing their meaning. A matching is precisely a face of the chessboard complex already used in H. Define a linear map \(\mathcal R\) on monomials by

\[ \mathcal R(cX^e)= \begin{cases}cM_{\operatorname{supp}(e)},&\operatorname{supp}(e)\text{ is a matching},\\ 0,&\text{otherwise},\end{cases} \qquad M_S=\prod_{x\in S}X_x. \]

First apply R05's Boolean reduction through \(\deg P\). A nonmatching squarefree support contains two distinct cells sharing a row or column. The checked pair certificate makes its monomial a single collision-generator multiple through its support cardinality, which is no larger than its original monomial degree. Summing gives

\[ P-\mathcal R(P)\in\mathcal I_{\deg P}(\mathcal A), \qquad \deg\mathcal R(P)\le\deg P. \]

Conversely \(\mathcal R\) annihilates every ordinary multiple of every generator of \(\mathcal A\), even without a degree bound. For a Boolean generator, multiplying an ordinary monomial by \(X_x^2\) or \(X_x\) gives the same squarefree support and hence the same image. For a collision generator, every monomial multiple still contains that conflicting pair and has image zero. Expand an arbitrary multiplier into monomials and use linearity. Consequently, for \(\deg P\le B\),

\[ P\in\mathcal I_B(\mathcal A)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\mathcal R(P)=0. \]

These normal-form facts also hold for empty boards; the later full marginal equivalence retains \(N\ge1\).

All row equations, with the original degree charge

For a matching \(T\), if row \(i\) is unused, the extension \(T\cup\{(i,j)\}\) is a matching exactly when column \(j\) is unused. Thus

\[ \mathcal R(M_T(\rho_i-1))= \sum_{j\notin\operatorname{col}(T)}M_{T\cup\{(i,j)\}}-M_T. \]

If row \(i\) is occupied at \((i,j_0)\), the only surviving term of \(\rho_iM_T\) is \(j=j_0\), which reduces to \(M_T\), so the displayed product reduces to zero. Both assertions are checked as polynomial identities.

An annihilator of the full system annihilates \(\mathcal A\), hence has the same value on \(P\) and \(\mathcal R(P)\) whenever \(\deg P\le B\). If \(|T|<B\), then \(M_T(\rho_i-1)\) is a legal multiple through \(B\). Applying the preceding identity therefore proves every stated marginal equation.

For the converse, take a linear functional annihilating \(\mathcal I_B(\mathcal A)\) whose matching moments satisfy the marginals. It annihilates every matching-monomial row multiple of cardinality below \(B\): use the unused-row identity and its marginal, or the occupied-row zero identity. Now consider any legal ordinary row multiple \(q(\rho_i-1)\) through \(B\). If \(q=0\), there is nothing to prove. Otherwise \(\rho_i-1\) is nonzero and has actual degree one because \(N\ge1\): one of its variable coefficients is one. The polynomial ring is an integral domain, so

\[ \deg(q(\rho_i-1))=\deg q+1\le B. \]

Multiplying the normal-form witness for \(q\) by \(\rho_i-1\) therefore stays in \(\mathcal I_B(\mathcal A)\). The functional has the same value on \(q(\rho_i-1)\) and \(\mathcal R(q)(\rho_i-1)\). The latter is a linear combination of the matching-monomial row multiples already checked, since every surviving support has size at most \(\deg q<B\). This exhausts all legal generators and then their span. The argument subtracts an actual degree, not a loose ceiling. For \(N=0\), the row generator would instead be the degree-zero constant \(-1\), so this reverse argument correctly does not assert that extra case.

Every moment assignment, and the actual bounded functional space

Given any matching moments satisfying the marginals, define \(L_z\) linearly on ordinary monomials by the rule in the statement. The implementation first applies \(\mathcal R\), then reads each remaining squarefree monomial's moment. It annihilates \(\mathcal A\) by the checked kernel statement, and the row argument proves that it annihilates the full ordinary NS space through \(B\). On a matching monomial \(M_T\) it returns exactly \(z_T\); on one it returns \(z_\varnothing\).

Conversely, start with a functional \(\lambda\) on \(\mathcal P_{\le B}\) annihilating the indicated NS subspace. The already verified R04 extension lemma supplies an ambient polynomial functional \(E\) agreeing with \(\lambda\) and annihilating the same NS space. Its well-definedness condition is exactly the supplied annihilation on the intersection: on \(\mathcal P_{\le B}+\mathcal I_B\), assign \(u+s\mapsto\lambda(u)\), then extend linearly. Set \(z_T=E(M_T)\). The preceding proof gives the marginals. For every polynomial in the bounded domain, normal-form invariance gives \(\lambda(P)=E(\mathcal R(P))=L_z(P)\). Hence the formal statement is about the actual bounded subspace, not an assumption that its functional was already globally defined. Evaluating on each legal matching monomial recovers its moment uniquely. The Lean array also permits arbitrary values on nonmatching or larger supports; these are unused auxiliary coordinates and impose no conditions on the bounded correspondence.

MatchingMomentCompleteness.lean proves both directions, constructs moment functionals, recovers moments, and proves the bounded-domain equivalence. These are project formalizations of the recorded normal-form and completeness arguments, without a novelty assertion. Exact types, transitive axiom reports, scope and source hashes preserve verification. All dependencies are checked, including R01/R02/R05 and R04 for the bounded extension; H's face definition is reused without assuming any unproved topology.

15 September 2026 — Canonical fresh ENS blocks and exact companion degrees

Status: complete Lean formalization of an extracted R07 degree claim; scalar PC cleanup remains separate.

Obligation and endpoint. Prove the exact original degrees asserted in the paper's scalar-cleanup discussion and the proper affine setup. The endpoint must use disjoint fresh variables and actual input degree, respecting the earlier equality-versus-ceiling correction. The canonical block representation also supports the fixed global coefficient registry needed by clause simulation.

Claim: fresh ENS block degrees and renaming

Let \(K\) be any field, let \((g_i)_{i\in I}\subseteq K[X_\sigma]\) be a finite input family with \(\deg g_i\le1\), and let \(h\ge0\). Adjoin distinct new variables \(r_{ui}\), disjoint from all old variables, and define

\[ F_u=1-\sum_i r_{ui}g_i,\qquad P=\prod_{u=1}^h F_u,\qquad C_i=g_iP. \]

Always \(\deg F_u\le2\), \(\deg P\le2h\), and \(\deg C_i\le2h+1\). If some selected input \(g_j\) has actual degree one, then

\[ \deg F_u=2,\qquad \deg P=2h,\qquad \deg C_j=2h+1. \]

The ordinary degree of any polynomial is preserved by injectively renaming its variables. Renaming the whole block through any variable map \(\rho\) gives exactly the product with coefficient variables \(X_{\rho(r_{ui})}\) and old inputs renamed through the composite old-variable injection. Thus an injective embedding into a global registry preserves these exact degrees. No identification of polynomial functions is used.

Full proof. For an injective variable map \(e:\alpha\hookrightarrow\beta\), the renamed polynomial has degree at most the original degree. Define a polynomial substitution back from target variables: a variable in the image of \(e\) maps to its unique original variable, and every other variable maps to zero. Every substitution image has degree at most one, and the substitution composed with renaming is the identity on every original variable, hence on every polynomial. The checked substitution degree bound therefore gives the reverse inequality. This argument also works when the original variable type is empty.

Each summand \(r_{ui}g_i\) has degree at most two, giving the factor upper bound; products add these upper bounds and multiplication by \(g_i\) adds at most one. Now assume \(\deg g_j=1\). In one factor, set all coefficient variables other than \(r_{uj}\) to zero and keep all old variables unchanged. The factor becomes \(1-r_{uj}g_j\). Injective old-variable renaming preserves \(\deg g_j=1\), so the product \(r_{uj}g_j\) has degree two in the integral domain \(K[X,r]\). Subtracting it from the degree-zero constant one cannot cancel its top degree. Thus the specialized factor has degree two. The specialization uses variable images of degree at most one and cannot increase degree, proving that the original factor has degree at least two; the upper bound makes this an equality.

Every such factor is nonzero. In a polynomial ring over a field, degrees add under multiplication of nonzero polynomials, so induction over the finite factor set gives \(\deg P=2h\), and its product is nonzero. Multiplication by the nonzero degree-one input \(g_j\) gives \(\deg C_j=2h+1\). When \(h=0\), the product is one and the formulas become \(\deg P=0\) and \(\deg C_j=1\). When all inputs vanish, or the family is empty, only the upper-bound statements apply. Finally, renaming is an algebra homomorphism: it distributes through the displayed sums, products and subtraction, proving the registry identity. \(\square\)

Connection to proper affine blocks. The preceding verified claim proves exact degree one for every nonzero input in a proper affine span. Applying the present companion theorem separately to each retained nonzero input therefore gives the paper's exact \(2h+1\) original degree. A loose degree-one ceiling alone is deliberately insufficient for the equality theorem.

Interface and evidence. FreshENSBlock.lean uses variables σ ⊕ (Fin h × ι), old renaming through Sum.inl, and individual fresh variables through Sum.inr. Its product-renaming identity directly embeds into a registry whose coefficient index is a dependent sum over blocks. The incremental report audits eight declarations with transitive axioms, and the reproduction record preserves the scope, original degree conventions, and complete checks.

Remaining route and process assessment. Scalar elimination of zero/unit blocks, including coefficient Boolean equations and degree-preserving PC replay, still remains in R07; R08/R16 remain assigned. Explicit coefficient specialization gave a short degree lower bound without expanding the full product. The distinction between actual degree and an upper ceiling was preserved, and no new mathematical gap or guidance change was needed. The coordinator owns living-section updates.

15 September 2026 — Degree-preserving scalar cleanup of complete ENS blocks

Status: complete Lean formalization of the remaining R07 scalar-cleanup dependency; together with the preceding releases, this covers the planned R07 obligations.

Obligation and endpoint. Formalize the paper's deletion of zero/unit-span blocks, including all coefficient Boolean equations and actual ordinary PC replay. Reuse the canonical fresh block; the retained variable type may include other blocks' coefficient variables, so preserving arbitrary retained polynomials explicitly ensures that their axioms are unchanged.

Claim: complete-block scalar cleanup

Let \(K\) be a field, \(F\subseteq K[X_\sigma]\) any retained axiom set, and \((g_i)\) any finite old-polynomial family. The block has fresh variables \(r_{ui}\), product \(P=\prod_u(1-\sum_i r_{ui}g_i)\), and complete axiom set

\[ \mathcal B=\{g_iP:i\in I\}\cup\{r_{ui}^2-r_{ui}:u\in[h],i\in I\}. \]

The product equation \(P=0\) is not an axiom. Let \(s_c\) fix every retained variable and replace the fresh coefficients by constants \(c_{ui}\). Suppose \(c_{ui}^2=c_{ui}\) for every slot and \(s_c(g_iP)=0\) for every companion. Then every ordinary degree-\(D\) PC derivation of \(p\) from the retained axioms and \(\mathcal B\) yields a degree-\(D\) derivation of \(s_c(p)\) from \(F\) alone. In particular retained conclusions and refutations are preserved at the same ceiling.

If all \(g_i=0\), take all \(c_{ui}=0\); this works over every field and for every \(h\ge0\). If \(K=\mathbb F_2\), \(h\ge1\), and \(1\) belongs to the linear span of the inputs, choose a unit combination \(\sum_i c_i g_i=1\), put \(c_i\) in the first coefficient row and zero in every other row. This also removes the whole block. The scalar cleanup itself needs no affine-degree assumption on the old inputs.

Full proof. Substitution fixes every old polynomial because it fixes each old variable and acts identically on constants. Its variable images have degree at most one. Every retained axiom therefore maps to itself; if active at source ceiling \(D\), its degree remains at most \(D\). Every companion maps to zero by hypothesis. Each coefficient-domain equation maps to the constant polynomial \(C(c_{ui}^2-c_{ui})=0\). Thus every substituted source axiom has a degree-\(D\) PC proof from the retained set: it is either a retained axiom or the zero line.

Apply the checked substitution/replay theorem with substitution degree bound one and constant weight one. Addition and scalar multiplication replay directly. At a nonzero variable-multiplication step, the source predecessor has degree at most \(D-1\), and its substituted multiplying variable has degree at most one; hence all primitive replay lines remain within \(D\). Zero predecessors remain zero. The final line is \(s_c(p)\), proving the general assertion. If \(p\) uses only retained variables, \(s_c(p)=p\); in particular \(s_c(1)=1\).

For a zero input family, every companion is already zero, and zero constants satisfy their Boolean equations. For a unit combination and \(h\ge1\), the first product factor specializes to \(1-\sum_i c_i g_i=0\); hence the product and all companions specialize to zero. Over \(\mathbb F_2\), every scalar satisfies \(c^2=c\), so the general cleanup theorem applies. Membership of one in the finite input span supplies the required constant combination. The unit case deliberately excludes \(h=0\), where there is no first coefficient row. Over a general field, idempotence of chosen constants remains an explicit hypothesis; characteristic two alone would not justify it. \(\square\)

Its complete block axiom set, scalar map and first-row unit assignment are explicit definitions. The incremental audit verifies five declarations: old-polynomial preservation, general cleanup with explicit idempotence, zero cleanup, binary unit-combination cleanup, and its unit-span corollary. The reproduction record retains exact hypotheses, scope and full measured outputs.

15 September 2026 — A fixed complete affine-clause ENS registry

Status: full formalization of the indexed clause-system definition and its degree interfaces; R18.

Affine maps over arbitrary finite coordinate types

Question and scope. Formalize the fixed affine-clause PC system in a form shared by semantic clause rules and the actual bit-variable system. The existing affine-form interface uses coordinates \(\mathrm{Fin}(v)\). Here we generalize only the coordinate index to an arbitrary finite type \(\sigma\), so product types such as pigeon–bit pairs need no artificial flattening. This is the same elementary coefficient representation, not a novelty claim.

For an affine map \(f:K^\sigma\to K\), over any field, define its ordinary polynomial

\[ \widehat f(X)=f(0)+\sum_{i\in\sigma}f_{\mathrm{lin}}(e_i)X_i. \]

It has total degree at most one. The coordinate expansion \(x=\sum_i x_i e_i\) and the affine identity \(f(x)=f_{\mathrm{lin}}(x)+f(0)\) show that \(\widehat f(x)=f(x)\) at every point. Addition and scalar multiplication of affine maps act coefficientwise, giving a linear conversion. If two converted polynomials agree, their evaluations show that the original maps agree, hence the conversion is injective. On \(\sigma=\mathrm{Fin}(v)\), the formula agrees exactly with the existing affinePolynomial (affineFormOfMap f); this compatibility is also checked. The separate FiniteAffinePolynomial.lean file records this reusable bridge.

One finite registry, with all companions and Boolean domains

Fix a finite list of binary affine clauses \((C_c)_{c<N}\) on \(\mathbb F_2^\sigma\), an old polynomial system \(\mathcal F\), and accuracy \(h\ge1\). Each clause is a finite set of true-indicator affine maps. Use the ordinary polynomial ring with variable type

\[ \sigma\;\sqcup\;\coprod_{c<N}\bigl([h]\times C_c\bigr). \]

The left summand holds old variables. A right-summand variable \((c,u,g)\) is the fresh coefficient \(r_{c,u,g}\). Different clause identifiers have disjoint coefficient scopes by their tags, even when their literal sets overlap. A clause with no literals contributes no coefficient variables. Convert each literal by \(g\mapsto\widehat g\) and include its polynomial through the old-variable injection. Thus every input is old-only and affine; the family has one extension level.

\[ P_c=\prod_{u<h}\left(1-\sum_{g\in C_c}r_{c,u,g}\widehat g\right),\qquad E_{c,g}=\widehat gP_c,\qquad U_{c,g}=\sum_{u<h}r_{c,u,g} \prod_{w<u}\left(1-\sum_{f\in C_c}r_{c,w,f}\widehat f\right). \]

The fixed system is exactly the lifted old system, Booleanity for every old and coefficient variable, and all \(E_{c,g}\). Clause values \(P_c\) are not introduced as an additional family of axioms; their derivations belong to subsequent rule simulations. If \(C_c=\varnothing\), every factor is one and \(P_c=1\), with no companion or coefficient in that scope. Each nonempty value also equals the injective renaming of the canonical fresh ENS block; the equality is proved by changing the product index from \(\mathrm{Fin}(h)\) to \(0,\ldots,h-1\) and checking each factor. It is valid for empty clauses too.

Prefix identity and ordinary bounds. Apply the checked ENS telescoping identity to obtain

\[ 1-P_c=\sum_{g\in C_c}U_{c,g}\widehat g,\qquad \deg P_c\le2h,\quad \deg U_{c,g}\le2h-1,\quad \deg E_{c,g}\le2h+1. \]

Indeed each old input and each coefficient variable has degree at most one, so each factor has degree at most two. The \(u\)-th prefix summand has degree at most \(1+2u\le2h-1\); multiplying \(P_c\) by an input costs at most one more. These are upper bounds, including zero and constant literals; no false exact-degree equality is introduced for degenerate clauses.

The PCClause interface packages the actual input polynomials, value, cofactors, identity, degree bounds, and primitive PC proofs of all companions. registryClauseData constructs it from this fixed system, and its value, input, and cofactor fields are checked equal to the registry definitions. This is a concrete reusable certificate interface, not an assumption that arbitrary abstract clause values have the required proofs. Later rule engines can operate on it while the registry supplies its hypotheses.

15 September 2026 — No-retained-core low-rank ENS packing

Status: complete Lean formalization of R08, including rank-only existence and ordinary Boolean NS companion certificates.

Obligation and endpoint. Formalize the low-rank part of the paper's weighted-removal lemma and the mixed-packing argument. The required endpoint assigns old polynomials to all coefficients of a low-rank block with no retained core. It does not invoke the stronger retained-core optimality theorem outside its stated positive-core range.

Claim: low-rank ENS specialization

Let \((g_i)_{i\in I}\) be a finite family of ordinary \(\mathbb F_2\)-polynomials of degree at most one in finitely many variables. Put \(r=\dim\operatorname{span}\{g_i\}\), and suppose \(r\le h(k+1)\), where \(h,k\ge0\). There exist coefficient polynomials \(\beta_{ui}\) and an ordinary polynomial \(Z\) such that

\[ \deg\beta_{ui}\le k,\qquad \prod_{u=1}^h\left(1-\sum_i\beta_{ui}g_i\right)=Z, \qquad \deg Z\le r. \]

At every Boolean point, \(Z\) equals one exactly when all inputs vanish, and equals zero otherwise. Every companion has an ordinary Boolean NS certificate

\[ g_iZ\in\mathcal I_{r+1}({\rm BOOL}). \]

The formal product identity is the actual specialization of the canonical fresh block, fixing all old variables. Properness and independence of the displayed input tuple are unnecessary. Empty inputs and \(r=0\) are included; \(h=0\) forces \(r=0\), and \(k=0\) permits only constant coefficient polynomials.

Full proof. Choose a basis \(F_1,\ldots,F_r\) of the input span. Every basis element is a constant combination \(F_j=\sum_i c_{ji}g_i\), and each original input is a constant combination of the basis. Since the degree-at-most-one polynomials form a vector subspace, \(\deg F_j\le1\).

The inequality \(r\le h(k+1)\) permits an injection of the basis indices into \([h]\times[k+1]\). Group indices by the first coordinate of this injection, obtaining disjoint bins \(J_u\), each of size at most \(k+1\). The second coordinate is injective within a bin, proving its capacity bound. Order basis indices by their natural order. For \(j\in J_u\), put \(Q_{uj}=\prod_{t\in J_u,\ t<j}(1-F_t)\), and define

\[ \beta_{ui}=\sum_{j\in J_u}c_{ji}Q_{uj}. \]

The prefix excludes \(j\) itself, so it has at most \(|J_u|-1\le k\) factors, each of degree at most one. Thus \(\deg Q_{uj}\le k\), and scalar multiplication and summation give \(\deg\beta_{ui}\le k\). For empty bins every coefficient is zero.

Ordered product telescoping gives

\[ 1-\prod_{j\in J_u}(1-F_j) =\sum_{j\in J_u}F_jQ_{uj} =\sum_i\beta_{ui}g_i. \]

Multiplying the bin identities and using the disjoint partition of all basis indices shows that the specialized block product is exactly \(Z=\prod_{j=1}^r(1-F_j)\), as an ordinary polynomial, and \(\deg Z\le r\).

At a Boolean point every \(F_j\) takes a value in \(\mathbb F_2\). If all values vanish, every product factor is one; otherwise some value is one and its factor is zero. Mutual span membership says that the basis and original family have identical common zero sets. Hence \(Z\) is the required indicator and \(g_iZ\) vanishes on the whole Boolean cube. Its ordinary degree is at most \(r+1\). The checked Boolean reduction theorem supplies an ordinary NS witness at that degree, with each generator multiple charged separately. No flattened PC assumption is used. \(\square\)

15 September 2026 — Primitive PC simulation of complementary-parity resolution

Status: full formalization of the indexed resolution degree lemma; R22.

Resolution preserves a fixed global degree ceiling

Question and scope. Formalize the complementary-parity resolution simulation in the actual fixed registry. The premises are \(A\lor(u=1)\) and \(B\lor(1-u=1)\), with old affine pivot \(u\), and the conclusion is \(A\lor B\). Contexts may overlap, and the conclusion may be empty. Accuracy satisfies \(h\ge1\). If both premise values already have primitive PC derivations through \(K\), the conclusion value has one through \(\max\{K,4h+1\}\).

Residual derivations. Write \(P\) for the conclusion value and \(P_A,P_B\) for the premise values. The checked prefixes yield \(1-P_A=\sum_iU_{A,i}g_{A,i}\), with distinguished pivot input \(u\); similarly the second pivot is \(1-u\). Every other premise input appears among the conclusion inputs, so its product with \(P\) is an actual conclusion companion. Multiplying the prefix identity by \(P\) and separating its pivot term gives

\[ R_A=P-U_{A,u}uP=P_AP+\sum_{i\ne u}U_{A,i}(g_{A,i}P),\qquad R_B=P-U_{B,1-u}(1-u)P=P_BP+\sum_{j\ne1-u}U_{B,j}(g_{B,j}P). \]

Each completed premise value has actual degree at most \(2h\), and \(\deg P\le2h\); their product costs at most \(4h\). A context companion has degree at most \(2h+1\), and its cofactor has degree at most \(2h-1\); multiplying those completed lines also costs at most \(4h\). Therefore \(R_A,R_B\) are derived through \(\max\{K,4h\}\). Independently of \(K\), their displayed ordinary expressions have degree at most \(4h\).

Eliminating the pivot. Since \(\deg u\le1\), the checked binary Boolean reduction supplies a degree-two primitive proof of \(u^2-u\) from the registry's Boolean equations. Ordinary algebra gives

\[ (1-u)R_A-U_{A,u}P(u^2-u)=(1-u)P. \]

The first product has degree at most \(4h+1\). The coefficient \(U_{A,u}P\) has degree at most \(4h-1\), so multiplying the completed quadratic Boolean line costs at most \(4h+1\) too. The resulting line \((1-u)P\) has actual degree at most \(2h+1\), although its derivation may have used the larger global ceiling. Multiply this completed line by \(U_{B,1-u}\), whose degree is at most \(2h-1\), and add \(R_B\):

\[ U_{B,1-u}(1-u)P+R_B=P. \]

The final product costs at most \(4h\). Consequently the entire rule preserves \(\max\{K,4h+1\}\). Every polynomial multiplication is implemented through the checked completed-line reuse theorem; earlier derivation lines are not multiplied, and no proof-height term is introduced.

Concrete registry instantiation. The general PCClause.resolve engine receives actual prefix identities and companion proofs from registryClauseData. The separate registry_resolution theorem instantiates it for registry clauses \(C_a=A\cup\{u\}\), \(C_b=B\cup\{1-u\}\), and \(C_t=A\cup B\). A nonpivot literal in either premise belongs to the corresponding context and therefore the conclusion. Its lifted old polynomial is identical across registry scopes, while the coefficient variables remain disjoint. The affine-to-polynomial bridge sends the opposite literal to \(1-u\). All Boolean and companion lines are members of the one fixed system. Thus the engine's data are supplied by checked definitions, rather than replacing the source system by assumptions. An empty conclusion uses its already defined value one and introduces no empty-clause block.

15 September 2026 — Semantic weakening and tautologies in the fixed registry

Status: full formalization of the indexed semantic-weakening degree lemma; R23.

Affine coefficient witnesses on arbitrary finite coordinates

Question and scope. Formalize the semantic-weakening PC simulation with actual registry inputs and all consistency cases. The registry accepts arbitrary finite old-coordinate types, so its affine linear-algebra dependency must do the same. The following is a coordinate generalization of the already checked affine-system witnesses, not a new mathematical principle.

Let \(g_i,f:K^\sigma\to K\) be affine maps, where \(\sigma\) and the input index set are finite. If the common zero set of the \(g_i\) contains a point and \(f\) vanishes on that zero set, then \(f=\sum_i c_i g_i\) for field constants \(c_i\). If the common zero set is empty, then \(1=\sum_i c_i g_i\).

Proof by coordinate transport. Choose a bijection \(e:\sigma\to\mathrm{Fin}(|\sigma|)\), and map a coordinate vector \(y\) to \(x_s=y_{e(s)}\). This is a surjective linear reindexing with inverse \(x\mapsto(j\mapsto x_{e^{-1}(j)})\). Compose every affine map with this reindexing and apply the checked finite-dimensional affine-form vanishing or unit-coefficient theorem. Evaluate the resulting coefficient identity at arbitrary reindexed vectors. Surjectivity gives the same identity at every original vector, hence equality of the original affine maps. The ordinary-polynomial conversion is linear, so these constant coefficient identities also hold as literal ordinary polynomial identities. No finite-field pointwise-to-polynomial principle for nonlinear polynomials is invoked. FiniteAffineSpan.lean records this reusable dependency.

Complete semantic weakening through \(\max\{K,4h\}\)

Suppose registry clause \(C\) semantically entails \(D\), accuracy \(h\ge1\), and \(P_C\) already has a primitive PC derivation through \(K\). If \(Z(D)\) is nonempty, then \(Z(D)\subseteq Z(C)\): a point falsifying \(D\) cannot satisfy \(C\). Thus each input \(g_{C,i}\) vanishes on \(Z(D)\). The preceding coefficient theorem yields constants with \(g_{C,i}=\sum_j\lambda_{ij}g_{D,j}\), as actual affine-map and ordinary-polynomial identities.

Multiply each identity by \(P_D\). The resulting \(g_{C,i}P_D\) is a constant linear combination of actual \(D\)-companions and therefore has a degree-\(2h+1\) PC derivation. The checked prefix identity gives

\[ P_D=P_CP_D+\sum_iU_{C,i}(g_{C,i}P_D). \]

The first term multiplies a completed premise value of actual degree at most \(2h\) by another polynomial of degree at most \(2h\). Each remaining term multiplies a completed degree-\(2h+1\) companion combination by a cofactor of degree at most \(2h-1\). By completed-line reuse, every term is derived through \(\max\{K,4h\}\), and their sum has the same ceiling.

If \(Z(D)\) is empty, the unit-coefficient identity \(1=\sum_j\lambda_jg_{D,j}\) instead gives

\[ P_D=\sum_j\lambda_j(g_{D,j}P_D). \]

It derives \(P_D\) directly through \(2h+1\), without any premise value. This is the separate tautology theorem and is at most \(4h\) for \(h\ge1\). The two cases prove the full semantic-weakening statement. An empty conclusion is included in the consistent case and has registry value one; its vacuous input set is handled by the same coefficient argument.

Concrete proof-system scope. PCClause.weaken_span and PCClause.tautology_span are the general coefficient engines. registry_semantic_weakening and registry_tautology construct every coefficient witness from actual clause semantics, convert it through the checked affine polynomial map and old-variable injection, and instantiate the engines with registryClauseData. No unproved span-membership premise remains in the concrete theorems, and no clause values are added as algebraic axioms.

15 September 2026 — Simultaneous weighted removal of a complete affine ENS family

Status: complete Lean formalization of R16 with supplied literal high-rank witnesses; their construction remains R15.

Obligation and endpoint. Assemble the verified low-rank specialization, high literal witnesses, every Boolean-domain equation, old axioms and one primitive weighted replay. This formalizes the paper's weighted-removal lemma and the corresponding ordinary-restriction audit; it does not assume the common-kernel existence argument has already been proved.

Claim: simultaneous affine family removal

Let \(F\) be an ordinary polynomial axiom set over \(\mathbb F_2\) on finitely many old variables, containing their Boolean equations. For each block \(b\), take a finite old-polynomial family \((g_{bi})\) with \(\deg g_{bi}\le1\). Give all blocks disjoint fresh coefficients \(r_{bui}\), \(u\in[h]\), and let \(P_b=\prod_u(1-\sum_i r_{bui}g_{bi})\). The complete source consists of the old axioms, all old and fresh Boolean variable equations, and all companions \(g_{bi}P_b\), with no product equations.

Suppose \(h,k\ge1\), \(D\ge2h+1\), and this source has an ordinary degree-\(D\) PC refutation. Let \(f\) be any old ordinary polynomial of degree at most \(k\). For every block of rank \(r_b>h(k+1)\), suppose supplied literal witnesses satisfy

\[ f=\sum_i a_{bi}g_{bi},\qquad \deg a_{bi}\le k-1. \]

Then \(f\) has an ordinary PC derivation from \(F\) through degree \(k(D+1)\). The formal theorem permits any block index type, since each block input tuple and every PC proof are finite. It does not require \(f\) to be multilinear or the blocks to be proper; it therefore recovers the paper's stated application while retaining the same ceiling.

Full proof: local assignments. Write \(d_f=\deg f\le k\) and \(W=kD+d_f\le k(D+1)\). If \(r_b\le h(k+1)\), use the low-rank theorem to choose coefficient images \(\beta_{bui}\) of degree at most \(k\), with specialized product \(Z_b\) and ordinary certificates \(g_{bi}Z_b\in\mathcal I_{r_b+1}({\rm BOOL})\). Multiplying these certificates by \(f\) costs at most \(r_b+1+d_f\). The elementary inequalities

\[ r_b+1\le h(k+1)+1\le k(2h+1)\le kD \]

put every low weighted companion within \(W\); the middle inequality is equivalent to \((k-1)(h+1)\ge0\).

For a high-rank block, put the supplied \(a_{bi}\) in one coefficient row and zero in all others. Since \(h\ge1\), such a row exists. The product becomes \(1-f\) exactly, and the coefficient-image degree is at most \(k\). A weighted companion equals

\[ f g_{bi}(1-f)=-g_{bi}(f^2-f). \]

Boolean reduction supplies \(f^2-f\) through \(2k\); multiplication by the degree-at-most-one input gives an ordinary NS certificate through \(2k+1\). Since \(D\ge3\) and \(k\ge1\), \(2k+1\le3k\le kD\le W\). This uses binary polynomial Booleanity with its checked degree bound, not a multilinearity assumption.

One global substitution and all remaining axioms. The variable type is the disjoint union of old variables and the dependent sum of all block coefficient slots. Fix each old variable, and assign each fresh slot the selected local \(\beta_{bui}\). All images are old polynomials of degree at most \(k\), so the local assignments define one substitution \(s\) even when input tuples overlap. Renaming compatibility of the canonical fresh product identifies every global block image with its local construction.

For any source variable whose image is \(\beta\), the weighted Boolean equation becomes \(f(\beta^2-\beta)\). Its Boolean NS certificate has cost at most \(2k+d_f\le kD+d_f=W\). This also handles old-variable Boolean equations in the complete registry. A used old axiom \(q\in F\) has actual degree at most \(D\), since the old-variable embedding preserves degree. Its weighted image \(fq\) is obtained by completed-line multiplication, through \(\max(D,\deg q+d_f)\le W\), using \(D\le kD\). All Boolean NS certificates transfer to \(F\) by inclusion and the checked NS-to-PC theorem. Thus every active source axiom has its weighted image derived through \(W\).

Primitive replay. Apply the checked weighted substitution theorem with coefficient-image bound \(k\) and weight \(f\). At a nonzero multiplication predecessor \(q\), the original degree satisfies \(\deg q+1\le D\). The weighted image has degree at most \(d_f+k\deg q\); multiplying its completed line by a variable image costs at most \(d_f+k(\deg q+1)\le W\). Zero predecessors and linear combinations are covered by the primitive rules. The final weighted image of one is \(f\). Increasing the ceiling from \(W\) to \(k(D+1)\) proves the claim. \(\square\)

The more general theorem here uses the explicit global assumption \(D\ge2h+1\); it does not infer that equality for zero or constant inputs. Old axiom activity and multiplication-predecessor degrees remain their actual ordinary degrees throughout replay.

Its representation matches the specialized clause registry, whose checked fresh-value identity provides the connection. The incremental audit checks the full refutation-to-old-consequence theorem and transitive dependencies; the reproduction record preserves all evidence and exact scope.

15 September 2026 — Prescribed matching moments extend, and old PC equals NS

R10 complete formalization · actual chessboard fillings · arbitrary row count

Full statement and useful generalization

Work over \(\mathbb F_2\) with the ordinary functional-unary polynomial system \(\mathcal F^{\mathrm{fun}}_{m,N}\). Assume \(N\ge1\), \(N\ge2B-1\), and \(0\le k\le B\). Every linear functional on \(\mathcal P_{\le k}\) annihilating \(\mathcal I_k\) extends to one on \(\mathcal P_{\le B}\) annihilating \(\mathcal I_B\), preserving every old value and hence the constant moment. Furthermore,

\[ \mathcal I_B(\mathcal F^{\mathrm{fun}}_{m,N})\cap\mathcal P_{\le k} =\mathcal I_k(\mathcal F^{\mathrm{fun}}_{m,N}), \qquad \mathcal C_B(\mathcal F^{\mathrm{fun}}_{m,N}) =\mathcal I_B(\mathcal F^{\mathrm{fun}}_{m,N}). \]

Normalized annihilators exist, span the full bounded annihilator space, and exclude a degree-\(B\) NS or ordinary-PC refutation. The formalization proves these statements for every natural row count \(m\), including zero. The original audit's additional hypothesis \(m\ge B\) is unnecessary: each top matching has its own row set, and levels above the available row count contain no new matching unknowns. This is a generalization, not a correction of the original result. It does not concern systems augmented with ENS equations.

Actual moment cycles and their checked fillings

For moment data \(z\) on an \(s\)-row board, define a coefficient function supported in cell count \(r\) by

\[ C_r(z)(T)= \begin{cases}z_T,&T\text{ is a matching and }|T|=r,\\0,&\text{otherwise}. \end{cases} \]

Suppose the matching marginals hold through degree \(s-1\). For \(s\ge2\), this makes \(C_{s-1}(z)\) a cycle for the exact augmented boundary from H01–H03. On a matching \(U\) of size \(s-2\), partition its boundary coefficient by the inserted cell's row. An occupied row contributes zero: its existing cell is excluded by the insertion boundary, while every other cell in that row would create a nonmatching support. An unused row contributes its full missing-row marginal, equal to \(z_U\). Injectivity of the row projection gives exactly \(s-|U|=2\) unused rows, so the coefficient is \(z_U+z_U=0\). On nonmatching faces or other sizes, the supported-boundary theorem gives zero. At \(s=2\), \(U\) is the empty face, and the same computation is the augmentation equation; it is not omitted.

For \(s=1\), the layer is supported on the empty face and has zero outgoing boundary by H01. The checked chessboard homological bound, specialized using \(N\ge2s-1\), fills \(C_{s-1}(z)\) with a chain in cell count \(s\) for every \(s\ge1\). At \(s=1\) this is the nonemptiness base: put the prescribed constant coefficient on one available vertex. At \(s\ge2\) it is the already proved chessboard filling theorem's range. The Lean implementation uses the proved H12 homological bound directly, with its exact boundary and degree conventions; no unproved filling predicate replaces this step.

Retained row sets and genuine chain transport

An injective row map \(f:[r]\hookrightarrow[m]\) induces the cell map \((i,j)\mapsto(f(i),j)\). It preserves matching faces in both directions, cardinalities, and the condition that a column is unused. Row \(i\) is unused before mapping exactly when \(f(i)\) is unused afterwards. Therefore pulling back moments by this map preserves every matching marginal: the summation still ranges over the same columns and each inserted face maps to the corresponding inserted face.

For a retained row set \(S\), enumerate it by \([|S|]\). The induced cell injection has image exactly the cells whose row lies in \(S\). Pull back the global lower moments to this board, obtain the checked local filling, and push its coefficients forward by the H03 chain map. The pushed filling is supported on matchings of size \(|S|\) using only rows in \(S\). For every matching \(T\) of size \(|S|-1\) using rows in \(S\), its boundary coefficient equals the prescribed \(z_T\): take the unique inverse-image face, use preservation of cardinality and matchings, and apply the checked boundary/push identity. This is an actual coefficient and boundary transport, not merely an isomorphism of face counts.

Global extension with cross-row-set consistency

Assume moments are known through degree \(s-1\), where \(1\le s\le B\). Choose the preceding pushed filling \(y_S\) for each row set \(S\) of size \(s\). Define new moments only on size-\(s\) matchings by

\[ z'_T=y_{\operatorname{row}(T)}(T)\qquad(|T|=s), \qquad z'_T=z_T\qquad(|T|<s). \]

A size-\(s\) matching has exactly \(s\) distinct occupied rows, hence has one and only one selector \(\operatorname{row}(T)\). Thus no new unknown is assigned by two fillings. In the implementation all other finite-set coordinates are also left unchanged.

To check a marginal for a matching \(T\), if \(|T|<s-1\), both \(T\) and all its one-cell extensions still have their old values, so its old equation remains valid. If \(|T|=s-1\) and row \(i\) is unused, every legal extension \(T\cup\{(i,j)\}\) has the same row set \(S=\operatorname{row}(T)\cup\{i\}\). Their new values therefore come from the same filling \(y_S\). In the boundary coefficient of \(y_S\) at \(T\), each occupied row contributes zero, and every other row outside \(S\) contributes zero by support. The remaining row is precisely \(i\), and used columns give nonmatching supports. Hence

\[ \sum_{j\notin\operatorname{col}(T)}z'_{T\cup\{(i,j)\}} = (\partial y_S)(T)=z_T=z'_T. \]

This proves all new equations with the globally shared lower values. Iterating from \(k+1\) through \(B\) works because \(N\ge2B-1\) implies every needed \(N\ge2s-1\). It preserves every prescribed moment of size at most \(k\), including \(z_\varnothing\). If \(s>m\), there are no size-\(s\) row sets or matchings; the construction is a function on an empty indexing type and adds no unknowns. A top marginal demanding an additional unused row would itself create such a row set, so it cannot introduce an unhandled case. No hypothesis \(m\ge B\) is used.

R09 turns the resulting moments into actual ordinary-NS annihilators. If two moment arrays agree on all matching supports of size at most \(k\), their canonical moment functionals agree on every polynomial of ordinary degree at most \(k\): expand into monomials, whose supports have no larger cardinality than their degree, and apply the exact R09 monomial rule. For a functional initially defined only on \(\mathcal P_{\le k}\), R04 first extends it to an ambient functional annihilating \(\mathcal I_k\); the construction then extends its low moments, and restriction to \(\mathcal P_{\le B}\) gives the desired bounded-domain extension. Thus the original bounded functional and all its values are recovered, not just its normalization.

Stable filtration, ordinary PC closure and normalization

If a degree-at-most-\(k\) polynomial \(P\) is outside \(\mathcal I_k\), R04 separates it by a functional that annihilates \(\mathcal I_k\) and takes value one on \(P\). The extension just proved preserves that value while annihilating \(\mathcal I_B\), so \(P\) is outside \(\mathcal I_B\). The reverse filtration inclusion follows by monotonicity of legal certificates. This proves the displayed subspace intersection identity.

Induct on an ordinary degree-\(B\) PC derivation. Zero, legal axioms and linear combinations lie in \(\mathcal I_B\). At a variable multiplication \(f\mapsto X_xf\), a zero predecessor is immediate. For a nonzero predecessor, the ordinary polynomial ring is an integral domain and

\[ \deg(X_xf)=1+\deg f\le B. \]

The induction hypothesis puts \(f\) in \(\mathcal I_B\), and stability moves it to \(\mathcal I_{B-1}\). Multiplying each of its legal generator multiples by \(X_x\) stays within \(B\), by the checked R02 NS multiplication rule. This proves \(\mathcal C_B\subseteq\mathcal I_B\); R02 supplies the other inclusion. There is no implicit multilinear multiplication rule or unsupported equality for augmented systems.

Starting at degree zero with constant moment one gives a normalized annihilator through \(B\), so neither NS nor PC can derive one. Finally fix a normalized bounded annihilator \(E\). For any bounded annihilator \(L\), set

\[ D=L+(1-L(1))E. \]

Then \(D(1)=1\), \(D\) still annihilates the same NS space, and \(L=D-(1-L(1))E\). Thus normalized annihilators span the entire bounded annihilator space, covering that assertion of the original audit as well. These statements retain \(N\ge1\), including when \(B=0\); at zero columns the ordinary row generator would be \(-1\), which is outside the source hypotheses.

MatchingMomentCycles.lean, MatchingMomentRelabeling.lean, and MatchingMomentExtension.lean are separately indexed dependencies; MatchingFiltration.lean supplies the full R10 endpoint. Their type/axiom audits, source hashes and complete measured evidence verify all dependencies without a custom axiom or unfinished proof. These are project formalizations of the recorded moment argument, using the attributed checked chessboard theorem; no novelty claim is made for the background topology.

15 September 2026 — Actual bit-PHP CNF clauses and their compact initial values

Status: verified extracted prerequisites for R24; the full DAG transfer remains separate.

Sharp prefixes for a product of affine-literal complements

Question and stopping point. Supply the concrete initial-clause boundary in the publication transfer proof, before assembling the finite source DAG. The first reusable helper is an ordinary identity over any field: if \(g_0,\ldots,g_{n-1}\) have degree at most one, there are polynomials \(U_i\) with

\[ 1-\prod_{i<n}(1-g_i)=\sum_{i<n}U_i g_i,\qquad \deg U_i\le n-1. \]

Complete recursive proof. For an empty family the identity is \(0=0\), with no coefficient obligation. For a nonempty family, apply induction to the tail, writing \(1-Q=\sum_{i>0}V_i g_i\). Set \(U_0=1\) and \(U_i=(1-g_0)V_i\) for tail indices. Then \(g_0+(1-g_0)(1-Q)=1-(1-g_0)Q\). The new coefficients have degree at most one plus the tail coefficient degree, hence at most \(n-1\); the first has degree zero. This is an equivalent orientation of the standard prefix identity and retains the sharper \(n-1\) bound needed here. AffineLiteralProduct.lean records the general helper.

The usual CNF and the genuine compact polynomial axiom

Use bit variables \(b_{it}\). Define the compact pair clause \(C_{ii'}\) by the affine true-indicators \(g_t=b_{it}+b_{i't}\), and define the usual CNF clause for a label \(z\in\mathbb F_2^\ell\) by all indicators \(b_{it}+z_t\) and \(b_{i't}+z_t\). The latter clause is false exactly when both bit rows equal \(z\); the compact clause is false exactly when the two rows agree. These two equivalences are explicitly checked, so the definitions retain the actual standard encoding.

It follows that \(C_{ii'}\) semantically entails every such CNF clause. For completeness, if the CNF clause is false, then \(b_{it}+z_t=b_{i't}+z_t=0\) for every \(t\). Cancelling \(z_t\) gives \(b_{it}=b_{i't}\), so every compact true-indicator is zero. Taking the contrapositive proves entailment.

Now let a clause in the fixed registry equal \(C_{ii'}\), with \(i<i'\), and write \(P\) for its actual registry value. The old compact system contains the ordinary degree-\(\ell\) axiom

\[ E_{ii'}=\prod_{t<\ell}(1+b_{it}+b_{i't}) =\prod_{t<\ell}(1-g_t). \]

It is not treated as an affine axiom. Apply the preceding literal-product identity to the old input polynomials lifted into the registry, and multiply by \(P\):

\[ P=E_{ii'}P+\sum_{t<\ell}U_t(g_tP). \]

The old axiom has degree at most \(\ell\) and \(\deg P\le2h\), so completed-line multiplication derives \(E_{ii'}P\) through \(2h+\ell\). Each \(g_tP\) is an actual registry companion through \(2h+1\), and \(\deg U_t\le\ell-1\), so every remaining product fits the same ceiling. If the index set is empty, no companion term is needed and the old product is one. Thus the formal local initial-value theorem includes all natural \(h,\ell\); the publication will use its stated positive-accuracy, large-bit regime.

Verification and remaining work. BitPHPInitialBridge.lean proves the two exact falsifying-set characterizations, semantic entailment, and the concrete fixed-registry initial-value certificate. The initial-bridge report, prefix report, and scope map preserve full statements and axiom audits. The staged builds and completed audits passed; no mathematical gap was found. Process assessment: explicit falsifying-set characterizations pin the formal clause definitions to the actual CNF, while the sharp literal-product prefixes avoid importing a looser ENS cofactor budget. R24 still needs global DAG normalization, \(3S+\binom m2\) node accounting, polynomial inventory, and height-independent replay.

15 September 2026 — Family removal also accepts unit-span high blocks

Status: verified generalization needed to compose the full clause registry with affine removal; the original theorem remains available.

Unit-or-literal high-block removal

Question and scope. The complete source-clause registry may contain tautological affine clauses. For their unit-span input families, a degree-\(k\) target need not have the degree-\(k-1\) literal coefficient witnesses supplied for proper high blocks. Extend the verified simultaneous removal theorem by treating a unit-span high block separately. This is a composition requirement, not a counterexample to the earlier theorem under its stated hypotheses.

Let \(\mathcal F\) contain the old Boolean equations, and let \((g_{b,i})_i\) be finite old-affine input families over \(\mathbb F_2\), with complete independent accuracy-\(h\) ENS blocks and all coefficient Boolean equations. Assume \(h,k\ge1\), \(D\ge2h+1\), and \(\deg f\le k\). Put \(r_b=\dim\operatorname{span}\{g_{b,i}\}\). For every block with \(r_b>h(k+1)\), require either

\[ 1\in\operatorname{span}_{\mathbb F_2}\{g_{b,i}\}, \qquad\text{or}\qquad f=\sum_i a_{b,i}g_{b,i},\quad \deg a_{b,i}\le k-1. \]

Then a degree-\(D\) primitive PC refutation of the full family implies \(\mathcal F\vdash_{k(D+1)}f\). The input family, coefficient inventory, old system, and degree conventions are unchanged.

Low blocks. If \(r_b\le h(k+1)\), use the already verified low-rank specialization. Its coefficient images have degree at most \(k\), and each specialized companion has an ordinary Boolean NS certificate through \(r_b+1\). Multiplying by \(f\) costs at most \(r_b+1+\deg f\le kD+\deg f\). The numerical inequality follows from \(h,k\ge1\) and \(D\ge2h+1\), exactly as in the original proof.

Unit-span high blocks. Choose field constants \(c_i\) with \(\sum_i c_i g_{b,i}=1\). In one coefficient row assign \(r_{b,u,i}=c_i\), and assign zero in every other row. The selected factor is \(1-\sum_i c_i g_{b,i}=0\), while the remaining factors are one, so the block value and every companion become zero. Every weighted companion image is therefore zero. The coefficient images have degree zero, and their Boolean equations also become zero because \(c_i\in\mathbb F_2\). No degree-\(k-1\) expression for \(f\) is needed in this branch.

Literal-witness high blocks. Use the original specialization: assign \(a_{b,i}\) to one coefficient row and zero to the others. Its value is \(1-f\), and

\[ f\,g_{b,i}(1-f)=-g_{b,i}(f^2-f). \]

The checked Boolean certificate for \(f^2-f\) costs at most \(2k\); multiplying by the affine input costs at most \(2k+1\le kD\). Coefficient images have degree at most \(k-1\le k\). These are the original high-block argument and budgets.

Complete replay. Choose all block substitutions simultaneously in their disjoint scopes and leave old variables unchanged. Every variable image has degree at most \(k\). A coefficient Booleanity image has a Boolean NS certificate through \(2k\), and multiplying it by \(f\) costs at most \(2k+\deg f\le kD+\deg f\). Every eligible old axiom remains itself, with its original degree retained by the injective old-variable inclusion; multiplying its completed line by \(f\) fits the same ceiling. The three block cases above cover all companions. Thus the checked weighted primitive PC substitution theorem maps the refutation to a derivation of \(f\) through \(kD+\deg f\le k(D+1)\).

Compatibility and verification. The stronger theorem lives in AffineFamilyRemovalWithUnits.lean. The original AffineFamilyRemoval.lean retains its theorem name and exact literal-only statement as a wrapper choosing the second disjunct. Public family definitions and namespaces remain unchanged through that import; there is no import cycle. The generalization report, original-wrapper report, and scope map preserve the checked statements. No source claim was invalidated. Process assessment: accepting a unit-span disjunct directly removes the concrete registry mismatch without a separate global pruning transformation or new DAG restrictions. The pending R24 DAG/counting proof can continue with tautological clauses present.

15 September 2026 — A compressed fixed registry for a finite affine proof DAG

Status: verified reusable DAG controller for R24; actual bit-PHP instantiation remains separate.

Three registry slots per source node, with no degree-height factor

Question and scope. Turn the checked local clause simulations into one finite fixed-registry construction. Represent a DAG by a topological list \((C_i)_{i<S}\), allowing any earlier node to be referenced repeatedly. The explicit source-step constructors are an initial clause, one-premise semantic weakening, complementary-parity resolution, and arbitrary two-premise semantic consequence. Thus both recorded proof-rule conventions are included. Let \(I\) be the source initial-clause set and let \((A_j)_{j\in J}\) be a finite covering family: every \(D\in I\) is semantically implied by some \(A_j\). Assume \(|A_j|\le w\), and write \(v=|\sigma|\) for the number of old variables.

The theorem constructs a registry \(R\), initial indices, and primary source-node indices with exactly \(N=3S+|J|\) slots. Each initial slot contains its \(A_j\). Each primary slot contains a semantically equivalent subclause of the original \(C_i\). Every registry clause has width at most \(\max\{w,v+2\}\). For any accuracy \(h\ge1\), old system, and global ceiling \(D\ge4h+1\), actual degree-\(D\) proofs of the initial-slot values imply degree-\(D\) proofs of every primary-node value.

Compression and local plans. Apply the already verified affine clause compression to each \(C_i\), obtaining \(Q_i\subseteq C_i\), \(|Q_i|\le v+1\), and identical truth sets. Semantic weakening transfers between these equivalent clauses. A complementary resolution step is a sound binary semantic step: either a context already holds, or both complementary pivot literals cannot simultaneously be true. For a general binary step, transfer its soundness to \(Q_a,Q_b,Q_i\) and apply the checked binary semantic affine cover. It yields either one weakening from one premise, or a pivot \(u\) such that

\[ Q_a\models Q_i\lor(u=1),\qquad Q_b\models Q_i\lor(1-u=1). \]

The latter case uses two weakenings and one complementary resolution. Source initial clauses instead use their covering \(A_j\), followed by equivalence to \(Q_i\). These choices define a finite plan for each original node and retain its earlier predecessor references.

One registry and its count. Use the tagged finite index type \(J\sqcup(\mathrm{Fin}(S)\times\mathrm{Fin}(3))\), reindexed as \(\mathrm{Fin}(N)\). The three slots for node \(i\) contain \(Q_i\) and the two auxiliary clauses in its plan. When the plan uses no auxiliary inference, the two spare slots may repeat \(Q_i\); they are unused in replay and still fit the same upper bound. The count is exactly \(|J|+3S\). An auxiliary clause adds at most one literal to \(Q_i\), so its width is at most \(v+2\), not \(v+1\). The indexed publication transfer requires polynomial inventory, so this actual bound suffices without another compression round.

The registry's coefficient variables are indexed by an accuracy row and one literal occurrence per slot. Consequently the exact total variable count is

\[ |\mathrm{Vars}(R,h)|=v+h\sum_{c<N}|R_c|. \]

The width bound therefore gives at most \(hN\max\{w,v+2\}\) fresh coefficient slots. This counts the ENS registry, not the monomial-expanded primitive PC derivation.

Replay in the original DAG order. Induct strongly on the original node index. An initial plan applies the concrete registry weakening theorem to its actual supplied initial-value proof. A one-premise plan applies the same theorem to its already derived earlier node. In the two-auxiliary case, derive both auxiliary values from the two earlier primary values, then apply concrete registry resolution with shared context \(Q_i\). All weakenings stay within \(D\), since \(4h\le D\), and resolution stays within \(D\), since \(4h+1\le D\). No clause value is added as an axiom, and no derivation is multiplied by a proof-height factor. Registry numbering need not be proof order: each node's auxiliaries are proved before its primary conclusion. Every derived value uses the same fixed family of old inputs, companions, and Boolean domains.

Completion boundary and verification. AffineDAGRegistry.lean proves this full conditional controller and the exact variable count. The verification report and scope map expose the initial-cover and initial-PC hypotheses. These have not been silently discharged: full R24 still must instantiate the actual bit-PHP initial family, prove its \(\binom m2\) count, supply the checked \(2h+\ell\) initial certificates, and use an empty final clause's value one. The first staged build needed only unused-section-instance cleanup; the complete theorem then verified. Process assessment: a finite typed plan keeps source-rule normalization, registry size, and primitive replay connected, while recording the actual \(v+2\) auxiliary width avoids overstating the compression bound.

15 September 2026 — Ordinary restriction witnesses and concrete kernel bounds

Status: four complete supporting formalizations for R15; the actual family joint-kernel assembly remains unfinished.

Obligation and endpoint. The full R15 assignment requires a nonzero row-linear polynomial with literal degree-controlled coefficients at the paper's concrete high-rank threshold and square-root/logarithmic parameter. This cycle checks the reusable coordinate, ideal and numerical components. It does not replace the final theorem by an abstract dimension assumption.

Finite-coordinate affine completion

Claim lem:finite-affine-coordinate-completion. For any field \(K\), finite coordinate type \(V\), and independent finite affine-map family \((g_i)\) on \(K^V\) whose span excludes the constant one, there exist an injection \(e:I\hookrightarrow V\) and an affine equivalence \(E:K^V\simeq K^V\) with \(E(x)_{e(i)}=g_i(x)\). This generalizes the previous coefficient-form completion to the actual bit-variable type.

Proof. If no common zero existed, the checked finite affine-span theorem would express the constant one as a combination of the inputs, a contradiction. Choose a common zero \(x_0\). On the input span, equality of linear parts implies equality of affine maps: evaluation at \(x_0\) also forces equality of the constants. Thus the independent affine family has independent linear functionals. Extend those functionals to a dual basis and reindex it by \(V\), placing the original functionals at distinct indices \(e(i)\). Evaluation of the dual basis is a linear equivalence by finite-dimensional double duality. Compose it with \(x\mapsto x-x_0\). Its selected coordinates are the original affine maps because those maps vanish at \(x_0\). \(\square\)

Literal coefficients from zero ordinary coordinate restriction

Claim lem:coordinate-restriction-ideal. Let \(K\) be a field and \(e:I\hookrightarrow V\) select finitely many variables. Set those variables to zero and retain every other variable as an ordinary indeterminate. If this ordinary restriction of \(p\) is zero and \(\deg p\le k\), then

\[ p=\sum_{i\in I}a_iX_{e(i)},\qquad \deg a_i\le k-1. \]

The formal statement permits arbitrary ambient variable types; only \(I\) is finite. Natural subtraction at \(k=0\) is harmless because the hypotheses force \(p=0\).

Proof. The coefficient of a monomial supported entirely on retained variables is unchanged by restriction. Therefore no such monomial can have a nonzero coefficient in \(p\). For each monomial in the finite support of \(p\), choose one selected variable occurring with positive exponent. Remove one copy of that variable. The remaining monomial has exponent sum one less, hence degree at most \(k-1\); multiplying it back by the chosen variable recovers the original monomial exactly. Group these remaining monomials, with their original coefficients, according to the selected variable chosen. Finite summation gives the displayed identity and preserves the coefficient-degree bound. Empty support yields all zero coefficients, covering the zero and degree-zero cases. \(\square\)

Ordinary affine pullbacks, literal ideal witnesses and image dimensions

Claim lem:ordinary-affine-restriction-ideal. Over \(\mathbb F_2\), an affine map \(A\) between finite coordinate spaces induces an ordinary polynomial pullback \(A^*\), substituting its degree-at-most-one coordinate polynomials. Pullbacks preserve evaluation, do not increase total degree, compose contravariantly and send identity maps to identity homomorphisms. An affine equivalence and its inverse therefore give inverse ordinary polynomial maps.

Suppose \(E(x)_{e(i)}=g_i(x)\). Define the ordinary free-coordinate restriction of \(p\) by first applying \((E^{-1})^*\), then setting selected coordinates to zero. If it vanishes and \(\deg p\le k\), then \(p=\sum_i a_i,\operatorname{poly}(g_i)\) literally, with \(\deg a_i\le k-1\). On any source subspace of degree at most \(k\), the image dimension of this restriction is at most

\[ \binom{|V|-|I|+k}{k}. \]

Proof. Evaluation of the substituted coordinate polynomials gives evaluation at \(A(x)\), and affine substitution cannot increase degree. To prove composition and identity as ordinary polynomial homomorphisms, it suffices to check their images of individual variables. Those images have total degree at most one and agree at every binary point. In this degree range they have individual degrees strictly below two, so the checked finite-field interpolation theorem identifies them as polynomials. This argument does not identify general polynomial functions with ordinary polynomials.

Apply the coordinate-ideal claim to \(q=(E^{-1})^*p\). Pulling its literal factorization back by \(E^*\) recovers \(p\), sends the selected variables to \(\operatorname{poly}(g_i)\), and preserves the coefficient-degree ceiling. There are exactly \(|V|-|I|\) retained coordinates. Both pullback and coordinate deletion preserve degree, so the image lies in their ordinary degree-at-most-\(k\) polynomial space. Reindex that finite variable type by a finite interval and apply the verified ordinary polynomial dimension bound. \(\square\)

Concrete binomial, exponential and ceiling estimates

Claim lem:ordinary-restriction-kernel-bound. Let \(m\ge1\), \(\ell\ge1\), \(M\ge1\), \(0\le k\le m\), \(r_*=3\ell(k+1)+1\), and suppose \(r_*\le m\ell\). If \(k^2\ge m\log(4M)\), then

\[ M\binom{m\ell-r_*+k}{k} \le\frac14\binom mk\ell^k. \]

The original choice \(k=\lceil\sqrt{m\log(4M)}\rceil\) satisfies the square condition and is at least one. The square-condition form allows a uniform inventory upper bound; the original ceiling specialization is also checked.

Full alternative estimate. More generally, write \(A=d+k\), \(B=m+1-k\), and \(t=1-k/m\ge0\). If \(A\le\ell(m-2k)\), then \(A\le\ell Bt\): after multiplication by \(m>0\), the difference between the latter right-hand side and \(\ell m(m-2k)\) is \(\ell(k^2+m-k)\ge0\). The standard descending-factorial bounds give

\[ k!\binom{d+k}{k}\le A^k, \qquad B^k\le k!\binom mk. \]

Raise the base inequality to the \(k\)-th power, combine these bounds and cancel the positive \(k!\). This yields \(\binom{d+k}{k}\le\binom mk\ell^k t^k\). The inequality \(1-x\le e^{-x}\), with \(x=k/m\), implies \(t^k\le e^{-k^2/m}\). Thus

\[ \binom{d+k}{k}\le\binom mk\ell^k e^{-k^2/m}. \]

For \(d=m\ell-r_*\), the assumptions \(r_*\le m\ell\) and \(\ell\ge1\) imply \(d+k+2\ell k\le m\ell\), exactly the required numerator inequality. Finally \(k^2\ge m\log(4M)\) gives \(e^{-k^2/m}\le e^{-\log(4M)}=1/(4M)\). Multiplying by \(M\) proves the claimed quarter bound. For the ceiling choice, nonnegativity and the defining ceiling inequality give \(k\ge\sqrt{m\log(4M)}\), so squaring proves the premise; positivity of \(\log(4M)\) also gives \(k\ge1\). This replaces the source's exact product-ratio calculation by a sufficient factorial comparison with the same final estimate. If \(r_*>m\ell\), the estimate is not invoked: the final family assembly must handle the absence of proper high-rank blocks separately. \(\square\)

They supply actual ordinary maps and the concrete numerical budget, but R15 still needs a restriction chosen for each proper input span, the finite joint-kernel argument on the row-linear space, and assembly of the original-tuple literal witnesses. 15 September 2026 — Disjoint coordinate pairs and a nonempty residual board

Verified R14 prerequisite · finite-family packing and exact bit differences · R14 separation still open

Statement and full packing proof

Let \(n=2^\ell\), identify its columns with \(\mathbb F_2^\ell\) using the checked decoder's label equivalence, and let \(S\) be a finite family of prescribed bit directions \(a_i\). If \(4(|S|-1)<n\), there are pairwise disjoint coordinate pairs

\[ C_i=\{c_i,c_i+e_{a_i}\},\qquad i\in S, \qquad \left|\bigcup_{i\in S}C_i\right|=2|S|. \]

The implementation permits any indexing type with a finite selected subset, not only a particular pigeon set. The empty family is included. A coordinate flip is an involution because adding its unit vector twice gives zero; it has no fixed point because its selected coordinate changes by one. Thus every pair has exactly two distinct columns.

For a forbidden column set \(F\) and one direction \(a\), the bad starting points lie in

\[ F\cup(F+e_a),\qquad |F\cup(F+e_a)|\le2|F|. \]

If \(2|F|<n\), choose a starting point outside this union. It is outside \(F\), and its flip is outside \(F\) as well, since flipping is an involution. Inductively, after \(j\) selected pairs the forbidden set has exactly \(2j\) points. Its bad starting set has at most \(4j\) points, fewer than \(n\) under the displayed hypothesis. Choose the next pair disjointly and continue. The exact union cardinality follows by summing the sizes of the pairwise disjoint two-point sets. This argument replaces the source's coset count with an equivalent direct count of bad vertices; it needs no quotient construction or division by two.

Bit isolation and the residual parameter ledger

For every bit coordinate \(u\), the pair sum is exactly

\[ \sum_{c\in C_i}c_u =(c_i)_u+((c_i)_u+\mathbf1_{u=a_i}) =\mathbf1_{u=a_i}. \]

This is the precise coordinate-difference identity required by the later cube coefficient isolation, not just disjointness of labels.

For the R14 parameters \(\ell\ge2\), \(1\le k\le B\), \(0\le t\le k\), \(4(k-1)<2^\ell\), and \(2B-1\le2^\ell\), the file also verifies

\[ n-2t\ge1, \qquad n-2t\ge2(B-t)-1. \]

Indeed \(n=4\cdot2^{\ell-2}\), so strict packing implies \(4k\le n\). Hence \(n-2t\ge n/2\ge2\). Subtracting \(2t\) from the original barrier inequality gives the second bound when \(B-t>0\); for \(B=t\), the natural-number version has right side zero and follows from positivity. This explicitly covers \(t=0\), \(t=1\), and \(t=B\). The residual normalized design supplied by R10 therefore has a nonempty column set; its degree-zero case is not justified by an unavailable column.

Verification and scope. DisjointCoordinatePairs.lean and its nine-declaration type/axiom audit check the exact flips, avoidance, finite-family packing, used-label cardinality, bit sums, and residual bounds. Scope and provenance retain the supporting evidence. This is a project formalization of the packing step of R14's recorded cube proof, without a novelty claim. The flip and small parameter facts stay together because they serve this one packing interface.

Remaining work and process assessment. R14 itself is not yet formalized: the actual residual/cube annihilator, its degree accounting, coefficient isolation, and PC exclusions remain. The bad-vertex formulation provided a short general finite-family proof and an exact residual nonemptiness check; existing guidance suffices, so no framework rule is needed. No mathematical discrepancy was found. A source-excerpt failure during a transient integration conflict was resolved after the parent completed its rebase; it was not a source or proof failure.

15 September 2026 — Binary cube differences lower ordinary degree and transport NS witnesses

Verified reusable R14 prerequisite · explicit restriction-sum operator · board-specific application remains

Statement and exact hypotheses

Let \(I\) be a finite set of selected groups, \(r=|I|\), and work over \(\mathbb F_2\). Each input variable \(X_v\) is either untagged or tagged by one \(i\in I\). For a cube choice \(\varepsilon\in\mathbb F_2^I\), define the ordinary polynomial substitution

\[ \sigma_\varepsilon(X_v)= \begin{cases} g_v,&v\text{ untagged},\\ a_v(\varepsilon_i),&v\text{ tagged by }i, \end{cases} \qquad \Delta(P)=\sum_{\varepsilon\in\mathbb F_2^I}\sigma_\varepsilon(P). \]

Each untagged \(g_v\) is one fixed polynomial of total degree at most one. Each \(a_v\) is an arbitrary scalar-valued function on \(\mathbb F_2\); it depends only on its own group's choice. No bound is imposed on the ignored \(g_v\) of a tagged variable. The input and output variable sets need not themselves be finite; every ordinary polynomial has finite support. The verified bounds are

\[ \deg\Delta(P)\le\max\{0,\deg P-r\}, \qquad \deg P<r\Longrightarrow\Delta(P)=0. \]

The second conclusion is proved directly, not inferred from a degree-at-most-zero bound. The empty selected family is included; its cube has one choice and its degree loss is zero.

Complete cancellation and degree proof

Flip one cube coordinate by \(\varepsilon_i\mapsto\varepsilon_i+1\). This map is a fixed-point-free involution. If a summand is unchanged by that flip, its whole cube sum is zero: partition the finite cube into the involution's two-point orbits and add each identical value twice in characteristic two. This argument applies to any \(\mathbb F_2\)-module, including the output polynomial space.

Consider one ordinary monomial \(cX^d\). If its support contains no variable tagged by some \(i\), changing \(\varepsilon_i\) leaves every substituted factor unchanged, so its cube sum is zero. Otherwise every selected group appears. Split its exponent sum into the untagged contribution \(D_{\rm out}\) and the tagged contribution \(D_{\rm in}\). For each selected group at least one supported exponent is positive, and distinct tags count disjoint contributions, so

\[ D_{\rm out}+D_{\rm in}=\sum_vd_v, \qquad D_{\rm in}\ge r. \]

All tagged variables become constants. The image of every untagged factor \(X_v^{d_v}\) has degree at most \(d_v\), so every corner image of the monomial has degree at most \(D_{\rm out}\le\sum_vd_v-r\). Taking their finite sum cannot increase this bound. Expanding \(P\) into its supported monomials, each of degree at most its actual total degree, proves the displayed degree inequality. If \(\deg P<r\), no supported monomial can contain every selected group; each therefore cancels exactly, proving the stronger zero conclusion. In particular a nonempty selected family kills the constant one.

Ordinary NS transport with every generator multiple charged

Let \(\mathcal F\) and \(\mathcal G\) be source and residual polynomial systems. Assume that for every \(f\in\mathcal F\) there is one fixed \(g_f\), either zero or an actual generator of \(\mathcal G\), such that \(\sigma_\varepsilon(f)=g_f\) for every cube choice. Then

\[ \Delta(qf)=\left(\sum_\varepsilon\sigma_\varepsilon(q)\right)g_f =\Delta(q)g_f. \]

For one legal ordinary NS generator multiple \(qf\) of actual degree at most \(B\), its image is zero if \(g_f=0\). Otherwise it is the displayed multiple of the supplied residual generator, and its actual ordinary degree is at most \(\max(0,B-r)\), by applying the proved degree-drop theorem to \(qf\) itself. Thus it is a legal residual NS multiple through that ceiling. Linearity and induction over the original NS span prove

\[ \Delta\bigl(\mathcal I_B(\mathcal F)\bigr) \subseteq\mathcal I_{\max(0,B-r)}(\mathcal G). \]

This accounts for every original generator multiple before summation; it does not allow cancellation between illegal higher-degree source multiples or subtract an inflated generator-degree budget. Consequently any residual functional annihilating the latter NS space gives a source annihilator by composition with \(\Delta\).

Verification and scope. BinaryCubeDegreeDrop.lean defines the actual cube homomorphisms and their linear sum, proves cancellation and ordinary-degree loss, proves fixed-factor extraction, and transports NS certificates and annihilators. The final fourteen-declaration audit checks the version bounding only untagged images; the preliminary all-image-bound audit is retained separately. Scope and source provenance record the evidence. This is a project-formulated finite-difference interface for the cube proof, without a novelty claim.

Remaining work and process assessment. R14 still requires its concrete board substitutions, proof that every unary generator has the stipulated cube-independent residual image, and isolation of the chosen coefficient in the actual R13 row-linear space through the R12 decoder. These hypotheses have not been assumed to declare R14 complete. The explicit operator separates the ordinary-degree argument from the board combinatorics, and removing the bound on ignored tagged-variable images gives its natural general scope. No framework rule or optional post-route sweep was added; no mathematical discrepancy was found.

15 September 2026 — Complete common affine-restriction kernel

Status: R15 fully formalized, including the concrete ceiling parameter and literal coefficient-degree bounds.

Obligation and endpoint. Assemble the previously checked ordinary restriction and numerical estimates into a nonzero row-linear common kernel on the actual bit variables. The endpoint is the full high-rank witness required by simultaneous affine-family removal, with no assumed dimension inequality.

Proper input spans admit ordinary restriction data

Claim lem:proper-affine-block-restriction. Let \((g_i)\) be a finite family of affine maps on \(\mathbb F_2^V\), with \(V\) finite. Its affine-map span and its ordinary polynomial span have the same rank \(r\), and contain the constant one simultaneously. If one is excluded, there are an injection \(e:\{1,\ldots,r\}\hookrightarrow V\) and an affine equivalence \(E\) such that the selected coordinates of \(E(x)\) vanish exactly when all \(g_i(x)\) vanish. In particular \(r\le |V|\). Let \(R\) be ordinary substitution by \(E^{-1}\) followed by deletion of these selected coordinates. For every \(p\) with \(\deg p\le k\) and \(R(p)=0\), there are literal ordinary coefficients

\[p=\sum_i a_i\operatorname{poly}(g_i),\qquad \deg a_i\le k-1.\]

Proof. The checked affine-to-polynomial map is linear and injective and sends constant one to polynomial one. Its restriction to the affine input span is a linear equivalence onto the polynomial input span, proving both rank equality and unit membership equivalence. Choose a basis \(G_1,\ldots,G_r\) of the affine span. It is independent and proper, so finite affine coordinate completion supplies \(e,E\) with selected coordinate functions \(G_j\). Each \(G_j\) is a constant linear combination of the original inputs, and every original input is a constant linear combination of the basis. These two identities prove equality of the common zero flats. The injection gives the rank bound. The checked ordinary affine-restriction ideal theorem gives \(p=\sum_j b_j\operatorname{poly}(G_j)\), with \(\deg b_j\le k-1\). Write \(G_j=\sum_i c_{ji}g_i\) and collect \(a_i=\sum_j c_{ji}b_j\). Linearity gives the literal identity, and constant scalar multiplication and finite addition preserve the degree ceiling. This also covers dependent inputs, empty bases and the zero polynomial. \(\square\)

Concrete common kernel and original-tuple witnesses

Claim lem:common-affine-restriction-kernel. Let \(m,\ell,M\ge1\), \(1\le k\le m\), and \(k^2\ge m\log(4M)\). On the ordinary bit polynomial ring \(\mathbb F_2[x_{ij}]\), consider an arbitrary finite family of finite affine input tuples \(g_b\), of polynomial-span ranks \(r_b\). Suppose at most \(M\) blocks are both proper (their span excludes one) and high, meaning \(r_b>3\ell(k+1)\). Then there exists a nonzero \(f\in\mathcal L_k\), the row-linear polynomial space of degree at most \(k\), such that every high block either has one in its input span or satisfies

\[f=\sum_i a_{bi}\operatorname{poly}(g_{bi}),\qquad \deg a_{bi}\le k-1.\]

The original parameter \(k=\lceil\sqrt{m\log(4M)}\rceil\), provided \(k\le m\), satisfies all the required numerical conditions. A bound of \(M\) on all positive-rank proper blocks implies the stated high-block bound by inclusion; a bound on the entire block inventory also suffices. Both the square-condition interface and the original ceiling specialization are checked. Thus a larger uniform inventory bound may be used without padding the family.

Proof. Write \(U=\mathcal L_k\), \(q=\binom mk\ell^k>0\), and \(v=m\ell\). The checked row-linear dimension formula gives \(\dim U=\sum_{j=0}^k\binom mj\ell^j\ge q\). For each proper high block choose the restriction data from the preceding claim and restrict its ordinary linear map to \(U\), obtaining \(L_b\). Its image dimension is at most \(\binom{v-r_b+k}{k}\), by the checked ordinary affine restriction dimension bound.

If there is a proper high block, its rank is at most \(v\). Consequently \(r_*=3\ell(k+1)+1\le v\). Every high integer rank is at least \(r_*\), and monotonicity of the binomial coefficient, the block count, and the concrete quarter estimate give

\[\sum_b\dim\operatorname{im}L_b\le M\binom{v-r_*+k}{k}\le\tfrac14q<\dim U.\]

If there are no proper high blocks, the same strict dimension comparison holds because the left side is zero and \(\dim U\ge q>0\); the numerical estimate is not invoked outside its rank hypothesis. Form the joint linear map \(T:U\to\prod_b\operatorname{im}L_b\). The target dimension is the displayed sum. An injective map would force the source dimension to be at most this smaller dimension, a contradiction. Choose distinct elements with equal image and subtract them. Their difference gives a nonzero \(f\in U\) in every kernel.

For each proper high block, its ordinary restriction of \(f\) is therefore zero. Since \(f\in\mathcal L_k\) implies \(\deg f\le k\), the preceding claim supplies coefficients in the original input tuple with degree at most \(k-1\). A unit-span block satisfies the other alternative directly. This is exactly the unit-or-literal interface of the checked family-removal theorem; it does not incorrectly demand degree-\((k-1)\) coefficients from unit membership alone. Finally, the checked ceiling bounds give positivity and the square condition for the original choice of \(k\). \(\square\)
