18 September 2026 — Importing the matching switching lemma: a switched wide reader of narrow literal terms gets a complete old-only image of polylogarithmic degree

Status: imported statement read from an open technical report (nonbipartite hypergraph-matching form); working image lemma with proof; parameter corollary; the bipartite PHP-board form is cited from paywalled sources and not verified locally. Spin cycle 175. Produced by Claude Code (Claude Fable 5.1 (claude-fable-5-1), low reasoning effort).

Question and stopping point. The frontier is a wide disjunction whose inputs are narrow terms. For literal terms this is the classical situation of bounded-depth Frege lower bounds, handled by a switching lemma over matching restrictions. This cycle retrieves an open source for that lemma, records its exact statement, and proves what it supplies to the present route: a complete old-only image of the reader block with all three certificate families at polylogarithmic degree. It stops at that lemma and its parameter corollary; the bipartite form and the parity case are recorded as open.

1. Imported statement

Source. P. Beame, A Switching Lemma Primer, technical report, 1994, Section 5, Lemma 4 (printed pages 13–17); reading locator and hash in the source audit. The journal versions of the bipartite PHP lemma, Pitassi–Beame–Impagliazzo, Computational Complexity 3 (1993) 97–140, and Krajíček–Pudlák–Woods, Random Structures and Algorithms 7 (1995) 15–39, were not obtainable; the Git-ignored request note lists the attempted links.

Setting (Beame, Section 5). Let \(D\) be a set of \(qn+1\) points. The \(q\)-variables are \(x_e\) for \(q\)-subsets \(e\subseteq D\). A \(q\)-term is a conjunction of variables with pairwise disjoint endpoint sets, so \(q\)-terms correspond to partial \(q\)-matchings; an \(r\)-disjunction is an OR of terms of size at most \(r\). \(\mathcal M^\ell_{D,q}\) is the set of partial \(q\)-matchings leaving \(q\ell+1\) points unmatched; each defines a restriction setting its edges to one, edges meeting them to zero, and the rest free. A \(q\)-matching decision tree queries a point and branches over the edges containing it that avoid the path's endpoints, so each path is a partial matching \(\pi\); it represents \(f\) if for every leaf \(v\) with path \(\pi\) and every assignment that is a matching on \(v(\pi)\) and satisfies \(\pi\), \(f\) equals the leaf label, and it refines a DNF \(F\) if every path to a 1-leaf forces some term of \(F\) to one. The canonical tree \(T_D(F)\) refines and represents \(F\).

Lemma 4 (Beame). Let \(|D|=qn+1\) and let \(F\) be an \(r\)-disjunction over \(D\). If \(s\ge0\) and \(6\le\ell=pn\le(n/r)^{1/q^2}/e\), then

\[ \frac{\bigl|\{\rho\in\mathcal M^\ell_{D,q}:\ |T_D(F\!\restriction_\rho)|\ge s\}\bigr|}{|\mathcal M^\ell_{D,q}|} <\bigl(4e^q\,r^{1/q}\,p^q\,n^{\,q-1/q}\bigr)^s . \tag{SW-Beame} \]

For \(q=2\) the base is \(4e^2\sqrt r\,\ell^2/\sqrt n\). The proof is a bijective encoding of bad restrictions, read in full. This is the nonbipartite form; the bipartite PHP board uses matching decision trees that query a pigeon or a hole, with the same shape of statement, which is what the two cited papers prove.

2. Working lemma: the image of a switched reader

Let \(\mathcal N\) be the old system of Boolean equations \(x_e^2-x_e\), exclusions \(x_ex_{e'}\) for \(e\ne e'\) with \(e\cap e'\ne\varnothing\), and point axioms \(\sum_{e\ni i}x_e-1\); on the bipartite board these are the functional PHP axioms. Let \(F=\bigvee_a{\rm term}(\tau_a)\) be a disjunction of terms of size at most \(r\), and let \(T\) be a matching decision tree of height at most \(s\) that represents and refines \(F\). Consider an ENS block whose inputs are the terms \({\rm term}(\tau_a)\), so its product is \(P=1-\sum_{u,a}r_{u,a}{\rm term}(\tau_a)\) with companions \({\rm term}(\tau_a)P\).

Lemma. Put \(\hat P=\sum_{\text{0-leaves }\pi}{\rm term}(\pi)\) and, choosing for each 1-leaf \(\pi\) one term \(\tau_{a(\pi)}\subseteq\pi\), \(\rho_a=\sum_{\text{1-leaves }\pi:\,a(\pi)=a}{\rm term}(\pi\setminus\tau_a)\). Assign the first coefficient row the images \(\rho_a\) and all other rows zero. Then \(\deg\hat P,\deg\rho_a\le s\), and

  • \({\rm term}(\tau_a)\hat P\) is a sum of exclusion multiples of degree at most \(r+s\);
  • \(1-\hat P-\sum_a\rho_a{\rm term}(\tau_a)\) is a combination of point-axiom and exclusion multiples of degree at most \(s\);
  • \(\rho_a^2-\rho_a\) is a combination of Boolean and exclusion multiples of degree at most \(2s\).

Proof. (i) If a 0-leaf path \(\pi\) were compatible with \(\tau_a\), the indicator of \(\pi\cup\tau_a\) would be a matching on \(v(\pi)\) satisfying \(\pi\) with \(F=1\), contradicting representation; so \({\rm term}(\tau_a){\rm term}(\pi)\) contains two edges sharing a point. (ii) At a node with path \(\pi\) querying \(i\), \({\rm term}(\pi)\sum_{e\ni i,\ e\cap v(\pi)=\varnothing}x_e={\rm term}(\pi)\bigl(\sum_{e\ni i}x_e-1\bigr)+{\rm term}(\pi)-\sum_{e\ni i,\ e\cap v(\pi)\ne\varnothing}{\rm term}(\pi)x_e\), and the last sum consists of exclusion multiples; induction down the tree gives \(\sum_{\text{leaves}}{\rm term}(\pi)\equiv1\) through degree \(s\). Refinement gives \(\sum_{\text{1-leaves}}{\rm term}(\pi)=\sum_a{\rm term}(\tau_a)\rho_a\). (iii) Two distinct leaves assigned to \(a\) diverge at a node with different edges \(e\ne e'\) at one point; neither lies in \(\tau_a\), since \(\tau_a\) is contained in both paths and is a matching, so the cross term contains \(x_ex_{e'}\); squares of monomials reduce by Boolean multiples. \(\square\)

The lemma uses only representation, refinement, point axioms, and exclusions; it holds verbatim for bipartite matching decision trees on the PHP board. At accuracy \(h\) the surplus rows are set to zero. Thus a switched reader has a complete old-only image whose degree is the tree height, independent of the number of terms it reads: this is the image asked for in the frontier statement, for literal terms.

3. Parameter corollary and scope

In the setting of (SW-Beame) with \(q=2\), let \(M\) readers be disjunctions of terms of size at most \(r\), and put \(\ell=\lfloor n^{1/4}/(2\sqrt2\,e\,r^{1/4})\rfloor\) and \(s=\lceil\log_2(2M)\rceil\). Then \(4e^2\sqrt r\,\ell^2/\sqrt n\le\tfrac12\), so by (SW-Beame) and a union bound some restriction in \(\mathcal M^\ell_{D,2}\) gives every reader a canonical tree of height below \(s\), provided \(6\le\ell\le(n/r)^{1/4}/e\), which holds for \(r\le n^{1/2}\) and large \(n\). On the residual \(2\ell+1\) points every reader then has the image of Section 2 with all certificates through \(r+2\log_2(2M)\). For polynomial \(M\) and polylogarithmic \(r\) this is polylogarithmic, while the residual keeps \(\Theta(n^{1/4}r^{-1/4})\) points. Iterating over a fixed number of levels leaves a polynomial residual.

Scope. This is verified in the nonbipartite form only; the bipartite board needs the cited lemma, whose constants were not checked. The tool covers readers all of whose inputs are terms of literals. It says nothing about a reader with one parity input, and a narrow term containing a parity of many cells survives every polynomial residual, as recorded in the previous decision. Composition with the weight step on the residual board, and the restriction's effect on the rest of the registry, are not carried out here.

Main-route assessment. The first obligation is unchanged, but its literal half now has a named tool inside the route's own language: after a matching restriction, wide readers of narrow literal terms cost the tree height, not the fan-in. The open core is exactly the parity half. The next step is to obtain or reprove the bipartite lemma, then to run the two-level source through restriction plus weight on the residual board and record the ledger.

Process assessment. The open primer was found and read within the cycle; the paywalled originals are recorded in the request note rather than guessed at, and the derived lemma is separated from the imported statement so that its verification status is clear.

18 September 2026 — A bipartite matching switching lemma on the PHP board, with an explicitly verified encoding

Status: working lemma with complete proof adapted from the imported nonbipartite argument; the encoding's injectivity was exercised by an exact round-trip test on small boards, which found and fixed two defects; constants are generous. Spin cycle 176. Produced by Claude Code (Claude Fable 5.1 (claude-fable-5-1), low reasoning effort).

Question and stopping point. The switched-reader image lemma needs a switching lemma on the bipartite \((n+1)\times n\) board, whose published versions were not obtainable. This cycle adapts the counting proof read from Beame's primer to the bipartite board with a simplified encoding, proves it, and tests the encoding exhaustively on small boards. It stops at the lemma and its parameter corollary.

1. Setting

Pigeons \([n+1]\), holes \([n]\), variables \(x_{ij}\). For \(0\le\ell\le n-1\), \(\mathcal M^\ell\) is the set of partial matchings \(\mu\) of size \(n-\ell\); each defines the restriction setting its edges to one, edges meeting a matched vertex to zero, and the remaining edges on the residual \((\ell+1)\times\ell\) board free. A term is a partial matching \(\tau\), \({\rm term}(\tau)=\prod_{(i,j)\in\tau}x_{ij}\); an \(r\)-disjunction \(F\) is an ordered list of terms of size at most \(r\). Under \(\mu\) a term is falsified if one of its edges is set to zero, and otherwise shortened to its free edges, kept in order. A matching decision tree on the residual board queries an uncovered residual vertex and branches over the uncovered residual vertices of the other side, so each path is a partial matching \(\pi\); representation and refinement are as in the imported setting. The complete tree for a vertex list \(K\) queries the first uncovered vertex of \(K\) in list order at each node. The canonical tree \(T(F\!\restriction_\mu)\): if \(F\!\restriction_\mu\) is constant, one leaf; otherwise, with \(C\) the first surviving term and \(\tau\) its free edges, take \(K=v(\tau)\) listed as pigeon then hole of each edge in term order, build the complete tree for \(K\), and at each leaf with path \(\sigma'\) attach \(T(F\!\restriction_{\mu\sigma'})\). It refines and represents \(F\!\restriction_\mu\) by the imported argument, unchanged.

2. The lemma

Lemma. Let \(F\) be an \(r\)-disjunction, \(1\le s\le\ell\le n-1\), and \(A=\dfrac{4r\,\ell(\ell+1)}{(n-\ell+1)\ln2}\). Then

\[ \frac{\bigl|\{\mu\in\mathcal M^\ell:\ {\rm height}\,T(F\!\restriction_\mu)\ge s\}\bigr|}{|\mathcal M^\ell|} \ \le\ (\ell+1)^s\!\!\sum_{j=\lceil s/2\rceil}^{\min(2s,\ell)}\!\!A^j \ \le\ 2\bigl((\ell+1)\sqrt A\bigr)^s\quad\text{if }A\le\tfrac12 . \tag{BSW} \]

Since \((\ell+1)\sqrt A\le2.41\,(\ell+1)^2\sqrt{r/(n-\ell+1)}\), the bound is nontrivial for \(\ell+1\) below about \(n^{1/4}r^{-1/4}/2.2\), matching the shape of the imported nonbipartite bound with \(r^{1/2}\) in place of Beame's tighter constants.

Proof: rounds. Let \(S\) be the bad set. For \(\mu\in S\) let \(\pi\) be the lexicographically first path of length at least \(s\) in \(T(F\!\restriction_\mu)\), trimmed to its first \(s\) edges. Define rounds: \(\mu_0=\mu\); in round \(i\), \(\nu_i\) is the index of the first term not falsified by \(\mu_{i-1}\), \(\tau_i\) its free edges, \(K_i=v(\tau_i)\), \(\pi_i\) the maximal prefix of the remaining path whose edges touch \(K_i\), and \(\mu_i=\mu_{i-1}\cup\pi_i\); stop at round \(k\) when \(\pi\) is exhausted. Since the path enters the complete tree for \(K_i\) and every edge in that tree touches \(K_i\), while after that tree all of \(K_i\) is covered, \(\pi_i\) is exactly the part of \(\pi\) inside that tree. Let \(\sigma_i\) be the edges of \(\tau_i\) with an endpoint in \(v(\pi_i)\). Facts: (F1) each edge of \(\pi_i\) touches \(K_i\) at a vertex of \(v(\pi_i)\cap K_i\subseteq v(\sigma_i)\), and distinct edges at distinct vertices, so \(|\pi_i|\le2|\sigma_i|\); (F2) \(|\sigma_i|\le|v(\pi_i)\cap K_i|\le2|\pi_i|\); (F3) for \(i<k\) the path traverses the whole complete tree, so \(\pi_i\) covers \(K_i\) and \(\sigma_i=\tau_i\); (F4) \(\tau_i\) is free under \(\mu_{i-1}\), so it avoids \(v(\pi_1\cup\dots\cup\pi_{i-1})\supseteq v(\sigma_1\cup\dots\cup\sigma_{i-1})\) by (F3); hence \(\sigma=\sigma_1\cup\dots\cup\sigma_k\) is a partial matching compatible with \(\mu\), \(\mu\sigma\in\mathcal M^{\ell-j}\) with \(j=|\sigma|\), and \(\lceil s/2\rceil\le j\le\min(2s,\ell)\) by (F1), (F2), \(\sum_i|\pi_i|=s\); (F5) a vertex of \(\pi_i\) is residual for \(\mu\) and, if it lies in some \(v(\sigma_{i'})\), then \(i'\le i\), since \(\tau_{i'}\) for \(i'>i\) avoids \(v(\pi_i)\). Write \(W_i\) for the vertices unset by \(\mu\sigma\) together with \(v(\sigma_1\cup\dots\cup\sigma_i)\); by (F5) every vertex of \(\pi_i\) lies in \(W_i\).

Proof: query order. Within round \(i\), list \(v(\sigma_i)\) as pigeon then hole of each edge of \(\sigma_i\) in term order; this is the order of \(K_i\) restricted to \(v(\sigma_i)\). The tree queries at each node the first uncovered vertex of \(K_i\), and the path's edge there contains it, so every queried vertex is touched by \(\pi_i\); an uncovered untouched vertex preceding a query would itself be queried, a contradiction. Hence the vertex queried at each step of \(\pi_i\) is the first vertex of \(v(\sigma_i)\), in this order, that is touched and not yet covered, and each edge of \(\pi_i\) contains that vertex; its other endpoint, the partner, lies in \(W_i\) on the opposite side by (F5).

Proof: code. Map \(\mu\mapsto(\mu\sigma,\beta,m,\delta)\): \(\beta=(\beta_1,\dots,\beta_k)\) with \(\beta_i\in\{*,-\}^r\) marking the positions of the edges of \(\sigma_i\) in the term \(C_{\nu_i}\), at least one star each, \(j\) stars in total; \(m=(m_1,\dots,m_k)\) with \(m_i\in\{0,1\}^{v(\sigma_i)}\) marking the touched vertices, in the order above; \(\delta\in[\ell+1]^s\) giving, for the edges of \(\pi\) in path order, the index of the partner among the sorted vertices of \(W_i\) on its side. By Beame's Lemma 2, \(\beta\) has fewer than \((r/\ln2)^j\) values; \(m\) has \(4^j\); \(\delta\) has at most \((\ell+1)^s\).

Proof: decoding. Put \(R_1=\mu\sigma\). In round \(i\), \(R_i=\mu\pi_1\cdots\pi_{i-1}\sigma_i\cdots\sigma_k\), and \(\nu_i\) is the first term not falsified by \(R_i\): earlier terms are falsified by \(\mu_{i-1}\subseteq R_i\), while \(C_{\nu_i}\) is not, because its free edges under \(\mu_{i-1}\) are set to one by \(\sigma_i\) or, in the last round, avoid \(v(\pi_k)\) and \(v(\sigma_k)\) and stay free. Then \(\beta_i\) gives \(\sigma_i\), \(m_i\) the touched set, and \(W_i\) is known from \(\mu\sigma\) and \(\sigma_1,\dots,\sigma_i\). Read edges: the first endpoint is the first touched uncovered vertex of \(v(\sigma_i)\), the partner comes from \(\delta\); each edge covers a previously uncovered touched vertex, and the round ends exactly when none remains or \(s\) edges have been read. Replace \(\sigma_i\) by \(\pi_i\) to obtain \(R_{i+1}\). At the end \(\mu=R_{k+1}\setminus\pi\). The map is therefore injective.

Proof: counting. \(|\mathcal M^{\ell-j}|/|\mathcal M^\ell|=(\ell+1)_j(\ell)_j/(n-\ell+j)_j\le\bigl(\ell(\ell+1)/(n-\ell+1)\bigr)^j\). Hence \(|S|/|\mathcal M^\ell|\le(\ell+1)^s\sum_j\bigl(\tfrac{4r}{\ln2}\cdot\tfrac{\ell(\ell+1)}{n-\ell+1}\bigr)^j\), which is (BSW); for \(A\le\tfrac12\) the tail sum is at most \(2A^{\lceil s/2\rceil}\le2A^{s/2}\). \(\square\)

3. Parameter corollary and round-trip evidence

Corollary. Let \(M\) readers be \(r\)-disjunctions on the board, \(\ell+1=\lfloor(n/2)^{1/4}/(2.2\,r^{1/4})\rfloor\ge s=\lceil\log_2(4M)\rceil\), and \(n\) large. Then \(A\le\tfrac12\) and \((\ell+1)\sqrt A\le\tfrac12\), so each reader has canonical tree height at least \(s\) with probability at most \(2^{1-s}\le1/(2M)\), and some \(\mu\in\mathcal M^\ell\) gives every reader height below \(s\). On the residual \((\ell+1)\times\ell\) board, with \(\ell=\Theta(n^{1/4}r^{-1/4})\), the image lemma then gives every reader a complete old-only image with certificates through \(r+2\log_2(4M)\), while the residual functional PHP keeps NS degree at least \(\ell/2+1\) by the imported bound used in the literal-family theorem.

Round-trip evidence. The checker builds canonical trees on small boards, and for every restriction with height at least \(s\) encodes the trimmed lexicographically first long path and decodes the code back. Seven runs (boards \(6\times5\) to \(8\times7\), \(\ell=2,3\), \(r=2,3\), \(s=2,3\), up to 58,800 restrictions and 21,450 bad ones) show zero decoding failures and the size range \(\lceil s/2\rceil\le j\le2s\) throughout; the output lists the disjunctions, height histograms, and bad fractions. The bound (BSW) is vacuous at these sizes, so the test checks the encoding, not the inequality. A first version of the encoding listed \(v(\sigma_i)\) in a different order from the tree's query order and indexed partners within the full residual of \(\mu\), which the decoder cannot know before the last round; the test exposed both, and the proof above uses the corrected rules.

Scope. The lemma concerns the canonical tree of one disjunction under a uniform restriction from \(\mathcal M^\ell\); readers whose inputs are not literal terms are outside it. It does not yet compose with the weight step: the effect of the restriction on the rest of a two-level registry, and the ledger on the residual board, are the next step.

Main-route assessment. The literal half of the frontier now has a locally verified tool on the actual board: after one matching restriction leaving \(\Theta(n^{1/4}r^{-1/4})\) residual holes, every wide reader of width-\(r\) literal terms has an old-only image at logarithmic degree. The first obligation is unchanged, and parity terms remain the open core.

Process assessment. Testing the encoding before writing the proof was decisive: both defects would have entered the record otherwise; an exact round trip is the right control for injectivity arguments and costs minutes.

18 September 2026 — Composing switching with the weight step: two alignment lemmas and an obstruction in the restriction family

Status: two working lemmas (decoder image of bit-literal readers; image lemma for sum inputs) and one precise obstruction; the planned ledger is not completed, for a stated reason. Spin cycle 177. Produced by Claude Code (Claude Fable 5.1 (claude-fable-5-1), low reasoning effort).

Question and stopping point. The plan was to run a two-level source through one matching restriction from the bipartite switching lemma and then the weight step on the residual board. Two encoding facts decide whether this composes: the source's readers have bit-literal terms while the switching lemma is stated for unary cell terms, and the weight step runs on compact boards. The stopping point is the first requirement the restriction breaks, with the pieces that survive proved.

1. Bit-literal readers decode to unary readers

Lemma. Let \(C\) be a conjunction of \(r\) bit literals \(b_{it}=c\) on \(\rho\le r\) rows, and let \(\tau\) be the affine decoder \(\tau(b_{it})=\sum_{z:z_t=1}X_{iz}\). Then, modulo \(\mathcal I_r(\mathcal F_n^{\rm fun})\),

\[ \tau(C)\ \equiv\ \sum_{\tau'\in T(C)}{\rm term}(\tau'), \tag{BT-decode} \]

where \(T(C)\) is the set of partial matchings \(\tau'\) that assign to each of the \(\rho\) rows a hole consistent with the row's literal pattern, at most \(n^\rho\) of them, pairwise incompatible. Proof. A negated literal decodes to \(\sum_{z_t=0}X_{iz}\) modulo the row axiom. On one row the product of its literal sums expands into diagonal terms \(X_{iz}^k\equiv X_{iz}\) for consistent \(z\) and cross terms \(X_{iz}X_{iz'}\), which are functional row exclusions; the reduction uses multiples of degree at most the number of literals on that row. The product over rows then expands into one unary term per choice of consistent holes, and choices with a repeated hole contain a column exclusion. All multiples have degree at most \(r\). \(\square\)

Hence a reader whose inputs are bit terms of width at most \(r\) is, modulo the functional base at degree \(r\), a reader whose inputs are sums of pairwise incompatible unary terms of size at most \(r\), and the union of all these terms is an \(r\)-disjunction in the sense of the switching lemma. The number of readers, not the number of decoded terms, enters the union bound.

2. The image lemma for sum inputs

Lemma. Let the reader's inputs be \(g_a=\sum_{\tau'\in T_a}{\rm term}(\tau')\) with each \(T_a\) a set of pairwise incompatible terms of size at most \(r\), let \(F=\bigvee_a\bigvee_{\tau'\in T_a}{\rm term}(\tau')\), and let \(T\) be a matching decision tree of height at most \(s\) representing and refining \(F\). Put \(\hat P=\sum_{\text{0-leaves}}{\rm term}(\pi)\) and, assigning each 1-leaf \(\pi\) an index \(a(\pi)\) with some \(\tau'\in T_{a(\pi)}\), \(\tau'\subseteq\pi\), put \(\rho'_a=\sum_{\pi:\,a(\pi)=a}{\rm term}(\pi)\). Then \(g_a\hat P\) is a sum of exclusion multiples of degree at most \(r+s\); \(1-\hat P-\sum_a\rho'_ag_a\) is a combination of point-axiom, exclusion, and Boolean multiples of degree at most \(r+s\); and \(\rho_a'^2-\rho'_a\) is a combination of Boolean and exclusion multiples of degree at most \(2s\).

Proof. Companions and Booleanity are as in the single-term lemma, since every term of every \(T_a\) is a term of \(F\) and distinct leaves conflict. For the identity, \(\rho'_ag_a=\sum_\pi{\rm term}(\pi)\sum_{\tau''\in T_a}{\rm term}(\tau'')\); the summand with \(\tau''=\tau'(\pi)\subseteq\pi\) reduces to \({\rm term}(\pi)\) by Boolean multiples, and every other \(\tau''\) conflicts with \(\tau'(\pi)\) on some row, so \({\rm term}(\pi){\rm term}(\tau'')\) contains an exclusion pair. Summing over \(a\) gives \(\sum_{\text{1-leaves}}{\rm term}(\pi)\), and the leaf partition identity supplies the rest. \(\square\)

Using full leaf terms as coefficient images, rather than the remainders \(\pi\setminus\tau'\), is what makes the cross terms vanish; it costs nothing in degree.

3. The obstruction: two restriction families

The weight step needs a compact board. The recorded compact subcube restriction fixes the pigeons outside a residual set bijectively to the labels outside a residual subcube \([N]\), \(N\) a power of two, and zeroes the residual pigeons' high bits; the residual is \(\mathcal Q_N\) in affine coordinates, which is what the kernel count and the coordinate-edge detector require. The switching lemma is proved for uniform partial matchings of size \(n-\ell\), whose residual hole set is an arbitrary \(\ell\)-set; its proof extends a bad restriction by \(j\) edges and gains the factor \(\bigl(\ell(\ell+1)/(n-\ell+1)\bigr)^j\) because the extended matchings, with fewer free holes anywhere, are that much rarer. In the subcube family the residual holes carry no such entropy: extensions leave the family, and the same count gives a ratio \(\binom{N}{j}(N+1)_j\ge1\), which proves nothing. Conversely, after a uniform restriction the residual holes are not a subcube; relabelling them to one is not affine, so bit-affine inputs become polynomials of degree up to \(\log N\) in the residual coordinates, the coordinate-edge trades leave the residual set, and the affine machinery has no flats to count.

Two ways around were checked and fail as stated. Running the weight step in unary cell variables after a uniform restriction: the ambient dimension is \(mn\), so a block is high only for rank at least \(mn\ln(16M)/k\), which exceeds the bit-affine dimension \(m\log n\) for every affordable \(k\). Using the decoded bit forms on the residual rows as coordinates: the kernel count then works, with threshold about \(2D\log n\log M\) on a residual of \(\Theta(n^{1/4})\) rows, but the detector needs to flip one bit of a residual label and stay in the residual set, which again requires a subcube.

The remaining opening is a switching lemma for the subcube family itself: uniform choice of \(N+1\) residual pigeons and of the bijection of the others onto the fixed outside labels, with only the pigeon side random. The notebook's positive-literal switching count is the width-one case of exactly this statement, proved by a swap encoding rather than an extension; and the literal-inventory theorem already removes bottom signed-bit families in this family. A width-\(r\) swap encoding, tested with the round-trip tool, is the natural next step.

Main-route assessment. The first obligation is unchanged. The literal frontier is now reduced to one combinatorial statement in the route's own restriction family, with the algebraic side (decoding, images, certificates) proved. Parity terms remain the open core.

Process assessment. Checking the encoding alignment before attempting the ledger found the family mismatch in one reading batch and saved a cycle of ledger writing that could not have closed; no framework change is needed.

18 September 2026 — A switching lemma for the subcube restriction family with light rows, and a refutation for rows pinned into a fixed subcube

Status: working lemma with a round-trip-tested encoding; one refutation (finite adversary argument, all sizes); one sharpened obstruction; the random-flat variant is a proposal, not a result. Spin cycle 178. Produced by Claude Code (Claude Fable 5.1 (claude-fable-5-1), low reasoning effort).

Question and stopping point. The previous cycle left one combinatorial statement on the literal frontier: a switching lemma for the compact subcube family, in which the residual holes are a fixed subcube \(Q\) and only the pigeon side is random. The allowed endpoints were a proved lemma or an explicit family of disjunctions whose bad probability stays large. Both occur, and the number of literals on a single row decides which: rows with at most about \(\tfrac13\log_2 n\) literals are switched by an extension encoding whose code lives in the same family with fewer free labels; a row pinned to a label of the fixed subcube cannot be encoded in any subcube family, and for the fixed subcube a wide reader of such rows is bad for essentially every restriction.

1. The family with slack, the residual instance, and the canonical tree

Labels are \(\{0,1\}^\ell\), \(n=2^\ell\); \(Q\) is a fixed subcube of size \(N=2^{\ell_2}\) (a set of \(\ell-\ell_2\) coordinates held at fixed values), \(O=\{0,1\}^\ell\setminus Q\), and rows are \([n+1]\). For \(e\ge0\) let \(\Phi_e\) be the set of pairs \(\rho=(R,\mu)\) with \(R\subseteq[n+1]\), \(|R|=N+1+e\), and \(\mu\) an injection of the other rows into \(O\); write \(E(\rho)=O\setminus\mu([n+1]\setminus R)\) for the \(e\) free outside labels. Then

\[ |\Phi_e|=\binom{n+1}{N+1+e}\frac{(n-N)!}{e!},\qquad \frac{|\Phi_{e-1}|}{|\Phi_e|}=\frac{e\,(N+e+1)}{n-N-e+1}. \]

\(\Phi_0\) is the compact subcube family of the weight step. A uniform element of \(\Phi_0\) is obtained from a uniform \(\rho\in\Phi_e\) followed by a uniform filling \(\rho''\), an injection of \(e\) rows of \(R\) onto \(E(\rho)\): every \(\rho'\in\Phi_0\) arises from exactly \(\binom{n-N}{e}\) pairs \((\rho,\rho'')\), the choices of which \(e\) matched rows were filled last, and \(|\Phi_e|\,(N+1+e)!/(N+1)!=|\Phi_0|\binom{n-N}{e}\).

The residual instance of \(\rho\) has pigeons \(R\) and holes \(Q\cup E(\rho)\). A bit term is a conjunction of literals \(b_{it}=c\); its rows are ordered, its pattern \(p_i\) on row \(i\) is the set of literals there, and \(C(p)\) is the set of the \(n2^{-|p|}\) labels consistent with \(p\). Under a partial assignment of rows to labels a term is falsified if an assigned row violates its pattern, satisfied if every row is assigned consistently, and otherwise alive with its uncovered rows. A disjunction \(F=(T_1,\dots,T_M)\) is ordered; it has at most \(r\) rows per term and at most \(w\) literals per row.

The canonical tree \(\mathcal T(F,\rho)\) has as nodes the partial matchings \(\pi\) of the residual instance (rows of \(R\) to distinct holes of \(Q\cup E(\rho)\)). At \(\pi\) take the first term not falsified by \(\rho\cup\pi\): if there is none the node is a 0-leaf; if it is satisfied, a 1-leaf; otherwise its uncovered rows are queried in the term's order, each branching over the holes unused by the path, and a row with no unused hole is a dead leaf. A dead leaf has depth \(N+e\), and its leaf term vanishes modulo the row axiom and the column exclusions at degree two, so it does not disturb the leaf-partition identity of the image lemma. The height is the largest depth of a node, and \(\mathrm{Bad}_s\) is the event that the height is at least \(s\). Say \(\rho\) is \(s\)-rich if \(|E(\rho)\cap C(p)|\ge s\) for every pattern \(p\) occurring on a row of some term of \(F\).

2. The lemma

Lemma (encoding). For \(1\le s\le e\),

\[ \bigl|\mathrm{Bad}_s\cap\{s\text{-rich}\}\bigr|\ \le\ |\Phi_{e-s}|\,(2r)^s\,(N+e)^s, \qquad\text{so}\qquad \Pr_{\rho\in\Phi_e}[\mathrm{Bad}_s\cap\{s\text{-rich}\}]\le A^s,\quad A=\frac{2r\,(N+e)\,e\,(N+e+1)}{n-N-e+1}. \]

Proof. Fix a rich \(\rho\in\mathrm{Bad}_s\) and the lexicographically first path \(\pi\) of length \(s\) in \(\mathcal T(F,\rho)\). The path splits into rounds: round \(i\) begins at the first term \(T_{t_i}\) not falsified by \(\rho\cup\pi_{<i}\), and its edges assign the uncovered rows \(\sigma_i\) of \(T_{t_i}\) in the term's order, all of them except in the last round, which the truncation to \(s\) edges may cut. Every row of \(T_{t_i}\) is covered after round \(i\), so no later round moves a row of \(T_{t_i}\).

The encoder processes the rounds in order. For each row \(j\in\sigma_i\) it picks the smallest label of \(E(\rho)\cap C(p_j(T_{t_i}))\) not yet picked; richness guarantees one, since at most \(s-1\) labels were picked before. The code is the triple \((\rho^\ast,\beta,\delta)\): \(\rho^\ast\in\Phi_{e-s}\) is \(\rho\) with every moved row \(j\) taken out of \(R\) and matched to its picked label; \(\beta\) lists, for the \(s\) moved rows in path order, the row's position among the at most \(r\) rows of its term and one bit marking the last row of a round, at most \((2r)^s\) values; and \(\delta\in(Q\cup E(\rho))^s\) lists the path's holes.

The decoder starts from the assignment \(\alpha=\rho^\ast\) and, for each round read off \(\beta\), finds the first term not falsified by \(\alpha\), identifies \(\sigma_i\) inside that term by the positions in \(\beta\), and reassigns those rows to their holes from \(\delta\). At round \(i\) the assignment \(\alpha\) extends \(\rho\cup\pi_{<i}\) as a function, since it agrees with \(\mu\) on matched rows and with the path on earlier moved rows, and additionally matches later moved rows; so every term before \(T_{t_i}\), falsified by \(\rho\cup\pi_{<i}\), stays falsified. \(T_{t_i}\) itself is not falsified by \(\alpha\): its rows covered by \(\rho\cup\pi_{<i}\) are assigned as before, its rows in \(\sigma_i\) carry consistent labels, and its remaining rows, present only in a cut last round, are unassigned. Hence the decoder recovers \(T_{t_i}\), then \(\sigma_i\) and its holes, and after the last round it deletes the moved rows from \(\alpha\) and recovers \(\mu\) and \(R\). Collisions between a hole in \(\delta\) and a picked label do not matter, because the decoder uses \(\alpha\) only to evaluate patterns row by row. The map \(\rho\mapsto(\rho^\ast,\beta,\delta)\) is therefore injective on rich bad restrictions, and the count follows from the ratio \(|\Phi_{e-s}|/|\Phi_e|=\prod_{j<s}(e-j)(N+e+1-j)/(n-N-e+1+j)\le\bigl(e(N+e+1)/(n-N-e+1)\bigr)^s\). \(\square\)

Lemma (richness). If \(w\le\ell-\ell_2-1\) and \(e\ge2^{w+2}s\), then \(\Pr_{\rho\in\Phi_e}[\rho\text{ not }s\text{-rich}]\le Mr\,e^{-e2^{-w-4}}\).

Proof. A pattern \(p\) with \(|p|\le w\) has \(|C(p)\cap Q|\le N2^{-|p_{\rm free}|}\), where \(p_{\rm free}\) collects its literals on the free coordinates of \(Q\), and \(|C(p)|=n2^{-|p|}=2^{-|p_{\rm free}|}\,n2^{-|p_{\rm fixed}|}\) with \(|p_{\rm fixed}|\le\ell-\ell_2-1\), so \(|C(p)\cap O|\ge2^{-|p_{\rm free}|}(n2^{-|p_{\rm fixed}|}-N)\ge n2^{-|p|-1}\). Given \(R\), the image of the uniform injection \(\mu\) is a uniform \((n-N-e)\)-subset of \(O\), so \(E(\rho)\) is a uniform \(e\)-subset of \(O\), and \(X_p=|E(\rho)\cap C(p)|\) is hypergeometric with mean \(\mu_p\ge e2^{-w-1}\ge2s\). Sampling without replacement obeys the multiplicative Chernoff bound (Hoeffding, Probability inequalities for sums of bounded random variables, JASA 58 (1963), Theorem 4), so \(\Pr[X_p<s]\le\Pr[X_p\le\mu_p/2]\le e^{-\mu_p/8}\le e^{-e2^{-w-4}}\). There are at most \(Mr\) patterns. \(\square\)

Theorem (switching in the subcube family). Let \(F\) have at most \(r\) rows per term and at most \(w\le\ell-\ell_2-1\) literals per row, and let \(1\le s\le e\) with \(e\ge2^{w+2}s\). Then

\[ \Pr_{\rho\in\Phi_e}\bigl[\mathcal T(F,\rho)\text{ has height}\ge s\bigr]\ \le\ A^s+Mr\,e^{-e2^{-w-4}}, \]

and with at least the same probability a uniform \(\rho'\in\Phi_0\) admits a matching decision tree over the holes \(Q\), of height below \(s\), whose 0-leaves falsify every term of \(F|\rho'\) and whose 1-leaves contain a satisfied term.

Proof. The first bound adds the two lemmas. For the second, draw \(\rho'=\rho\cup\rho''\) as in Section 1 and restrict \(\mathcal T(F,\rho)\) by \(\rho''\): at a node querying a row filled by \(\rho''\) follow the branch of its filled hole, which is unused because the surviving path assigns filled rows to filled holes and other rows to holes of \(Q\); at a node querying another row keep only the branches into \(Q\). Depth does not increase, every surviving leaf's path together with \(\rho''\) is a leaf path of the original tree, so it still falsifies every term or contains a satisfied term, and the surviving nodes query only rows of \(R\setminus\mathrm{dom}\,\rho''\) with holes in \(Q\). \(\square\)

Parameters. Take \(e=N\) with \(4N\le n\): then \(A\le24rN^3/n\), which is at most \(\tfrac12\) once \(N^3\le n/(48r)\); with \(w\le\log_2N-\log_2s-6\) the richness failure is at most \(Mr\,e^{-4s}\). With \(s=\lceil\log_2(8M)\rceil\) one restriction \(\rho'\in\Phi_0\) gives all \(M\) readers of a source trees of height \(O(\log M)\) with probability at least \(3/4\) (for \(r\le8M^3\)). The residual subcube may thus have size up to \((n/48r)^{1/3}\), far above the polylogarithmic size the high threshold needs, the terms may have \(r\le n^{\varepsilon}\) rows, and each row may carry about \(\tfrac13\log_2n-\log_2\log_2M\) literals. The decoder lemma at degree \(rw\), the sum-input image lemma with companions through \(r+s\), and the weight step on the residual subcube then compose for such readers.

Verification. check_subcube_switching_encoding.py enumerates every \(\rho\in\Phi_e\) for small \(\ell,\ell_2,e\) and a random ordered disjunction, builds the canonical tree of Section 1, and for every bad restriction whose encoder finds its labels (the per-path form of richness) encodes the trimmed lexicographically first long path and decodes it. The eight recorded runs cover \(n\in\{8,16\}\), \(N\in\{2,4\}\), \(e\in\{1,2,3,4,10,12\}\), \(r\in\{2,3\}\), \(s\in\{2,3,4\}\): 76,418 rich bad restrictions were encoded and decoded with zero failures (one run is vacuous, with no rich bad restriction). The tool's first version omitted the marks \(\beta\) and failed 1,348 of 7,234 round trips, because the decoder could not tell moved rows from rows that \(\mu\) had already assigned consistent outside labels; that failure fixed the code's shape before the proof was written. The ratio and the richness bound were not tested numerically; the bound \(A^s\) is vacuous at these sizes.

3. Refutation: rows pinned into a fixed subcube

The lemma needs, for every moved row, a consistent free label outside \(Q\), so it says nothing about a row whose consistent labels lie in \(Q\). Such rows are on the frontier: a row pinned to one label is a flat of rank \(\ell\le r_{\rm high}\). For the fixed subcube they defeat every switching lemma.

Claim. Enumerate \(Q=\{q_0,\dots,q_{N-1}\}\) and let \(F_Q=\bigvee_{i\in[n+1]}[\text{row }i\text{ pinned to }q_{i\bmod N}]\), a reader with \(n+1\) terms of one row and \(\ell\) literals each. For \(\rho'\in\Phi_0\) let \(t(\rho')\) be the largest number of rows of \(R'\) sharing a target. Then every matching decision tree, with pigeon and hole queries, whose leaves each falsify every term of \(F_Q|\rho'\) or contain a satisfied term has height at least \((N+1)/(t(\rho')+1)\); and the fraction of \(\rho'\in\Phi_0\) with \(t(\rho')\ge t\) is at most \(N\,8^t/t!\), below \(N^{-1/10}\) for \(t=2\lceil\log_2N\rceil+32\).

Proof. Matched rows have labels in \(O\), so \(F_Q|\rho'=\bigvee_{i\in R'}X_{i,q_{i\bmod N}}\). An adversary answers a pigeon query \(i\) with an unused hole other than the target of \(i\), possible while fewer than \(N-1\) holes are used, and a hole query \(z\) with an uncovered row whose target is not \(z\), possible while more than \(t(\rho')\) rows are uncovered. After \(h\) answers no term is satisfied, at least \(N+1-h\) rows are uncovered, and at most \(h\,t(\rho')\) of them have a used target; if \(h<(N+1)/(t(\rho')+1)\) some uncovered row keeps an unused target, so its term is alive and the node is not a leaf of the stated kind. For the fraction: a target class has at most \(2n/N\) rows, a fixed set of \(t\) rows lies in the uniform \((N+1)\)-set \(R'\) with probability at most \(((N+1)/(n+1-t))^t\), so a class contributes at most \(\binom{2n/N}{t}((N+1)/(n+1-t))^t\le8^t/t!\) for \(t\le(n+1)/2\), and there are \(N\) classes. \(\square\)

Hence for all but an \(N^{-1/10}\) fraction of \(\Phi_0\), \(F_Q|\rho'\) has no representing tree of height below \(N/(2\log_2N+35)\). The claim concerns trees whose leaves decide the terms syntactically, the form used by the image lemmas; it does not exclude a representation of \(F_Q|\rho'\) modulo the residual ideal by other means.

4. Why the encoding stops exactly there

In the encoding lemma the whole gain \(\bigl((N+e+1)/(n-N-e+1)\bigr)^s\) comes from the residual pigeons: a code removes \(s\) rows from \(R\). It is paid for by the factor \(e^s\) of extra injections and by \((2r)^s(N+e)^s\) of side information, and the residual holes contribute nothing, because in every subcube family they are fixed. A row whose consistent labels lie in \(Q\) can only be recorded by matching it into \(Q\), and no element of any family with residual holes a flat does that; the family of "flat minus \(j\) points" has ratio \(\binom Nj(N+1+e)_j\ge1\), as recorded, and identifying the displaced pigeon of a swap costs the factor \(N+1+e\) that the swap saves. So an extension encoding covers exactly the rows with consistent free labels outside \(Q\), that is, rows with at most about \(\log_2(e/s)\) literals, and the bound \(N^3\lesssim n/r\) caps this at \(\tfrac13\log_2n\).

5. The way around the refutation: a random flat

Section 3 uses that \(F_Q\) knows \(Q\). If instead \(Q\) is a uniformly random affine subspace of \(\mathbb F_2^\ell\) of dimension \(\ell_2\), followed by uniform \((R,\mu)\), then each label lies in \(Q\) with probability \(N/n\), a term of \(F_Q\) is alive only if its row is residual and its target lies in \(Q\), and the expected number of alive terms is at most \((N+1+e)N/n\). The weight step should accept a random flat: a basis of the direction of \(Q\) gives coordinates in which \(Q\) is \(\mathcal Q_N\), old affine forms restricted to \(Q\) are affine in them, the new bits are affine in the unary variables, and flipping a new coordinate is a translation inside \(Q\). This must be checked against the exact form of the kernel count and the coordinate-edge detector; it is not verified here. The theorem of Section 2 holds conditionally on \(Q\), hence in the random-flat family. For a heavy row \((i,p)\) with \(|p|>w\), the union bound gives \(\Pr[i\in R\text{ and }C(p)\cap(Q\cup E)\ne\emptyset]\le(N+1+e)(N+2e)2^{-|p|}/(n+1)\) for \(N\le n/2\), so rows with \(2^{|p|}\ge8Mr(N+1+e)(N+2e)/n\) are, with probability \(7/8\), all matched by \(\mu\) (satisfying or falsifying their term) or dead (residual with no consistent available hole, so their term vanishes modulo the residual axioms at degree \(rw+1\)). What remains open in the random-flat family is the middle range \(\log_2(e/s)\lesssim|p|\lesssim\log_2(Mr(N+e)^2/n)\), about \(\tfrac13\log_2n\) to \((c-\tfrac13)\log_2n\) for \(M=n^c\): such rows have typically no consistent free label, so the code cannot move them, and they are too many for the union bound. Deleting dead terms inside the canonical tree also needs the decoder to see the same dead rows, which the picked code labels can spoil.

Main-route assessment. The first obligation is unchanged. On the literal frontier, the compact subcube family is now settled in both directions: readers whose rows carry at most \(\tfrac13\log_2n\) literals switch and compose with the weight step; readers with rows pinned into the fixed subcube do not switch, so the composition must randomize the flat and still handle the middle range of row widths. Parity terms remain the open core.

Process assessment. The round-trip tool again fixed the code's shape before any proof text existed, but the fifth test case was launched without estimating its enumeration size (\(6188\cdot14!/2!\) restrictions) and had to be stopped after twenty minutes; the tester now prints the size and refuses cases above a limit, and the computation rules gain one sentence asking for that estimate.

18 September 2026 — The random-flat family: base preservation, switching for all row widths below a size-dependent window, and a refuted shortcut

Status: two working lemmas and one working theorem (encoding round-trip tested in the random-flat family); one refuted method (round-trip failures, mechanism identified); the size window is an explicit remaining gap. Spin cycle 179. Produced by Claude Code (Claude Fable 5.1 (claude-fable-5-1), low reasoning effort).

Question and stopping point. The previous cycle left three items: check that the weight step accepts a uniformly random flat in place of the fixed subcube, carry the subcube switching lemma into that family, and handle rows with more than about \(\tfrac13\log_2n\) literals. The first two are done here. For the third, a canonical tree that skips terms with a dead row looked like the natural tool and was refuted by the round-trip test before any proof was written; the tool that survives is a dichotomy for heavy terms that needs no change to the tree, and it closes the literal frontier for sources of size \(n/\mathrm{polylog}(n)\), leaving for larger sources a window of row widths whose length grows with the size exponent.

1. A random flat preserves the compact base and the weight step's objects

Let \(Q=q+V\subseteq\mathbb F_2^\ell\) be an affine flat of dimension \(\ell_2\), \(N=2^{\ell_2}\), with a basis \(v_1,\dots,v_{\ell_2}\) of \(V\), and write \(y(z)\in\mathbb F_2^{\ell_2}\) for the coordinates of \(z\in Q\), so \(z=q+\sum_ay_a(z)v_a\). The flat restriction chooses \(N+1\) live rows, matches the other rows bijectively to the labels outside \(Q\) and fixes their bits, and on a live row \(i\) substitutes \(b_{it}=q_t+\sum_a(v_a)_t\,y_{ia}\), renaming live rows canonically.

Lemma. (i) An old-bit polynomial of degree \(d\) restricts to a polynomial of degree at most \(d\) in the residual bits \(y\). (ii) The image of \(\mathcal Q_n\) lies in the ideal generated by \(\mathcal Q_N\) in the variables \(y\), with certificates of degree at most \(\ell\): a live–live collision generator restricts to the residual collision generator plus a Boolean multiple, a live–fixed or fixed–fixed generator to a Boolean multiple or to zero, and Booleanity to a sum of residual Booleanity generators. (iii) The residual affine decoder \(y_{ia}=\sum_{z\in Q:\,y_a(z)=1}X_{iz}\) agrees with the restriction of the old decoder modulo the residual row axiom. Consequently the multiplier space, the flat count of the high threshold, and the signed cube detector, all defined in the residual instance's own coordinates, apply verbatim on \(Q\).

Proof. (i) is the affine substitution. (ii) In characteristic two, \((q_t+\sum_ac_ay_a)^2+(q_t+\sum_ac_ay_a)=\sum_ac_a(y_a^2+y_a)\), which is Booleanity. For two live rows, \(E_{ii'}=\prod_t(1+L_t(d))\) with \(d=y_i+y_{i'}\) and \(L_t(d)=\sum_a(v_a)_td_a\); the linear forms \(L_t\) span the dual of \(\mathbb F_2^{\ell_2}\) because the \(v_a\) are independent, so the product is the indicator of \(d=0\) as a function, hence equals \(\prod_a(1+d_a)\) modulo the ideal of \(d_a^2+d_a=(y_{ia}^2+y_{ia})+(y_{i'a}^2+y_{i'a})\), with cofactors of degree at most \(\ell-2\). For a live row and a fixed row with label \(u\notin Q\), \(\prod_t(1+b_{it}+u_t)\) is the zero function on \(\mathbb F_2^{\ell_2}\), so it lies in the Boolean ideal at degree \(\ell\); two fixed rows have distinct labels and give zero. (iii) Modulo \(\sum_{z\in Q}X_{iz}=1\) and \(X_{iz}=0\) for \(z\notin Q\), \(q_t+\sum_a(v_a)_ty_{ia}=\sum_{z\in Q}X_{iz}\bigl(q_t+\sum_a(v_a)_ty_a(z)\bigr)=\sum_{z\in Q}z_tX_{iz}\). The last sentence holds because those objects (IQ-space, the flat count, the cubes with free axes) are stated for a compact base of \(N\) labels with bits \(y\), and a coordinate cube in \(y\) is a subflat of \(Q\). \(\square\)

The recorded coordinate restriction is the case \(V=\mathbb F_2^{\ell_2}\times0\), \(q=0\), where the mixed generators vanish syntactically. Switched-reader images, which are sums of leaf terms in the residual unary variables, become polynomials of degree at most \(s\ell_2\) in \(y\), since \(X_{iz}=\prod_a(1+y_{ia}+y_a(z))\) modulo the residual axioms.

The random-flat family draws \(Q\) uniformly among the affine flats of dimension \(\ell_2\), then \((R,\mu)\) uniformly as in \(\Phi_e\) or \(\Phi_0\) with the labels outside \(Q\) as the outside labels. Every label lies in \(Q\) with probability \(N/n\), so for a pattern \(p\), \(\Pr[C(p)\cap Q\ne\varnothing]\le N2^{-|p|}\).

2. The light-row lemma transfers

The encoding and richness lemmas use of \(Q\) only that \(|C(p)\cap Q|\le N\), so that \(|C(p)\cap O|\ge n2^{-w-1}\) for \(w\le\ell-\ell_2-1\), and that moved rows receive labels outside \(Q\). Conditioning on \(Q\), the theorem of the previous cycle therefore holds in the random-flat family with the same bound \(A^s+Mr\,e^{-e2^{-w-4}}\) and the same transfer to \(\Phi_0\). Verification. The round-trip tool gained --flat random, which draws \(Q\) as a random affine subspace; the three recorded random-flat runs (\(n\in\{8,16\}\), \(N\in\{2,4\}\), \(e\in\{2,10,12\}\), \(r\in\{2,3\}\), \(s\in\{2,3,4\}\)) encode and decode 54,713 rich bad restrictions with zero failures.

3. Heavy terms: satisfied, falsified, or vanishing

Fix \(w_0\ge1\). Call a row of a term heavy if its pattern has at least \(w_0\) literals, a term heavy if it has a heavy row, and let \(F_{\rm light}\) be the terms of \(F\) with no heavy row; \(M_h\) counts the heavy terms. Write \(\rho'=(Q,R',\mu')\) for an element of the random-flat family \(\Phi_0\).

Theorem. Let \(F_{\rm light}\) have at most \(r\) rows per term and at most \(w=w_0-1\) literals per row, with \(w\le\ell-\ell_2-1\) and \(e\ge2^{w+2}s\). With probability at least

\[ 1-A^s-Mr\,e^{-e2^{-w-4}}-\frac{M_h\,r\,(N+1+e)(N+2r)}{2^{w_0}\,n}, \qquad A=\frac{2r(N+e)e(N+e+1)}{n-N-e+1}, \]

the restriction \(\rho'\) admits a matching decision tree over the holes \(Q\), of height below \(s\), whose 1-leaves contain a term of \(F\) satisfied by \(\rho'\) and the leaf, and whose 0-leaves falsify every light term while every heavy term is either falsified or, as a polynomial in the residual bits, lies in the residual Boolean ideal at degree at most its number of literals.

Proof. If some term of \(F\) is satisfied by \(\rho'\), a single 1-leaf serves. Otherwise consider the events \(B_1\): some heavy term has a heavy row \(i\) with \(\mu'(i)\in C(p_i)\) and another row in \(R'\); and \(B_2\): some heavy term has a heavy row \(i\in R'\) with \(C(p_i)\cap Q\ne\varnothing\). Given \(R'\), \(\mu'(i)\) is uniform on the labels outside \(Q\), so \(\Pr[\mu'(i)\in C(p_i)]\le n2^{-|p_i|}/(n-N)\le2\cdot2^{-w_0}\); a fixed other row is residual with probability at most \((N+1+e)/n\) after the filling; and \(\Pr[i\in R']\le(N+1+e)/(n+1)\) is independent of \(Q\). Summing over at most \(r\) heavy rows of each of the \(M_h\) heavy terms,

\[ \Pr[B_1]+\Pr[B_2]\ \le\ M_hr\Bigl(2\cdot2^{-w_0}\frac{(r-1)(N+1+e)}{n}+\frac{N+1+e}{n+1}\,N2^{-w_0}\Bigr) \ \le\ \frac{M_hr(N+1+e)(N+2r)}{2^{w_0}n}. \]

Outside \(B_1\cup B_2\), with no term satisfied, every heavy term \(T\) is falsified or has a heavy row \(i\in R'\) with \(C(p_i)\cap Q=\varnothing\): if a heavy row is matched consistently, then by \(\lnot B_1\) every other row is matched, so \(T\) is satisfied or falsified; if a heavy row is residual, then by \(\lnot B_2\) its pattern misses \(Q\). In the second case \(T\) restricted by \(\rho'\) is a product of affine forms in the residual bits that vanishes identically on \(\mathbb F_2^{\ell_2}\) at row \(i\), hence lies in the Boolean ideal at degree at most the number of literals of \(T\), whatever the remaining rows do; in the unary encoding it vanishes outright, since every decoded unary term contains a variable \(X_{iz}\) with \(z\notin Q\), which \(\rho'\) sets to zero. Now take the canonical tree of \(F_{\rm light}\) under \(\rho'\). Its 1-leaves contain a satisfied light term, its 0-leaves falsify every light term, and the heavy terms stay falsified or vanishing at every leaf, because both properties are preserved under extending the assignment. The height is below \(s\) outside the event of the light-row lemma, whose bound is uniform in \(Q\). \(\square\)

In the sum-input image lemma a vanishing heavy term contributes nothing at a 0-leaf: its decoded unary terms are zero after the restriction, so the companion and identity certificates are unchanged.

4. Parameters: complete below \(n/\mathrm{polylog}\), a window above

Take \(N\) polylogarithmic, as the high threshold needs, \(e=\lfloor(n/48r)^{1/3}\rfloor\ge N\), so that \(A\le\tfrac12\), and \(s=\lceil\log_2(8S)\rceil\) for a source with \(S\) readers of at most \(S\) terms each. The light range is \(2^{w}\le e/(64s)\), about \(\tfrac13\log_2n\) literals per row, where the richness failure is at most \(Mr\,e^{-4s}\); the heavy bound, summed over all heavy terms of all readers, is at most \(1/8\) once \(2^{w_0}\ge8Sr(N+1+e)(N+2r)/n\). Both hold with \(w_0=w+1\) exactly when

\[ S\ \le\ \frac{n\,e}{512\,s\,r\,(N+1+e)(N+2r)}\ \approx\ \frac{n}{768\,s\,r\,(N+2r)}, \]

and then every reader of the source, whatever its row widths, has a tree of height \(O(\log S)\) under one common restriction, with probability at least \(5/8\) (for \(r\le S^3\)). For \(S=n^c\) with \(c>1\) the two ranges leave a window of about \((c-1)\log_2n\) row widths, from \(\log_2(e/64s)\) to \(\log_2(8Sr(N+1+e)(N+2r)/n)\), in which rows are neither light enough to move nor rare enough to ignore. The window does not depend on \(e\), which cancels, and shrinking \(N\) below \(2r\) does not help.

5. A refuted shortcut: skipping dead terms inside the canonical tree

The first attempt at Section 3 changed the canonical tree to skip a term having an uncovered row with no consistent hole of \(Q\) unused by the path, expecting the decoder to see the same dead rows because moved rows receive outside labels. The round-trip tool with --skip-dead refutes this: 114, 1,206, 108, 883, and 359 failures in five runs (two with zero failures are too small to exercise the rule). The mechanism, read off a failing case at \(n=8\): the term \([b_{2,1}=1]\wedge[b_{0,1}=0]\) is skipped under \(\rho\) because row 2 is residual and no label of \(Q=\{0,1\}\) has second bit one, while row 0 is matched consistently; a later round moves row 2 to the outside label 2, consistent with its own term and, by chance, with the skipped term, which the decoder then finds satisfied. Moved rows can revive skipped terms, and choosing code labels that avoid every dead pattern on that row costs richness the adversary can destroy with extensions of light terms. Section 3 avoids the issue by never skipping: the light tree is fixed, and dead heavy terms vanish modulo the residual axioms instead.

Main-route assessment. The first obligation is unchanged. On the literal frontier the composition switching–decoder–image–weight step is now complete in the random-flat family for sources of size at most \(n/\mathrm{polylog}(n)\); for larger sources the open part is exactly the row-width window of Section 4. Parity terms remain the open core.

Process assessment. The round-trip tool refuted the skip rule before any proof text existed and pointed to the actual mechanism within one diagnostic run, which is the intended use of the tool; no framework change is needed this cycle.

18 September 2026 — The row-width window: sharper heavy-term bound (complete up to size \(n^{4/3}\)), hole queries without onto axioms, and what the window would need

Status: one dated refinement of a working theorem's parameters; one working lemma (hole-query nodes modulo the functional base); one observation on the window with a refuted variant of the family. Spin cycle 180. Produced by Claude Code (Claude Fable 5.1 (claude-fable-5-1), low reasoning effort).

Question and stopping point. The remaining literal-frontier obligation is the window of row widths left open for sources of size \(n^c\). The plan was to sharpen the bounds that define the window, to check whether a variant of the restriction family widens the light range, and to determine what a proof for the window must control. The stopping point is a refined statement of the window and a named mechanism for the next attempt.

1. The heavy-term bound on the compact family is sharper than stated

The proof of the heavy-term dichotomy bounds the probability that a row is residual under \(\rho'\in\Phi_0\) by \((N+1+e)/n\), carried over from the slack family. On \(\Phi_0\) the residual set \(R'\) has exactly \(N+1\) rows, so \(\Pr[i\in R']=(N+1)/(n+1)\) and \(\Pr[j\in R'\mid i\notin R']=(N+1)/n\). The same argument therefore gives

\[ \Pr[B_1]+\Pr[B_2]\ \le\ M_hr\Bigl(2\cdot2^{-w_0}\frac{(r-1)(N+1)}{n}+\frac{N+1}{n+1}\,N2^{-w_0}\Bigr)\ \le\ \frac{M_hr\,(N+1)(N+2r)}{2^{w_0}\,n}, \]

and the theorem holds with \((N+1)\) in place of \((N+1+e)\). Since \(N\) is polylogarithmic while \(e=\lfloor(n/48r)^{1/3}\rfloor\), this changes the parameters of Section 4 of the previous entry: the heavy bound summed over a source of size \(S\) is at most \(1/8\) once \(2^{w_0}\ge8Sr(N+1)(N+2r)/n\), and with the light range \(2^w\le e/(64s)\) the two ranges meet exactly when

\[ S\ \le\ \frac{n\,e}{512\,s\,r\,(N+1)(N+2r)}\ =\ \frac{n^{4/3}}{512\,(48r)^{1/3}\,s\,r\,(N+1)(N+2r)}(1+o(1)). \]

So the whole literal frontier switches under one restriction for sources of size up to \(n^{4/3}/\mathrm{polylog}(n)\), and for \(S=n^c\) the window runs from about \(\tfrac13\log_2n\) to \((c-1)\log_2n+O(\log\log n)\) literals per row, nonempty only for \(c>\tfrac43\). The previous entry's remark that the window does not depend on \(e\) is withdrawn: its lower end is \(\log_2(e/64s)\), and the complete regime grows with \(e\); only the upper end is independent of \(e\).

2. Hole queries need no onto axiom

Matching decision trees that query holes as well as pigeons are the natural tool for readers whose terms crowd one residual hole, but a hole query has an "empty" outcome, and the functional base has no axiom forcing a hole to be filled. The following lemma removes the concern.

Lemma. On the residual instance (pigeons \(R'\), holes \(Q\)), let a node with partial matching \(\pi\) query a hole \(q\) unused by \(\pi\), with branches \(X_{jq}\) for the pigeons \(j\in R'\) uncovered by \(\pi\) and one further branch with factor \(u_q(\pi)=1-\sum_{j}X_{jq}\), the sum over the same pigeons. Then the branch factors sum to one identically, any two of them multiply to zero modulo Boolean and exclusion axioms at degree two, and for every pigeon \(i\) uncovered by \(\pi\), \(X_{iq}u_q(\pi)\) lies in the same ideal. Consequently a tree with such nodes, of height \(h\), has leaf terms of degree at most \(h\) that satisfy the leaf-partition identity and pairwise incompatibility used by the switched-reader image lemma and the sum-input lemma, and in the empty branch every term containing a variable \(X_{iq}\) with \(i\) uncovered vanishes modulo those axioms.

Proof. \(\sum_jX_{jq}+u_q=1\) is an identity. For \(j\ne j'\), \(X_{jq}X_{j'q}\) is a column exclusion. \(X_{iq}u_q=X_{iq}-X_{iq}^2-\sum_{j\ne i}X_{iq}X_{jq}\equiv X_{iq}-X_{iq}=0\). Since \(u_q^2-u_q=-\sum_jX_{jq}u_q\), \(u_q\) is idempotent modulo the same axioms. A leaf term is a product of at most \(h\) factors, each a variable or some \(u_q\), hence of degree at most \(h\); the partition identity follows by induction over the tree, as for pigeon queries, and two distinct leaves share a node at which their branch factors differ, so their product contains an incompatible pair. \(\square\)

A pigeon covered by \(\pi\) sits at a hole other than \(q\), so its variable \(X_{iq}\) is already excluded on the path. The image lemmas use of leaf terms only their degree, the partition identity, incompatibility, and idempotence, so they extend verbatim; the factor \(u_q\) is affine in the residual unary variables and adds nothing to the certificate degrees beyond the height.

3. What the window would need

The light range cannot be widened by fixing the free pool. One might hope to remove the factor \(e\) from \(A=2r(N+e)e(N+e+1)/(n-N-e+1)\) by drawing the free labels from a fixed pool \(E_0\) of size \(e\) instead of anywhere outside \(Q\). Counting the family \(\Phi'(k)\) with \(k\) unused pool labels, \(|\Phi'(k)|=\binom ek\binom{n+1}{N+1+k}(n-N-k)!\), gives \(|\Phi'(k-1)|/|\Phi'(k)|\approx k(N+1+k)/(e-k+1)\), which for a pool of size \(e\le n-N\) is at least the ratio \(k(N+1+k)/(n-N-k+1)\) of the family \(\Phi_k\) with \(k\) free labels anywhere, and a smaller pool only raises it. In \(\Phi_k\) the ratio is small because a smaller free set has \(\binom{n-N}{k-1}/\binom{n-N}{k}\approx k/n\) times as many positions; that entropy of the free set, not the residual pigeons alone, is what pays for a moved row. So the light range \(2^w\lesssim e/s\) with \(e^3\lesssim n/r\) is intrinsic to extension encodings in flat families, and the window's lower end stays at \(\tfrac13\log_2n\).

Per-term rarity. For a term \(T\) whose rows have patterns \(p_j\), being alive but unsatisfied under \(\rho'\) with a residual heavy row that is \(Q\)-consistent has probability at most \(r4^r(N+1)N/n\) times \(\prod_j2^{-|p_j|}\) (each other row is matched consistently or residual, at most \(4\cdot2^{-|p_j|}\) each), while \(T\) is satisfied with probability at least \(2^{-2r-1}\prod_j2^{-|p_j|}\) when every \(2^{|p_j|}\le n/4rN\). Hence if the expected number \(\mu_{\rm sat}\) of satisfied terms is at most \(n/(2^{4r+4}r(N+1)N)\), the expected number of window-alive terms is at most \(1/8\) and the window is harmless; and if \(\mu_{\rm sat}\) is large and the satisfaction events were independent, the reader would be satisfied outright. The window is therefore a problem only for readers with \(\mu_{\rm sat}\) in between, whose satisfied events are positively correlated; a family of terms sharing one heavy row is the extreme case, and there the tree needs one query for the shared row. The natural attempt is a second-moment or Janson bound on "no term satisfied" over the flat and the matching, with shared rows handled by the tree; a code-based proof is unavailable, since a code in a flat family cannot move a \(Q\)-consistent heavy row (code obstruction), and shared-hole configurations, which pigeon-only trees resolve slowly, are exactly where the hole queries of Section 2 apply.

What suffices. The goal needs the frontier for every fixed size exponent \(c\). Section 1 settles \(c\le\tfrac43\); the remaining obligation is a bound on the probability that some reader has, under \(\rho'\), at least \(k_0\) alive window terms with pairwise distinct heavy rows and no satisfied term, for \(k_0\) below the tree height budget, since paths with fewer than \(k_0\) heavy queries are paid by the encoding at a factor \((2r(N+e))^{k_0}\) with \(A^{s-k_0}\) to spare.

Main-route assessment. The first obligation is unchanged, but the literal frontier is now closed for sources of size up to \(n^{4/3}/\mathrm{polylog}(n)\) rather than \(n/\mathrm{polylog}(n)\), the window for larger sources is located exactly, and its resolution has a named mechanism (correlated satisfaction of window terms) and a named tool (hole queries, now available under the functional base). Parity terms remain the open core.

Process assessment. The refinement came from rereading the previous proof with the compact family's exact residual count, a one-line check that should accompany every transfer from the slack family; no framework change is needed, and no computation was run this cycle.

18 September 2026 — Pigeon-only trees fail in the random-flat family at source size \(n^2\): hole queries are necessary, and the window obligation is corrected to distinct holes

Status: one refutation (working proof, explicit readers); one correction of the obligation named in the previous cycle; two failed counterexample constructions recorded; the corrected obligation is open. Spin cycle 181. Produced by Claude Code (Claude Fable 5.1 (claude-fable-5-1), low reasoning effort).

Question and stopping point. The previous cycle named as sufficient obligation a bound on the probability that a reader has at least \(k_0\) alive window terms with pairwise distinct heavy rows and no satisfied term. The plan was to attack it, first by trying to falsify it. The attempt found that the event is not rare when the alive terms share one residual hole, that this makes pigeon-only trees fail while one hole query succeeds, and that the obligation must therefore be restated with distinct holes. The stopping point is that restatement, with the failed constructions recorded so they are not retried.

1. The single-target reader is bad for pigeon-only trees with probability \(N/n\)

For a label \(x^\ast\in\{0,1\}^\ell\) let \(F_{x^\ast}=\bigvee_{i\in[n+1]}[\text{row }i\text{ pinned to }x^\ast]\), the reader of the fixed-subcube refutation with one target. Draw \(\rho'=(Q,R',\mu')\) from the random-flat family \(\Phi_0\) with \(N\ge s+1\).

Claim. With probability exactly \(N/n\), the event \(x^\ast\in Q\), no term of \(F_{x^\ast}\) is satisfied by \(\rho'\), and every matching decision tree with pigeon queries only whose leaves decide \(F_{x^\ast}|\rho'\) (0-leaves falsify or annihilate every term, 1-leaves contain a satisfied term) has height at least \(N-1\ge s\); a tree with the single hole query at \(x^\ast\) has height one. Consequently, for the \(n\) readers \(F_{x^\ast}\), \(x^\ast\in\{0,1\}^\ell\), of total size \(n(n+1)\), some reader is bad for every \(\rho'\).

Proof. A uniformly random flat contains a given point with probability \(N/n\). When \(x^\ast\in Q\), every matched row has a label outside \(Q\), so its term is falsified, and no term is satisfied; the \(N+1\) residual rows have alive terms \(X_{ix^\ast}\). An adversary answers a pigeon query \(i\) with an unused hole other than \(x^\ast\), possible while fewer than \(N-1\) holes are used; at depth \(h<N-1\) at least two residual rows are uncovered and \(x^\ast\) is unused, so their terms are alive and the node is not a deciding leaf. The hole query at \(x^\ast\) has branches \(X_{jx^\ast}\), each a 1-leaf containing the satisfied term of row \(j\), and the empty branch \(u=1-\sum_jX_{jx^\ast}\), at which every term \(X_{ix^\ast}\) is annihilated by \(X_{ix^\ast}u\equiv0\). Since \(Q\) is nonempty, some \(x^\ast\) lies in it. \(\square\)

This is consistent with the heavy-term dichotomy, whose event \(B_2\) for \(F_{x^\ast}\) has probability at most \((n+1)(N+1)N/n^2\), and with its size regime: the family of all \(F_{x^\ast}\) has size \(n^2\), above the regime. What the claim adds is that no improvement of the probabilistic argument can rescue pigeon-only trees beyond size about \(n^2/N\): the bad readers exist and are hit with probability one. The window analysis must be carried out for trees with hole queries, which Section 2 of the previous entry made available under the functional base.

2. The corrected obligation: distinct holes

In a tree with hole queries, a window row \(i\) of an alive term, residual and with \(C(p_i)\cap Q\) a single point \(q\) (the typical case for \(|p_i|>\ell_2\)), is handled by querying \(q\): the branch \(X_{iq}\) satisfies the row, every other branch falsifies the term, and every other term wanting \(q\) is decided at the same node. A path therefore contains at most one query per hole, and a path with \(k_0\) heavy queries exhibits \(k_0\) alive window terms whose heavy rows are distinct and whose consistent holes are distinct. The obligation named last cycle is corrected accordingly: bound the probability that, under \(\rho'\), no term is satisfied and at least \(k_0\) distinct holes of \(Q\) are each the consistent hole of an alive window term. Paths with fewer heavy queries are paid by the encoding, with the answer to a hole query recorded in \(\delta\) (at most \(N+e+2\) values) and the row left unmoved.

Why distinct holes are rare. For unary rows the consistent holes are the pinned labels themselves, and \(k_0\) distinct pinned labels \(x_1,\dots,x_{k_0}\) all lie in the random flat with probability \(\prod_{t}(N-2^{t})/(n-2^{t})\) over the affine rank \(d\) of the set, about \((N/n)^{d}\): a set of \(k_0\) affinely independent labels costs \((N/n)^{k_0}\), and even the cheapest configuration, a \(d\)-dimensional subflat of \(2^d=k_0\) labels, costs \((N/n)^{\log_2k_0}=n^{-\Theta(\log\log n)}\), superpolynomially small. For window rows of width \(w\) below \(\ell\), the analogous count is over the projections of \(Q\) onto the patterns' coordinates, with \(N2^{-w}\) in place of \(N/n\). A proof must combine this rank effect with the per-term rarity of the previous entry and with negative association of satisfaction events for terms on disjoint rows (the residual set and matching together form a uniform injection, whose indicator entries are negatively associated); shared rows and shared holes are handled by the tree rather than by probability.

3. Two constructions that do not refute the corrected obligation

(i) A shared light row \(j\) with one literal and \(n/2\) two-row terms \([j\in p']\wedge[i_k\in p]\), \(p\) of the first width above the light range: with \(2^w\approx n^{1/3}\) about \(n^{2/3}\) of the rows \(i_k\) are matched consistently, so the reader is satisfied whenever row \(j\) is, and when \(j\) is residual the tree queries \(j\) once. (ii) The same with a residual shared row: alive terms with matched-consistent heavy rows reduce to \([j\in p']\), decided by one query. In both, satisfaction of a window term is about \(n/(N+1)N\) times as likely as being alive with a residual consistent heavy row, as the per-term rarity predicts; a counterexample needs many alive terms with distinct residual heavy rows and no satisfied term, which single-target readers achieve only by sharing the hole.

Main-route assessment. The first obligation is unchanged. On the literal frontier the switching machinery must use hole queries (now available); the window obligation is corrected to distinct holes, with a named rank mechanism that makes it plausible; the complete regime \(n^{4/3}/\mathrm{polylog}\) is unchanged. Parity terms remain the open core.

Process assessment. Trying to falsify the stated obligation before proving it found in one cycle that it was mis-stated, at the cost of two discarded constructions whose failure modes are now recorded; no framework change is needed, and no computation was run.

18 September 2026 — The window obligation is a matching bound: alive pinned pairs form a bipartite graph whose matching number is the tree height, and dense pinned classes are satisfied by matched edges

Status: one correction (the obligation of the previous cycle is restated as a matching bound, with two readers showing that neither distinct rows nor distinct holes alone suffice); one working reduction principle with proof sketch for unary heavy rows; the general bound remains open. Spin cycle 182. Produced by Claude Code (Claude Fable 5.1 (claude-fable-5-1), low reasoning effort).

Question and stopping point. The plan was to prove the distinct-holes obligation for unary heavy rows. Testing it against readers first showed that it is again mis-stated: a residual row pinned to many labels realizes many distinct holes but is decided by one pigeon query. The correct quantity is the matching number of the alive pinned-pair graph, and the stopping point is a proof strategy for it: pinned pairs that are frequent enough are satisfied by the matched part of the restriction, and pairs that are rare contribute few alive pairs.

1. The alive pinned-pair graph and its matching number

For a reader \(F\) whose heavy rows are unary, let \(P_F\) be the set of pairs \((i,x)\) such that some term pins row \(i\) to label \(x\). Under \(\rho'=(Q,R',\mu')\) a pair is matched-consistent if \(\mu'(i)=x\) (then \(x\notin Q\)), alive if \(i\in R'\) and \(x\in Q\), and otherwise falsified or dead (a residual row pinned outside \(Q\) makes its term vanish, as in the dichotomy). The alive pairs form a bipartite graph \(B(\rho')\subseteq R'\times Q\). A decision tree decides every alive pair incident to a vertex by querying that vertex: a pigeon query at \(i\) decides all \((i,\cdot)\), a hole query at \(x\) decides all \((\cdot,x)\). Hence the pinned part of \(F|\rho'\) is decided by a tree of height equal to the vertex cover number of \(B(\rho')\), which by König's theorem is its matching number \(\nu(B(\rho'))\); conversely an adversary who answers each query with a partner outside \(B\) keeps an alive pair as long as the queried vertices do not cover \(B\), so no tree of the stated kind does better when no term is satisfied. The obligation for unary heavy rows is therefore: bound \(\Pr[\text{no term satisfied}\wedge\nu(B(\rho'))\ge k_0]\).

Two readers show that the earlier formulations were too weak. \(F=\bigvee_{x\in L}[i_0\mapsto x]\) with \(|L|=n/2\): with probability \((N+1)/(n+1)\) row \(i_0\) is residual, no term is satisfied, and about \(N/2\) distinct holes carry alive pairs, yet \(\nu(B)=1\) and one pigeon query decides \(F\). The single-target reader \(F_{x^\ast}\) of the previous cycle has \(N+1\) alive pairs on distinct rows and \(\nu(B)=1\). So the obligation must involve a matching, distinct rows and distinct holes at once.

2. Reduction principle: dense pinned classes are satisfied, sparse ones are rare

Group the terms of \(F\) by tail, the conjunction of their light rows: a class \(\tau\) consists of the terms \([i\mapsto x]\wedge\tau\) for \((i,x)\in P_\tau\). Under \(\rho'\), the class is satisfied as soon as one of its pairs is matched-consistent and \(\tau\) is satisfied; its alive pairs are those of \(P_\tau\cap(R'\times Q)\) with \(\tau\) alive or satisfied.

Lemma (matched edges hit dense pair sets). Fix \(Q\) and \(R'\), and let \(P\) be a set of pairs \((i,x)\) with \(i\notin R'\) and \(x\notin Q\). Under the uniform bijection \(\mu'\) of the matched rows onto the labels outside \(Q\), the probability that no pair of \(P\) is matched is at most \(\exp(-|P|/(n-N))\).

Proof. The indicators \(1[\mu'(i)=x]\) of a uniformly random bijection are negatively associated (Joag-Dev and Proschan, Negative association of random variables, with applications, Ann. Statist. 11 (1983), permutation distributions; imported statement). For each row \(i\) the event \(\mu'(i)\in P_i\), with \(P_i\) the labels paired with \(i\), is an increasing function of the entries of row \(i\), and different rows use disjoint entries, so these events are negatively associated and \(\Pr[\text{none}]\le\prod_i(1-|P_i|/(n-N))\le\exp(-\sum_i|P_i|/(n-N))\). \(\square\)

The two sides of a class. Write \(\lambda_\tau=\Pr[\tau\text{ satisfied}]\ge2^{-|\tau|-2r}\) and \(\lambda'_\tau=\Pr[\tau\text{ alive or satisfied}]\le4^r\lambda_\tau\) (each light row is residual with probability \((N+1)/n\le2^{-|p|}\) or matched consistently with probability at most \(2\cdot2^{-|p|}\)). A class with \(|P_\tau|\ge n\ln(8SK)\), where \(K\) is the number of classes, has a matched pair with probability at least \(1-1/(8SK)\) after discarding the at most \((N+1)n+nN\) pairs touching \(R'\) or \(Q\), so the class is satisfied whenever its tail is, and otherwise its alive pairs are irrelevant only if the tail is not alive either. A class with \(|P_\tau|<n\ln(8SK)\) has at most \(|P_\tau|(N+1)N/n^2\cdot\lambda'_\tau\le4^r(N+1)N\ln(8SK)\lambda_\tau/n\) alive pairs in expectation. Summing, the expected number of alive pairs in sparse classes is at most \(4^r(N+1)N\ln(8SK)\,\mu_{\rm sat}^{\rm sparse}/n\), where \(\mu^{\rm sparse}_{\rm sat}\le\sum_\tau\lambda_\tau\) bounds the expected number of satisfied terms among them; and the dense classes are, up to probability \(1/8\), reduced to their tails, a light disjunction handled by the light-row lemma.

What remains. For the sparse classes one needs \(\Pr[\nu(B)\ge k_0]\) exponentially small in \(k_0\), not just \(\mathbb E|B|/k_0\), because the union over \(S\) readers costs a factor \(S\). Given \(Q\) the alive-pair indicators are negatively associated in \(R'\), which gives \(\Pr[|B|\ge k_0\mid Q]\le(e\,\mathbb E[|B|\mid Q]/k_0)^{k_0}\), so what is missing is control of \(\mathbb E[|B|\mid Q]=\frac{N+1}{n}\sum_{x\in Q}w(x)\) with \(w(x)=\sum_{(i,x)\in P^{\rm sparse}}\lambda'_{(i,x)}\), that is, of how much sparse-class weight a random flat can capture; the crude bound \(N\max_xw(x)\) is too weak when the weight concentrates on few labels, and concentration on few labels is exactly the single-target situation, where \(\nu(B)=1\) although \(|B|\) is large. A proof must therefore bound the matching number directly, for instance through the weights of the labels and rows separately: \(\nu(B)\le\min(\)number of rows touched, number of holes touched\()\), and a hole \(x\in Q\) is touched only if some row pinned to \(x\) is residual, an event of probability at most \((N+1)\deg(x)/n\), while a row is touched only if one of its labels lies in \(Q\). This is the next cycle's target, with tails on shared rows handled by the tree as before.

Main-route assessment. The first obligation is unchanged. On the literal frontier the window obligation is now stated as a matching bound on the alive pinned-pair graph, which the known readers cannot violate, and the proof is reduced to bounding \(\nu(B)\) for sparse pinned classes under a random flat; dense classes are reduced to their light tails by the matched part of the restriction. Parity terms remain the open core.

Process assessment. Two more constructions were discarded by the same per-term rarity check before any proof text, and a near-contradiction with the bipartite switching lemma was resolved by noticing that matched pairs satisfy sub-terms; both are recorded here so the reader family is not re-examined. No framework change is needed, and no computation was run.
