18 September 2026 — Switching for unary readers at every polynomial source size: dense labels are satisfied, sparse labels give an exponential tail for the matching number, and dense labels in the flat are bounded by affine rank

Status: working theorem with full proof (hole-query trees, random-flat family) for readers all of whose terms pin one row to one label, and for readers whose terms are either such or light; one imported lemma (negative association of a uniform bijection). Mixed terms (a pinned row with a light tail) remain open. Spin cycle 183. Produced by Claude Code (Claude Fable 5.1 (claude-fable-5-1), low reasoning effort).

Question and stopping point. The previous cycle reduced the window obligation for unary heavy rows to an exponential tail for the matching number of the alive pinned-pair graph. The plan was to prove that tail. It follows from three facts: the events that different labels are occupied by rows pinned to them are negatively associated; a flat has exactly \(N\) points, so the elementary symmetric sums of label degrees over the flat are bounded without any rank consideration; and a set of \(k\) labels lies in the flat with probability at most \((N/n)^{\lceil\log_2k\rceil+1}\). The stopping point is a switching theorem for unary readers, valid at every polynomial source size, which is the first result on the literal frontier not limited by a size regime.

1. Setting

A unary reader is a disjunction \(F=\bigvee_{(i,x)\in P_F}[\text{row }i\text{ pinned to }x]\) over a set \(P_F\) of pairs; \(\deg(x)\) is the number of rows pinned to \(x\). In the random-flat family \(\rho'=(Q,R',\mu')\), a pair is satisfied if \(\mu'(i)=x\), alive if \(i\in R'\) and \(x\in Q\), and otherwise falsified (\(\mu'(i)\ne x\)) or annihilated (\(i\in R'\), \(x\notin Q\): every \(X_{ix}\) with \(x\) matched to another row is zero after the restriction). The alive pairs form the bipartite graph \(B(\rho')\subseteq R'\times Q\) with matching number \(\nu(B)\). Fix \(k_1\ge1\), \(k_2\ge2\), and a source size \(S\); put

\[ D^\ast=\frac{k_1(n-k_1)}{2e(N+1)N},\qquad \Delta_0=N+\frac{2(n-N)\ln(8S)}{D^\ast}, \]

and assume \(D^\ast\ge2(N+1)\). Call a label dense if \(\deg(x)\ge D^\ast\), sparse otherwise, and let \(D\) be the set of dense labels.

2. Lemma: many dense labels force a satisfied term

Lemma. Conditionally on any \((Q,R')\), if \(|D|\ge\Delta_0\) then some term of \(F\) is satisfied by \(\mu'\) with probability at least \(1-1/(8S)\).

Proof. For a label \(x\notin Q\) let \(A_x\) be the event that the row \(\mu'^{-1}(x)\) is pinned to \(x\). Given \((Q,R')\), \(\mu'\) is a uniform bijection from the \(n-N\) matched rows onto the labels outside \(Q\), so \(\Pr[A_x]=\deg_{R'^c}(x)/(n-N)\), where \(\deg_{R'^c}(x)\ge\deg(x)-(N+1)\) counts matched rows pinned to \(x\). The indicators of a uniform bijection are negatively associated (Joag-Dev and Proschan, Negative association of random variables, with applications, Ann. Statist. 11 (1983), permutation distributions; imported statement), \(A_x\) is an increasing function of the entries of column \(x\), and distinct labels use disjoint columns; hence \(\Pr[\bigcap_{x}A_x^c]\le\prod_x(1-\Pr[A_x])\le\exp(-\sum_x\Pr[A_x])\). At least \(|D|-N\) dense labels lie outside \(Q\), each with \(\deg_{R'^c}(x)\ge D^\ast-N-1\ge D^\ast/2\), so the exponent is at most \(-(|D|-N)D^\ast/(2(n-N))\le-\ln(8S)\). \(\square\)

3. Lemma: sparse labels give an exponential tail for the matching number

Lemma. Let \(B_{\rm sp}\) be the alive pairs whose label is sparse. Then \(\Pr[\nu(B_{\rm sp})\ge k_1]\le2^{-k_1}\).

Proof. A matching of size \(k_1\) in \(B_{\rm sp}\) consists of pairs \((i_1,x_1),\dots,(i_{k_1},x_{k_1})\) with distinct rows in \(R'\) and distinct sparse labels in \(Q\). For a fixed label set \(X\) the number of such row choices is at most \(\prod_{x\in X}\deg(x)\), fixed distinct rows all lie in the uniform \((N+1)\)-set \(R'\) with probability at most \(\bigl((N+1)/(n+1-k_1)\bigr)^{k_1}\), and \(R'\) is independent of \(Q\). Hence the expected number of \(k_1\)-matchings is at most

\[ \Bigl(\frac{N+1}{n+1-k_1}\Bigr)^{k_1}\ \mathbb E\Bigl[\sum_{X\subseteq Q\cap{\rm sparse},\ |X|=k_1}\ \prod_{x\in X}\deg(x)\Bigr] \ \le\ \Bigl(\frac{N+1}{n+1-k_1}\Bigr)^{k_1}\binom{N}{k_1}(D^\ast)^{k_1} \ \le\ \Bigl(\frac{eN(N+1)D^\ast}{k_1(n+1-k_1)}\Bigr)^{k_1}\le2^{-k_1}, \]

because \(Q\) has exactly \(N\) points, whatever they are, and each sparse degree is below \(D^\ast\). Markov's inequality on the count of matchings finishes. \(\square\)

No affine structure of \(Q\) enters: the bound uses only \(|Q|=N\). This is where the rank difficulties of the previous cycles disappear, because a matching needs distinct labels and the elementary symmetric sum over \(N\) points is bounded uniformly.

4. Lemma: few dense labels lie in the flat

Lemma. For any set \(D\) of labels, \(\Pr[|D\cap Q|\ge k_2]\le|D|^{k_2}(N/n)^{\lceil\log_2k_2\rceil+1}\).

Proof. A \(k_2\)-subset \(X\subseteq D\) has affine rank \(d\ge\lceil\log_2k_2\rceil\), since a \(d\)-dimensional flat has \(2^d\) points; it contains \(d+1\) affinely independent points \(x_0,\dots,x_d\), and \(Q\supseteq X\) forces \(Q\supseteq\{x_0,\dots,x_d\}\). By transitivity of the affine group, given that \(Q\) contains the \(t\)-dimensional flat spanned by \(x_0,\dots,x_{t-1}\), the next point lies in \(Q\) with probability \((N-2^t)/(n-2^t)\le N/n\); so \(\Pr[X\subseteq Q]\le(N/n)^{d+1}\). Sum over the at most \(|D|^{k_2}\) subsets. \(\square\)

5. Theorem: unary readers switch at every polynomial size

Theorem. Let \(F\) be a unary reader and \(\rho'\) uniform in the random-flat family with \(D^\ast\ge2(N+1)\). With probability at least \(1-1/(8S)-\Delta_0^{k_2}(N/n)^{\lceil\log_2k_2\rceil+1}-2^{-k_1}\), \(F|\rho'\) has a matching decision tree with pigeon and hole queries of height at most \(k_1+k_2\) whose 1-leaves contain a satisfied term and whose 0-leaves falsify or annihilate every term.

Proof. If some term is satisfied by \(\rho'\), one 1-leaf serves. Otherwise, by the first lemma applied for each \((Q,R')\), we are outside an event of probability \(1/(8S)\) unless \(|D|<\Delta_0\); assume the latter. A matching of \(B\) uses at most one alive pair per label, so \(\nu(B)\le\nu(B_{\rm sp})+|D\cap Q|\), which is below \(k_1+k_2\) outside events of probability \(2^{-k_1}\) and \(\Delta_0^{k_2}(N/n)^{\lceil\log_2k_2\rceil+1}\). Take a minimum vertex cover \(C\) of \(B\), of size \(\nu(B)\) by König's theorem, and query its vertices in a fixed order. A pigeon query at \(i\in C\) has branches over the unused holes \(z\in Q\): if \((i,z)\in P_F\) the branch is a 1-leaf, otherwise every pair \((i,\cdot)\) is falsified on it. A hole query at \(x\in C\) has branches \(X_{jx}\) over uncovered residual rows: a 1-leaf if \((j,x)\in P_F\), otherwise every pair \((\cdot,x)\) is falsified; on the empty branch every \(X_{ix}\) is annihilated by \(X_{ix}u_x\equiv0\). Along a path with no 1-leaf, every alive pair is incident to a queried vertex and is falsified or annihilated, and every other pair was already falsified or annihilated by \(\rho'\), so the end of the path is a 0-leaf of the stated kind. \(\square\)

Corollary (all unary readers of a polynomial source). Let \(N\) be polylogarithmic and \(S=n^c\). Take \(k_1=\lceil\log_2(16S)\rceil\) and \(k_2=2^{c+2}\). Then \(D^\ast\ge2(N+1)\) for large \(n\), \(\Delta_0\le N+4e(N+1)N\ln(8S)(1+o(1))\) is polylogarithmic, and \(S\Delta_0^{k_2}(N/n)^{c+3}\to0\); so one restriction gives every unary reader of the source a tree of height at most \(\log_2(16S)+2^{c+2}+1\), with probability at least \(3/4\) for large \(n\). The height depends on the size exponent only through the additive constant \(2^{c+2}\), which bounds how many dense labels a flat may contain when the number of dense labels is polylogarithmic.

Corollary (separate light and unary terms). If every term of a reader is either light (rows with at most \(w\) literals, as in the subcube switching lemma) or unary, the tree that first queries the vertex cover \(C\) of the unary part and then continues with the canonical tree of the light part has height at most \(\nu(B)+s\), and the extension encoding applies to the light part with the cover queries recorded in \(\delta\) as unmoved rows: the decoder recovers \(C\) from the code, because pinned rows are never moved, \(Q\) is fixed, and the cover is a fixed function of \(B\); the cost is a factor \((N+e+2)^{\nu(B)}\) against \(A^{s}\) with \(s\) light queries. Hence such readers switch at every polynomial size with height \(O(\log S+2^c)\).

What is not covered. Mixed terms, a pinned row together with a light tail, are the general case of the window. For them the alive graph must be taken with tails alive, which the decoder cannot always evaluate when tails share rows with conflicting patterns, and the dense-label lemma needs the tail satisfied as well. The class reduction of the previous cycle is the intended route: dense classes reduce to their tails, sparse classes have few alive pairs, and the present lemmas supply the missing exponential tail once the alive graph is defined through a decoder-computable proxy.

Main-route assessment. The first obligation is unchanged. On the literal frontier, readers of unary terms, and readers mixing unary and light terms without mixed terms, now switch under one random-flat restriction at every polynomial source size, with hole-query trees; this removes the size regime for that term class and leaves mixed terms and parity terms. Parity terms remain the open core.

Process assessment. Stating the obligation as a matching bound made the proof a matter of three standard tools, whereas the earlier formulations had invited rank calculations that led nowhere; the lesson, that the tree height is a covering number and should be bounded as such, is recorded in the working context. No framework change is needed, and no computation was run.

18 September 2026 — Mixed terms: an adaptive heavy-query rule makes the heavy queries of the canonical tree a matching in the alive pinned-pair graph, with a decoder-computable proxy; the remaining probabilistic bound is decomposed

Status: one working lemma (tree rule and its encoding, proof by the invariant that heavy queries have distinct rows and holes); the probabilistic bound for mixed readers is decomposed into three named parts and left open; working-context consolidation done separately. Spin cycle 184. Produced by Claude Code (Claude Fable 5.1 (claude-fable-5-1), low reasoning effort).

Question and stopping point. The unary theorem used a minimum vertex cover of the alive graph, which the decoder can recompute because pinned rows are never moved. For mixed terms, a pinned row with a light tail, the alive graph depends on tails, which the decoder cannot always evaluate: a moved light row shows a code label consistent with its own term but possibly inconsistent with another term's pattern on that row, so alive tails may look falsified (the mirror image of the revival problem). The stopping point is a tree rule that avoids evaluating tails and still bounds the heavy queries by a matching number, plus the decomposition of the bound that remains.

1. The rule and its invariant

Let \(B_0(\rho')\) be the set of pinned pairs \((i,x)\) of the reader with \(i\in R'\) and \(x\in Q\), tails ignored; along a path, a pair is killed once its row or its hole has been queried. The canonical tree takes the first term not falsified by \(\rho'\cup\pi\), queries its uncovered light rows in order (pigeon queries, moved in the code as in the light lemma), and then, if its pinned pair \((i,x)\) is still unkilled and in \(B_0\), makes one heavy query: the pigeon \(i\) if \(i\) has at least two unkilled pairs in \(B_0\), otherwise the hole \(x\). Branches are as in the unary theorem.

Lemma. (i) The heavy queries of any path are triggered by pairs with pairwise distinct rows and pairwise distinct holes, each the pinned pair of a term not falsified by \(\rho'\); hence their number is at most \(\nu(B_{\rm t})\), the matching number of the pairs of \(B_0\) whose term's tail is not falsified by \(\rho'\). (ii) The extension encoding of the light lemma applies with the heavy queries recorded in \(\delta\) as unmoved (at most \(N+e+2\) values each): the decoder recomputes the rule from the code, because pinned rows are never moved, \(Q\) is fixed, and killed pairs are read off the path.

Proof. (i) Holes are distinct because a queried hole kills every pair at it. Suppose two triggers share a row \(i\), at rounds \(m<m'\). At round \(m\) the rule queried the hole, so \(i\) had exactly one unkilled pair, \((i,x_m)\); killed pairs stay killed and no pair becomes unkilled, so \((i,x_{m'})\) was unkilled at round \(m\) as well, a contradiction. A trigger is the pinned pair of the round's first non-falsified term, whose tail is not falsified by \(\rho'\cup\pi\), hence not by \(\rho'\). (ii) At round \(m\) the decoder's assignment extends \(\rho'\cup\pi_{<m}\), agrees with it on pinned rows, and matches later moved light rows consistently with their own terms; the first non-falsified term is found as in the light lemma, its light rows by \(\beta\), and the rule's test uses only \(R'\cap\{\text{pinned rows}\}\), \(Q\), and the path. \(\square\)

Consequently, for a mixed reader, \(\Pr[\text{no short tree}]\le\Pr[\text{no term satisfied}\wedge\nu(B_{\rm t})\ge k_0]+\sum_{k<k_0}\binom sk A^{s-k}\bigl(2r(N+e+2)\bigr)^k+Mr\,e^{-e2^{-w-4}}\), and the whole difficulty sits in the first term.

2. The remaining bound, decomposed

Condition on \(Q\), \(R'\), and the labels of every light row that occurs in a tail; the pinned rows' matching is then a uniform bijection on the remaining rows and labels. Each tail class is satisfied, falsified, or alive (some residual tail row). (a) Satisfied classes behave as a unary reader: the dense-label lemma gives a satisfied term when at least \(\Delta_0\) labels have degree at least \(D^\ast\) within them, and the sparse and rank lemmas bound the matching number of their alive pairs, with \(R'\) restricted to the non-tail rows still uniform. (b) Alive classes with a matched pinned pair are harmless along a path: after the tail's residual rows are queried, a consistent answer satisfies the matched-pair terms, so the adversary answers inconsistently and the class dies; the only cost is that alive-pair terms of the class may precede its matched-pair terms in the fixed order, and since labels and rows are exchangeable, at most \(k\) such terms precede the first matched-pair term with probability about \(n\bigl((N+1)N/n\bigr)^k\). (c) Alive classes without a matched pair supply the genuinely heavy queries; a class with \(|P_\tau|\) pairs is unmatched with probability about \(e^{-|P_\tau|/n}\) and has \(|P_\tau|(N+1)N/n^2\) alive pairs in expectation, so the matching number of their union is bounded by the sparse lemma with per-label degrees counted over unmatched alive classes, and dense labels there are limited because a label of degree \(D\) over alive classes is the hole of a matched pair of one of them with probability about \(D/n\), leaving the other classes at that hole to a single hole query. The three parts must be assembled with the conditioning made uniform over paths; this is the next cycle's task, and it is expected to give \(\Pr[\text{no short tree}]\le2^{-\Omega(k_0)}+\mathrm{polylog}\cdot(N/n)^{2}\) for every polynomial source size.

Main-route assessment. The first obligation is unchanged. The mixed-term case is reduced to a tree rule whose heavy queries are a matching (proved) and a probabilistic bound decomposed into three parts, two of which are the unary lemmas verbatim; the remaining assembly is bounded work. Parity terms remain the open core.

Process assessment. The working context was consolidated this cycle (switching material condensed into one paragraph with record links); it still exceeds the soft target because the older fresh-block, weight-step, and source-audit paragraphs have not been revisited, which is a bounded editorial task for a later cycle. No framework change is needed, and no computation was run.

18 September 2026 — Matched-first preference: heavy queries come only from classes without a matched pinned pair, a candidate counterexample fails through the occupants of labels outside the flat, and the remaining step is a rank bound for survivor sets

Status: one working lemma (tree rule refinement, decoder-computable, with proof); one analyzed non-counterexample; the probabilistic assembly for mixed readers remains open with its last missing step named. Spin cycle 185. Produced by Claude Code (Claude Fable 5.1 (claude-fable-5-1), low reasoning effort).

Question and stopping point. The plan was to assemble the three-part bound for mixed readers. Part (b), alive classes with a matched pinned pair, had an order effect that the fixed term order could not control: alive-pair terms of such a class may precede its matched-pair terms and cost heavy queries, and a union bound over the path's light answers would have forced \(A\) far below what the light range allows. The stopping point is a rule that removes part (b) entirely, and the identification of the last probabilistic step through a reader that looked bad and is not.

1. The matched-first preference

Refine the adaptive rule: at a node, among the terms not falsified by \(\rho'\cup\pi\), take the earliest whose pinned pair is matched by \(\mu'\) if there is one, and otherwise the earliest term. The decoder can apply the same preference, since pinned rows are never moved and the matched status of a pinned pair is read off the code.

Lemma. Under the preference, a heavy query at a round is triggered by the pinned pair of a term whose class (its tail) contains no term with a matched pinned pair; consequently the number of heavy queries on a path is at most \(\nu(B_{\rm um})\), the matching number of the alive pairs of classes without a matched pair whose tail is not falsified by \(\rho'\).

Proof. Suppose the round's term \(T\) has an alive pinned pair and its class \(\tau\) contains a term \(T'\) with a matched pinned pair. By the preference, \(T'\) is falsified by \(\rho'\cup\pi\); its pinned part is satisfied, so its tail \(\tau\) is falsified by \(\rho'\cup\pi\), and then \(T\), with the same tail, is falsified too, a contradiction. The distinctness of rows and holes among triggers is as in the adaptive-rule lemma. \(\square\)

So along any path, an alive class that has a matched pair is decided by its tail alone: its residual tail rows are light queries, a consistent answer produces a 1-leaf at the matched-pair term, and an inconsistent answer kills the class. Part (b) of the decomposition disappears, and the bound needed is \(\Pr[\nu(B_{\rm um})\ge k_0]\).

2. A candidate counterexample and why it fails

Fix a row \(j\) and, for every label \(x\), a distinct light pattern \(p_x\) on row \(j\); let \(F^{(j)}=\bigvee_x\bigvee_{i}[i\mapsto x]\wedge[j\text{ satisfies }p_x]\), a reader of \(n(n+1)\) mixed terms, one class per label. With probability \((N+1)/(n+1)\) row \(j\) is residual, every class is alive, no term is satisfied, and the classes whose label lies in \(Q\) are unmatched with all \(N+1\) residual rows alive at that label, so \(\nu(B_{\rm um})=N\); the \(n+1\) readers \(F^{(j)}\), of total size \(n^3\), always contain one in this situation. This looked like a refutation at size \(n^3\). It is not: every class whose label \(x\) lies outside \(Q\) is matched, because the occupant of \(x\) is pinned to \(x\), so after the tail query \(j\mapsto z\) every class with \(z\in C(p_x)\) and \(x\notin Q\) gives a 1-leaf under the preference. The adversary must answer with a \(z\) all of whose surviving classes have labels in \(Q\); if the patterns are designed so that the survivors of \(z\) are the \(k_0\) labels sharing a prefix with \(z\), this needs those labels inside \(Q\), which happens with probability about \((N/n)^{\log_2k_0+1}\) per prefix class by the rank lemma, so over the \(n/k_0\) prefix classes with probability at most \(n(N/n)^{\log_2k_0+1}\). Two lessons: alive pairs must always be weighed against the matched pairs of the same class, and the last probabilistic step is a rank bound for survivor sets, the labels of the classes kept alive by one light answer, all of which must fall inside the flat.

3. What remains for mixed readers

With the preference, \(\Pr[\text{bad}]\le\Pr[\nu(B_{\rm um})\ge k_0]+\text{(encoding terms)}\). A matching in \(B_{\rm um}\) consists of alive pairs \((i_m,x_m)\) of unmatched classes with tails not falsified; for each such class the label side must be handled through the flat: a class with label set \(L_\tau\) (labels of its pairs) is unmatched only if no label of \(L_\tau\setminus Q\) is occupied by a row pinned to it, which for classes pinned to all rows means \(L_\tau\subseteq Q\), and in general has probability at most \(\exp(-|P_\tau\setminus(\cdot\times Q)|/n)\); so the labels of the matching's classes are forced into \(Q\) or the classes are sparse, and the sparse lemma and the rank lemma apply to these two kinds. The assembly, with the conditioning on the tail rows' labels and the case that many rows occur in tails, is the remaining work; it is bounded and uses no new idea.

Main-route assessment. The first obligation is unchanged. For mixed readers the tree is now fixed (light rows, matched-first preference, adaptive heavy query) and the bound is reduced to the unmatched-class matching number, with the sparse and rank lemmas as the tools; the remaining assembly is technical. Parity terms remain the open core.

Process assessment. The candidate counterexample was checked against the matched classes before being written up as a refutation, which is the same check that caught the previous constructions and should be the first check for any reader family in this route; no framework change is needed, and no computation was run.

18 September 2026 — The window's height budget is a constant fraction of the board, the trivial heavy-query count already gives height \(O(N)\), and rows that are pinned in one term and light in another need a recording rule in the decoder

Status: one working observation with proof (budget and trivial bound); two corrections with fixes (the order of the separate-terms corollary of the unary entry, and part (ii) of the adaptive-rule lemma); the mixed-reader bound remains open with a sharpened statement and a named failed route. Spin cycle 186. Produced by Claude Code (Claude Fable 5.1 (claude-fable-5-1), low reasoning effort).

Question and stopping point. The plan was to bound \(\Pr[\nu(B_{\rm um})\ge k_0]\). Before assembling it, this cycle asked what tree height the goal needs, since the window entries never stated a budget and the unary theorem's \(O(\log S+2^c)\) may be a convenience. The stopping point is the budget, its consequence for the obligation, and a check of the decoder claims on which the mixed-term tree rests.

1. What suffices: height a constant fraction of \(N\)

After switching, every reader is a matching decision tree of height \(s\) whose image has companions through \(r+s\) and Booleanity through \(2s\), and the argument continues with the weight step on the compact board of \(N\) labels. There the cube-volume multiplier range is \(k'=\lfloor(N/4-D')/(2D'+1)\rfloor\) with \(D'\) at least the image degrees (PT-choice on the board of \(N\) labels, multiplier space), so the residual step needs \(2s+r\le N/4\) and nothing smaller: height at most \(N/8-r\) suffices, and any bound \(o(N)\) is a convenience. \(N\) is a free polylogarithmic parameter, since the light range, the heavy dichotomy, the sparse and rank lemmas lose only polylogarithmic factors in \(N\); it may be taken as a large constant multiple of \(r_{\rm high}+c\log n\).

Observation (trivial heavy count). On any path of the canonical tree with the adaptive rule, the heavy queries number at most \(2N+1\): every heavy query is a pigeon query at a residual row or a hole query at a hole of \(Q\), and no row or hole is queried twice. Hence, recording each heavy answer in \(\delta\) (at most \(N+e+2\) values) and the interleaving pattern, \(\Pr[\text{height}\ge s+2N+1]\le\sum_{k\le2N+1}\binom{s+k}{k}A^{s}\bigl(2r(N+e+2)\bigr)^{k}+Mr\,e^{-e2^{-w-4}}\), which is at most \(n^{-c}/8\) once \(s\ge3c+2N+1+o(N)\) (the heavy factor is \(n^{(2N+1)/3+o(N)}\) against \(A^s=n^{-s/3+o(s)}\)). So every literal reader of the window already switches at every polynomial size with height \(4N+3c+O(1)+o(N)\), and the open obligation is a constant-factor one: heavy queries at most \(N/24-c\), which with \(s=2k+3c\) light queries gives height at most \(N/8\). A heavy hole query's answer needs only \(N+2\) values (a row residual in the decoder's current assignment, or the empty branch), so hole queries are polylogarithmically cheap; pigeon queries cost \(N+e+1\).

2. Correction: rows with two roles, and the recording rule

The decoder of the light lemma sees the code restriction \(\rho^\ast\), whose matched rows include the light rows moved in later rounds; a row residual under \(\rho'\) that is light in a later term therefore appears matched, at a label outside \(Q\) consistent with that later term's pattern but in general not with a wide pattern the same row carries elsewhere. Two recorded claims assumed that pinned rows are visible to the decoder.

(a) The corollary on separate light and unary terms queried the vertex cover of the alive graph \(B(\rho')\) first, "recovered by the decoder because pinned rows are never moved". If a pinned row of a unary term is a light row of a light term, the decoder computes \(B(\rho^\ast)\), which lacks the pairs at later-moved rows, and may choose a different cover. Fix: reverse the order. Run the canonical tree of the light part first; at each of its 0-leaves, with light answers \(\pi\), query a minimum vertex cover of \(B(\rho'\cup\pi)\subseteq B(\rho')\). The light part's encoding is the light lemma's, unchanged, and the unary part is bounded probabilistically by \(\nu(B(\rho'))\) with no decoding, so the corollary holds as stated with height \(s+\nu(B)\). The claim index is annotated.

(b) Part (ii) of the adaptive-rule lemma claimed the decoder recomputes the rule "because pinned rows are never moved". At a heavy round the current term's pinned row \(i\) is residual and, after a hole query answered by another row or by the empty branch, stays unassigned; if a later round moves \(i\) as a light row, the decoder sees the term falsified at round \(m\) and identifies a later term, possibly with a different hole. Fix (recording rule): a light query at a row that was the pinned row of an earlier heavy round of the same path is recorded in \(\delta\) (at most \(N+e\) values) instead of moved, and \(\beta\) marks it. Each heavy round has one pinned row and a row is light-queried at most once, so at most one recorded light query per heavy query; in the code such a row stays residual, the decoder's current assignment agrees with \(\rho'\cup\pi_{matched-first preference are unaffected; the pure unary theorem has no light rows and is unaffected.

3. The sharpened obligation and a route that does not work

By Section 1 with the recording rule, it remains to show: with probability at least \(1-n^{-c}/8\) per reader, no path has \(k\ge N/24-c\) heavy queries together with at most \(3k+3c\) light queries (paths with more light queries are paid by the encoding). On such a path the \(k\) triggers are alive pairs \((i_t,x_t)\), with distinct rows and distinct holes, of classes without a matched pair whose tails are satisfied by \(\rho'\cup\pi\), and every class with a matched pair is falsified by \(\rho'\cup\pi\). The naive route enumerates the light answers: given \(\rho'\), a path's light answers are at most \(3k+3c\) holes among \(N+e\), a union of size \(n^{k+c+o(k)}\), against which the rank mechanism supplies only \(\Pr[k\text{ labels of one survivor set lie in }Q]\le(N^2/n)^{\log_2k+1}\), superpolynomially but not exponentially small in \(k\). The two do not combine for any \(k\ge2\); the reader \(F^{(j)}\) of the previous entry is harmless only because its paths have one light answer, so the union has \(n\) members. Hence the assembly cannot enumerate light answers; it must charge each light answer to the survivor set it keeps alive, and the quantity to bound is the affine rank in \(Q\) of the holes of surviving unmatched classes accumulated over at most \(3k+3c\) answers, with each answer's survivors weighed against the matched classes it also keeps alive. This is the open step; no part of it is proved here.

Main-route assessment. The first obligation is unchanged. On the literal frontier the target is now correctly sized: trees of height \(N/8\) suffice, height \(6N+3c\) is already proved for every literal reader at every polynomial size by the trivial count, and the mixed-reader obligation is a constant-factor improvement of the heavy count, not an \(O(\log S)\) bound. Two decoder claims were corrected with fixes that do not change any parameter regime. Parity terms remain the open core.

Process assessment. Three cycles refined a target (\(O(\log S+2^c)\)) that the goal never required because the window entries stated no height budget; the budget now stands in the working context, and the rule "select a sufficient endpoint before proof-conversion steps" was the one not applied. No framework change beyond the notebook is needed, and no computation was run.

18 September 2026 — Trigger-eligibility comparison: an alive unmatched class is at most \(45(N+1)^2\ln n/n\) times as likely as a matched one, an alive unsatisfied tail at most \(r2^wN/n\) times as likely as a satisfied one, and the expected number of eligible classes is bounded by that of satisfied terms

Status: two working lemmas with full proofs (pair-side and tail-side comparisons, random-flat family), one working corollary in expectation; the constant-factor heavy bound for mixed readers remains open, with the obstacle to the natural conditioning named. Spin cycle 187. Produced by Claude Code (Claude Fable 5.1 (claude-fable-5-1), low reasoning effort).

Question and stopping point. The sharpened obligation asks for at most \(N/24\) heavy queries on paths with few light answers. A trigger is an alive pair of a class without a matched pair whose tail is satisfied by \(\rho'\cup\pi\); a satisfied term is a matched pair whose tail is satisfied by \(\rho'\). The per-term rarity of the window entry compared single terms; the tree works with classes, whose pair sets can be large, so the comparison must hold for a class's whole pair set. The stopping point is a class-level comparison on the pair side and on the tail side, and what it gives in expectation.

1. Lemma: alive and unmatched against matched, for any pair set

Fix a set \(P\) of pairs \((i,x)\) (rows \([n+1]\), labels \(\{0,1\}^\ell\)). Under uniform \(\rho'=(Q,R',\mu')\) in the random-flat family let \(M=\{\exists(i,x)\in P:\ i\notin R',\ \mu'(i)=x\}\) (a pair of \(P\) is matched) and \(A=\{\exists(i,x)\in P:\ i\in R',\ x\in Q\}\) (a pair of \(P\) is alive). Assume \(n\ge16(N+1)\).

Lemma. \(\Pr[A\wedge\neg M]\le\theta\Pr[M]\) with \(\theta=45(N+1)^2\ln n/n\).

Proof. Write \(m=|P|\) and, given \((Q,R')\), \(P_{\rm m}=P\cap(R'^{c}\times Q^{c})\) for the matchable pairs; \(\mu'\) is then a uniform bijection of the \(n-N\) matched rows onto \(Q^c\), and \(M\) is the event that some pair of \(P_{\rm m}\) is realized. Two conditional estimates: by inclusion–exclusion over the pairs of \(P_{\rm m}\) (two compatible pairs are realized together with probability \(1/((n-N)(n-N-1))\), incompatible ones never), \(\Pr[M\mid Q,R']\ge|P_{\rm m}|/(2(n-N))\) whenever \(|P_{\rm m}|\le n-N-1\), and by monotonicity in the pair set \(\Pr[M\mid Q,R']\ge1/2-1/(2(n-N))\ge1/5\) whenever \(|P_{\rm m}|\ge n-N-1\); and by negative association of the entries of a uniform permutation matrix (Joag-Dev and Proschan, imported as in the dense-label lemma), applied to the decreasing events "entry \(e\) is zero" on the distinct coordinates \(e\in P_{\rm m}\), \(\Pr[\neg M\mid Q,R']\le(1-1/(n-N))^{|P_{\rm m}|}\le e^{-|P_{\rm m}|/(n-N)}\). Since \(R'\) and \(Q\) are independent, \(\Pr[i\in R',x\in Q]=(N+1)N/((n+1)n)\) and \(\Pr[i\notin R',x\notin Q]\ge1/2\), so \(\Pr[A]\le m(N+1)N/(n(n+1))\) and \(\mathbb E|P_{\rm m}|\ge m/2\).

(i) \(m\le n-N\). Then \(|P_{\rm m}|\le n-N\) always; dropping one pair if necessary, \(\Pr[M]\ge\mathbb E[|P_{\rm m}|-1]/(2(n-N))\ge m/(5(n-N))\), while \(\Pr[A\wedge\neg M]\le\Pr[A]\le m(N+1)N/(n(n+1))\); the ratio is at most \(5(N+1)N/n\).

(ii) \(n-N

(iii) \(m>4(n-N)\ln n\). Let \(H_R\) be the rows of \(P\)-degree at least \(m/(4(N+1))\) and \(H_Q\) the labels of degree at least \(m/(4N)\); \(|H_R|\le4(N+1)\) and \(|H_Q|\le4N\). If \(R'\cap H_R=\emptyset\) and \(Q\cap H_Q=\emptyset\) then fewer than \(m/4\) pairs have a row in \(R'\) and fewer than \(m/4\) a label in \(Q\), so \(|P_{\rm m}|>m/2\ge2(n-N)\ln n\) and \(\Pr[\neg M\mid Q,R']\le n^{-2}\). Hence \(\Pr[A\wedge\neg M]\le\Pr[R'\cap H_R\ne\emptyset]+\Pr[Q\cap H_Q\ne\emptyset]+n^{-2}\le4(N+1)^2/(n+1)+4N^2/n+n^{-2}\le9(N+1)^2/n\), while \(\Pr[M]\ge1/5\); the ratio is at most \(45(N+1)^2/n\). \(\square\)

The lemma is sharp up to the logarithm: for a single pair both sides are exact with ratio \((N+1)N/n\); for all pairs at one label the ratio is \(N/n\). No structure of \(P\) is assumed, and the affine structure of \(Q\) is not used, only \(\Pr[x\in Q]=N/n\) and the independence of \(R'\) and \(Q\).

2. Lemma: an alive unsatisfied tail against a satisfied one

Let \(\tau\) be a tail with rows \(J\), \(|J|\le r-1\), and patterns \(p_j\) of at most \(w\) literals, and let \(S_\tau\) (satisfied by \(\rho'\): every row of \(J\) matched consistently) and \(N_\tau\) (not falsified by \(\rho'\): every matched row of \(J\) consistent) be as before. Assume \(2^{w}(N+r)\le n/8\).

Lemma. \(\Pr[N_\tau\wedge\neg S_\tau]\le\varepsilon_w\Pr[S_\tau]\) with \(\varepsilon_w=2(r-1)2^{w}(N+1)/n\), and the same holds conditionally on any event determined by the rows outside \(J\) and by \(Q\) (up to replacing \(n\) by \(n-r\) in the constant).

Proof. Given \(Q\) and \(J\cap R'=\emptyset\), the labels \(\mu'(J)\) form a uniform injection into \(Q^c\), so \(\Pr[S_\tau\mid Q,J\cap R'=\emptyset]\ge\prod_{j\in J}(|C(p_j)|-N-r)/(n-N)\ge\prod_j2^{-|p_j|}(1-2^{w}(N+r)/n)^{r}\), and \(\Pr[J\cap R'=\emptyset]\ge1-(r-1)(N+1)/(n+1)\). On \(N_\tau\wedge\neg S_\tau\) some \(j\in J\) is residual and the other rows are matched consistently; for a fixed \(j\), the consistency of the others has conditional probability at most \(\prod_{j'\ne j}|C(p_{j'})|/(n-N-r)\le\prod_{j'\ne j}2^{-|p_{j'}|}(1+2(N+r)/n)\), and \(\Pr[j\in R']=(N+1)/(n+1)\). Summing over \(j\) and comparing, the ratio is at most \((N+1)/(n+1)\sum_j2^{|p_j|}\) times \((1+o(1))\), at most \(\varepsilon_w\). Conditioning on the rows outside \(J\) and on \(Q\) leaves \(\mu'(J)\) a uniform injection into the remaining labels and \(R'\cap J\) a hypergeometric set, and the same computation applies. \(\square\)

With \(2^w\le e/(64s)\) and \(e=\lfloor(n/48r)^{1/3}\rfloor\), \(\varepsilon_w\le rN\,n^{-2/3}\): an alive tail is almost always alive because a tail row is residual, not because a matched row happens to be consistent, and such tails are \(n^{2/3}/(rN)\) times rarer than satisfied ones.

3. Corollary: eligible classes against satisfied terms, in expectation

For a class \(\tau\) with pair set \(P_\tau\) (rows disjoint from \(J_\tau\) after the normalization of the adaptive-rule entry) call \(\tau\) \(\rho'\)-eligible if \(A_\tau\wedge\neg M_\tau\wedge S_\tau\), \(\pi\)-eligible if \(A_\tau\wedge\neg M_\tau\wedge N_\tau\wedge\neg S_\tau\), and satisfied if \(M_\tau\wedge S_\tau\) (some term of the class is satisfied by \(\rho'\)). Every trigger of a path is the pair of a \(\rho'\)-eligible or \(\pi\)-eligible class.

Corollary. \(\Pr[\tau\ \rho'\text{-eligible}]\le\theta'\Pr[\tau\text{ satisfied}]\) and \(\Pr[\tau\ \pi\text{-eligible}]\le\theta'\varepsilon_w\Pr[\tau\text{ satisfied}]\), with \(\theta'=\theta(1+o(1))\); hence, for any reader, the expected number of eligible classes is at most \(\theta'(1+\varepsilon_w)\) times the expected number of satisfied classes.

Proof. Condition on the exposure \(E_J\) of the tail rows: \(R'\cap J_\tau\) and \(\mu'\) on \(J_\tau\setminus R'\). Given \(E_J\), the pairs of \(P_\tau\) live on the other rows, where \(R'\) is a uniform set of the remaining size, \(Q\) is a uniform flat avoiding at most \(r-1\) labels, and \(\mu'\) is a uniform bijection; Section 1 applies to this family with \(n\) replaced by \(n-r\) and \(\Pr[x\in Q]\le(N/n)(1+rN/n)\), so \(\Pr[A_\tau\wedge\neg M_\tau\mid E_J]\le\theta'\Pr[M_\tau\mid E_J]\). Since \(S_\tau\) and \(N_\tau\) are determined by \(E_J\), \(\Pr[A\wedge\neg M\wedge S]=\mathbb E[1_S\Pr[A\wedge\neg M\mid E_J]]\le\theta'\Pr[M\wedge S]\), and likewise \(\Pr[A\wedge\neg M\wedge N\wedge\neg S]\le\theta'\Pr[M\wedge N\wedge\neg S]\le\theta'\varepsilon_w\Pr[M\wedge S]\) by Section 2 conditioned on the pair rows and \(Q\). Sum over classes. \(\square\)

4. What the corollary does not give, and why the natural conditioning fails

The bad event needs \(k\ge N/24-c\) eligible classes with alive pairs at distinct holes and no satisfied class. In expectation eligible classes are \(\theta'\approx N^2\ln n/n\) times rarer than satisfied ones, so if the classes' events were independent the bound \(\min_\mu(e^{-\mu},(\theta'\mu)^k/k!)\le(e\theta')^{k}\) would follow. They are not: the reader \(F^{(j)}\) of the matched-first entry has all its satisfied and eligible events correlated through one tail row, and there the bad event is excluded by the survivor-rank mechanism, not by expectations. The natural repair, conditioning on the fates of all tail rows and applying the unary theorem to the pairs of the classes with satisfied tails, is not available: \(Q\) is the complement of \(\mu'\)'s image, so conditioning on \(\mu'\) at all tail rows of a reader, which may be every row, determines \(Q\) and destroys the rank lemma. Only a limited exposure can be used, and which rows to expose depends on the path. The correct organization, suggested by \(F^{(j)}\), is by rows: for every assigned row \(j\), all classes with a tail on \(j\) consistent with its label are unmatched, and a row whose consistent classes have labels of affine rank \(d\) outside \(Q\) forces \(d+1\) points into \(Q\). Turning this into a bound over all rows at once, with the bijection's dependence between rows, is the open step.

Main-route assessment. The first obligation is unchanged. The mixed-reader obligation now has its class-level comparison lemmas, which are the correct replacement for the per-term rarity and hold for arbitrary pair sets; the remaining step is a correlation argument organized by rows, and the reason the obvious conditioning fails is recorded. Parity terms remain the open core.

Process assessment. The cycle first tried an exposure argument and found that it pins the flat, which the earlier entries never stated as a constraint; it is now recorded so that later cycles do not retry it. No framework change is needed, and no computation was run.

18 September 2026 — Mixed readers with single-row tails on distinct rows and full classes switch at every polynomial size: negative association forces a satisfied term when the labels are many, and affine rank bounds the trigger holes when they are few

Status: working theorem with full proof for a named subclass of mixed readers (random-flat family, hole-query trees); the two mechanisms that the general case must combine, shared tail rows and non-full pair sets, are identified with the reason each is excluded here. Spin cycle 188. Produced by Claude Code (Claude Fable 5.1 (claude-fable-5-1), low reasoning effort).

Question and stopping point. The row-organized argument of the previous entry was to be carried out. It closes cleanly when the tails of different classes lie on different rows, where negative association applies, and when every class pins all rows to one label, where a class is unmatched exactly when its label lies in the flat. The stopping point is the theorem for this subclass, and the exact point where each hypothesis is used.

1. The subclass

A class is a triple \(\tau=(j_\tau,p_\tau,x_\tau)\): a tail row, a light pattern (at most \(w\) literals) on it, and a label; its terms are \([i\mapsto x_\tau]\wedge[\text{row }j_\tau\text{ satisfies }p_\tau]\) for every row \(i\ne j_\tau\) (a full class). A reader \(F\) of this kind is a set of classes with pairwise distinct tail rows; labels may repeat. Let \(X=\{x_\tau\}\) be its label set. The tree is the canonical tree with the adaptive rule, the matched-first preference and the recording rule; \(\rho'\) is uniform in the random-flat family, \(2^w\le n^{1/3}\), and \(n\) is large.

Two facts used below. Under \(\rho'\), a class with \(x_\tau\notin Q\) is matched unless the occupant of \(x_\tau\) is \(j_\tau\) itself, and a class with \(x_\tau\in Q\) is unmatched. A heavy query is triggered by an alive pair \((i,x_\tau)\) of an unmatched class, so its hole is \(x_\tau\in X\cap Q\); heavy queries have distinct holes, hence their number on any path is at most \(|X\cap Q|\).

2. Theorem

Theorem. For \(F\) as above and \(k\ge2^{2c+2}\), the probability that some path of the tree has at least \(k\) heavy queries and no 1-leaf before them is at most \(n^{-c-1}+n^{-2c-2}\). Consequently every such reader of a source of size \(n^c\) switches with at most \(2^{2c+2}\) heavy queries and, by the encoding with the recording rule, height \(O(c\log n+2^{2c})\), under one restriction with probability at least \(3/4\).

Proof. Put \(m_w=N+8(c+1)2^{w}\ln n\).

Case A: \(|X|\ge m_w\). Given \(Q\), at least \(|X|-N\ge8(c+1)2^w\ln n\) labels of \(X\) lie outside \(Q\); pick one class \(\tau_x\) for each such label \(x\). The pair \((R',\mu')\) is a uniform bijection of the rows onto \(Q^c\) together with \(N+1\) residual slots, whose indicator matrix is negatively associated (Joag-Dev and Proschan, imported as before). For each chosen class the event \(E_x\) that row \(j_{\tau_x}\) is sent into \(C(p_{\tau_x})\setminus(Q\cup\{x\})\) is increasing in the entries of that row, the rows are distinct, and \(\Pr[E_x\mid Q]\ge(n2^{-w}-N-1)/(n+1)\ge2^{-w}/3\). On \(E_x\) the class \(\tau_x\) has a satisfied tail and is matched (its label is outside \(Q\) and its occupant is not \(j_{\tau_x}\)), so a term is satisfied and the tree is a 1-leaf. Hence \(\Pr[\text{no term satisfied}\mid Q]\le\prod_x(1-2^{-w}/3)\le\exp(-8(c+1)\ln n/3)\le n^{-2c-2}\).

Case B: \(|X| Then \(|X|\le9(c+1)2^w\ln n\). By the rank lemma in its independent-points form, \(\Pr[|X\cap Q|\ge k]\le|X|^{d+1}(N/n)^{d+1}\) with \(d=\lceil\log_2k\rceil\), because \(k\) points of a flat have affine rank at least \(d\) and \(d+1\) affinely independent points of \(X\) lie in \(Q\) with probability at most \((N/n)^{d+1}\). With \(2^w\le n^{1/3}\) this is at most \((9(c+1)N\ln n\,n^{-2/3})^{d+1}\le n^{-c-1}\) once \(d+1\ge\tfrac32(c+1)+1\), which \(k\ge2^{2c+2}\) gives for large \(n\). Outside this event every path has fewer than \(k\) heavy queries. \(\square\)

The rank lemma is used in the form that counts only \(d+1\) independent points, not all \(k\)-subsets; the form recorded in the unary entry has the factor \(|D|^{k_2}\), which would not suffice here.

3. Where each hypothesis enters, and what the general case must add

Distinct tail rows make the satisfaction events of different classes depend on disjoint rows, which is what negative association needs. With a shared tail row the events are positively correlated through that row: the reader \(F^{(j)}\) of the matched-first entry has \(|X|=n\) and no satisfied term whenever \(j\) is residual, and its harmlessness comes from the survivor sets of the answers at \(j\), each a fixed set that must lie in \(Q\). The general single-row case therefore needs, per row, the survivor-rank bound, and across rows the product bound of Case A restricted to the rows that host a class with a label outside the flat; the two are compatible, since the rows are disjoint, but the count of rows carrying triggers through answered rows must be charged to the light budget, and this bookkeeping is not done here.

Full classes make "unmatched" equivalent to "label in \(Q\)". For a general pair set the comparison lemma replaces this equivalence in expectation, and a class contributes at most one heavy query per label of a vertex cover of its alive pairs; the general case must combine the lemma's factor \(\theta\) with the rank of the trigger holes, which are no longer the classes' labels.

Multi-row tails add the mixed case where some tail rows are matched and some residual; by the tail comparison this is \(rN\,n^{-2/3}\) times rarer than the fully matched case per class, so it changes Case A only by a constant, but the per-row survivor structure becomes a per-class condition.

Main-route assessment. The first obligation is unchanged. On the literal frontier a second class of mixed readers now switches at every polynomial size with \(O(1)\) heavy queries; the two remaining mechanisms for the general window obligation are named with the exact hypotheses that remove them. Parity terms remain the open core.

Process assessment. The cycle reached a theorem by restricting to the hypotheses under which the two available tools apply, instead of attempting the general assembly again; this is the restricted-case testing that the task-selection guidance asks for. No framework change is needed, and no computation was run.

18 September 2026 — Shared tail rows: the loading of a reader controls both mechanisms, bounded loading gives switching with polylogarithmic heavy queries, and out-loading forces a satisfied term

Status: one working theorem with full proof (single-row full classes on arbitrary, possibly shared, rows under a loading hypothesis) and one working lemma (out-loading forces satisfaction); the gap between them, readers of large loading whose loading outside the flat is small, is stated exactly. Spin cycle 189. Produced by Claude Code (Claude Fable 5.1 (claude-fable-5-1), low reasoning effort).

Question and stopping point. The distinct-rows hypothesis of the previous theorem was to be removed. The right parameter turns out to be the loading of a row, the fraction of labels consistent with some class on it: negative association still applies row by row, and a row's answers are controlled by the survivor sets of its labels, whatever the number of classes on it. The stopping point is a theorem under a loading bound, a lemma showing what unbounded loading forces, and the exact residual case.

1. Loading

Classes are as in the previous entry (full, single-row light tails), but several classes may share a tail row; classes on a row have distinct patterns. For a row \(j\) let \(U_j=\bigcup_{\tau:j_\tau=j}C(p_\tau)\) and \(f_j=|U_j|/n\) (the loading of \(j\)); \(\Lambda(F)=\sum_jf_j\) is the loading of the reader, \(J_F\) the set of rows hosting a class, and \(L_j(z)=\{x_\tau:\ j_\tau=j,\ z\in C(p_\tau)\}\) the survivor set of a label \(z\) at row \(j\). Since \(|C(p)|\ge n2^{-w}\), \(f_j\ge2^{-w}\) for \(j\in J_F\), so \(|J_F|\le2^w\Lambda(F)\).

Two facts. If row \(j\) is assigned a label \(z\) by \(\rho'\cup\pi\) on a path with no 1-leaf, then \(L_j(z)\setminus\{z\}\subseteq Q\): a class on \(j\) consistent with \(z\) whose label lies outside \(Q\) is matched (its occupant is not \(j\) when \(z\ne x_\tau\)) with a satisfied tail, so its term is satisfied if \(j\) is matched and its class is preferred and yields a 1-leaf if \(j\) is residual. The trigger holes of the path are contained in \(\bigcup_j(L_j(z_j)\cap Q)\) over assigned rows, and heavy queries have distinct holes.

2. Theorem: bounded loading

Theorem. Let \(F\) be as above with \(\Lambda(F)\le\lambda_0\), \(2^w\le n^{1/3}\), and \(n\) large. Put \(m=2c+2\), \(k'=\max(4e\lambda_0,(c+1)\log_2n)\), \(k''=2^{c+3}\). Then with probability at least \(1-3n^{-c-1}\), every path of the tree has fewer than \((m+k')k''\) heavy queries before any 1-leaf. In particular such readers of a source of size \(n^c\) switch with \(O((\lambda_0+c\log n)2^{c})\) heavy queries, within the height budget once \(N\) exceeds a constant multiple of this.

Proof. (i) Few residual hosting rows. \(|R'\cap J_F|\) is hypergeometric with \(|J_F|\le2^w\lambda_0\), so \(\Pr[|R'\cap J_F|\ge m]\le\binom{|J_F|}{m}\bigl(\tfrac{N+1}{n+1-m}\bigr)^m\le(2\lambda_0Nn^{-2/3})^m\le n^{-c-1}\).

(ii) Few matched loaded rows. Given \(Q\), the pair \((R',\mu')\) is a uniform bijection of the rows onto \(Q^c\) and \(N+1\) residual slots, negatively associated. For \(j\in J_F\) the event that \(j\) is matched into \(U_j\) is increasing in the entries of row \(j\) and has probability at most \(|U_j|/(n-N)\le2f_j\); for distinct rows these events are on disjoint coordinates, so \(\Pr[\text{all rows of }T\text{ loaded}]\le\prod_{j\in T}2f_j\) and \(\Pr[\ge k'\text{ matched loaded rows}]\le\sum_{|T|=k'}\prod_{j\in T}2f_j\le(2\lambda_0)^{k'}/k'!\le(2e\lambda_0/k')^{k'}\le2^{-k'}\le n^{-c-1}\).

(iii) Few survivors per assigned row. The sets \(L_j(z)\setminus\{z\}\) are fixed by the reader. If one of them has at least \(k''\) elements and lies in \(Q\), then \(Q\) contains \(d+1=\lceil\log_2k''\rceil+1\) affinely independent points of it, an event of probability at most \((N/n)^{d+1}\); over the \(n(n+1)\) pairs \((j,z)\), \(\Pr[\exists(j,z):\ |L_j(z)\setminus\{z\}|\ge k'',\ L_j(z)\setminus\{z\}\subseteq Q]\le n^2(N/n)^{c+4}\le n^{-c-1}\).

Outside these three events, on a path with no 1-leaf every assigned row \(j\) has \(L_j(z_j)\setminus\{z_j\}\subseteq Q\), hence fewer than \(k''\) trigger holes; a row contributes trigger holes only if it hosts a class, and such rows are either residual (fewer than \(m\)) or matched and loaded (fewer than \(k'\)). So the trigger holes number fewer than \((m+k')k''\). \(\square\)

No satisfied term is needed in this theorem: bounded loading alone bounds the heavy queries, through the scarcity of hosting rows among the residual ones and of loaded rows among the matched ones. The distinct-rows theorem is not implied (its readers may have \(\Lambda(F)\) up to \(n\)); the two overlap on readers with few classes.

3. Lemma: loading outside the flat forces a satisfied term

For a row \(j\) and a flat \(Q\) let \(U^{\rm out}_j(Q)=\bigcup\{C(p_\tau)\setminus\{x_\tau\}:\ j_\tau=j,\ x_\tau\notin Q\}\), the labels consistent with a class of \(j\) whose label is outside the flat.

Lemma. \(\Pr[\text{no term of }F\text{ satisfied}\mid Q]\le\exp\bigl(-\sum_{j}|U^{\rm out}_j(Q)\setminus Q|/(n+1)\bigr)\).

Proof. If row \(j\) is matched into \(U^{\rm out}_j(Q)\setminus Q\), a class on \(j\) with label outside \(Q\) has a satisfied tail and an occupant other than \(j\), so a term is satisfied. These events are increasing in disjoint rows, each of probability \(|U^{\rm out}_j(Q)\setminus Q|/(n+1)\) (a uniform bijection onto \(Q^c\) and \(N+1\) slots), and negative association gives the product bound. \(\square\)

Hence a bad reader satisfies \(\sum_j|U^{\rm out}_j(Q)\setminus Q|\le(c+1)(n+1)\ln n\) outside probability \(n^{-c-1}\): its loading outside the flat is at most \((c+1)\ln n+o(1)\) even when \(\Lambda(F)\) is large. Since \(Q\) has \(N\) labels, this means that all but \((c+1)\ln n\) of the loading is carried by classes whose labels lie in \(Q\) or whose consistent sets are covered by those classes.

4. The residual case

What remains for single-row full classes is a reader with \(\Lambda(F)>\lambda_0\) whose loading outside \(Q\) is below \((c+1)\ln n\). Its rows split into those whose union is covered, up to \((c+1)\ln n\) in total, by the consistent sets of classes with labels in \(Q\). If every row's dominant classes (those whose consistent sets cover half its union) have at most \(\rho\) distinct labels and the set \(X_{\rm dom}\) of all dominant labels has at most \(n^{2/3}\) elements, the rank lemma bounds \(|X_{\rm dom}\cap Q|\) by \(2^{c+2}\), each such label dominates at most \(\rho'\) rows by a degree hypothesis, and the remaining loading is outside the flat; the theorem of Section 2 then applies to the rest. The general case has no such degree hypothesis: one label may dominate every row, and a row's union may be covered by many classes with overlapping consistent sets (nested patterns give multiplicity \(\binom{\ell-w+t}{t}\) on a union only \(2^t\) times a single pattern), so the loading carried by labels in \(Q\) need not be small. This is the open step for single-row full classes; non-full classes and multi-row tails remain as before.

Main-route assessment. The first obligation is unchanged. For mixed readers the window obligation is now settled for two overlapping subclasses, distinct tail rows and bounded loading, by two different mechanisms, and the residual single-row case is reduced to the interaction of loading with the flat's labels. Parity terms remain the open core.

Process assessment. Identifying the loading as the parameter took most of the cycle, after a false start on unions over answer sequences that the sharpened obligation had already ruled out; the working context now names the parameter so the next cycle starts from it. No framework change is needed, and no computation was run.

18 September 2026 — For full classes the trigger holes are labels of the reader inside the flat, so single-row full-class readers with at most \(n^{2/3}\) labels switch outright, and the residual case is a reader with many labels whose out-classes sit on few rows

Status: one working observation with corollary (label-set bound, full proof), one working reduction lemma (many out-rows force a satisfied term), and a sharpened statement of the residual case with its two remaining estimates. Spin cycle 190. Produced by Claude Code (Claude Fable 5.1 (claude-fable-5-1), low reasoning effort).

Question and stopping point. The residual case of the previous entry was to be closed. A simpler observation reorganizes it: for full classes every trigger hole is a label of the reader that lies in the flat, so the affine-rank lemma settles readers with few labels, and the loading matters only for readers with many labels, where the out-loading lemma forces the out-classes onto few rows. The stopping point is this reduction, with the residual case and its two estimates stated exactly.

1. Trigger holes are labels in the flat

Let \(F\) be a single-row full-class reader with label set \(X=\{x_\tau\}\). A heavy query is triggered by an alive pair \((i,x_\tau)\), whose hole is \(x_\tau\in Q\); heavy queries have distinct holes. Hence on every path the heavy queries number at most \(|X\cap Q|\), whatever the tails, rows, or loading.

Corollary. If \(|X|\le n^{2/3}\), then \(\Pr[\text{some path has at least }2^{c+3}\text{ heavy queries}]\le\Pr[|X\cap Q|\ge2^{c+3}]\le|X|^{c+4}(N/n)^{c+4}\le n^{-c-1}\) for large \(n\), by the rank lemma in its independent-points form. This contains the distinct-rows theorem's Case B and the bounded-loading theorem whenever \(|X|\le n^{2/3}\), with a better constant and no loading hypothesis.

2. Lemma: many rows with an out-class force a satisfied term

Given \(Q\), call a row an out-row if it hosts a class whose label is outside \(Q\), and let \(J_{\rm out}(Q)\) be their set. Each out-row \(j\) has \(|U^{\rm out}_j(Q)\setminus Q|\ge n2^{-w}-N-1\ge n2^{-w}/2\), so the out-loading lemma gives \(\Pr[\text{no term satisfied}\mid Q]\le\exp(-|J_{\rm out}(Q)|\,2^{-w}/3)\). Put \(r_w=3(c+1)2^{w}\ln n\): if \(|J_{\rm out}(Q)|\ge r_w\), a term is satisfied except with probability \(n^{-c-1}\).

3. The residual case

By Sections 1 and 2, a single-row full-class reader can be bad only if \(|X|>n^{2/3}\) and, for the given flat, its at least \(|X|-N\) out-labels have all their classes on fewer than \(r_w\le n^{1/3}\mathrm{polylog}(n)\) rows, while its in-labels, at most \(N\) of them, have classes on arbitrary rows. The trigger holes are in-labels \(x\) with a class whose tail row is assigned a label consistent with it: on a matched out-row the label \(\mu'(j)\) must avoid \(U^{\rm out}_j(Q)\); on a matched row without out-classes every consistent class gives a hole; on a residual row the answer must avoid \(U^{\rm out}_j(Q)\) and each such row gives fewer than \(2^{c+3}\) holes outside probability \(n^{-c-1}\) (survivor rank, as in the bounded-loading theorem). Two estimates remain.

(a) Rows without out-classes. Such a row has all its labels \(X_j\) in \(Q\). Rows with a single label \(x_j\) give holes in \(X_1\cap Q\), \(X_1=\{x_j\}\), which is small by rank when \(|X_1|\le n^{2/3}\) and otherwise puts at least \(|X_1|-N\ge r_w\) single-label rows in \(J_{\rm out}\), contradicting the residual case. Rows with at least two labels have \(\Pr[X_j\subseteq Q]\le(N/n)^2\), so the expected number of such rows that are matched into their union is at most \((N/n)^2\Lambda(F)\); a high-probability bound on the labels they contribute, a union of fixed sets \(X_j\) inside \(Q\), is the first missing estimate.

(b) Gaps at out-rows. On a matched out-row, \(\mu'(j)\) avoids \(U^{\rm out}_j(Q)\) with probability at most \(1-|U^{\rm out}_j(Q)\setminus Q|/(n+1)\), and the holes it yields are the in-classes consistent with it; on a residual out-row the adversary chooses a gap in \(Q\). The number of residual out-rows is hypergeometric with mean below \(r_w(N+1)/n\), so at most \(2c+2\) of them outside probability \(n^{-c-1}\), giving fewer than \((2c+2)2^{c+3}\) holes. For the fewer than \(r_w\) matched out-rows, the holes are survivors of \(\mu'(j)\) inside \(Q\); each row contributes fewer than \(2^{c+3}\), and the number of matched out-rows whose label is consistent with an in-class is, by negative association, at most \(k'\) outside probability \((2u_{\rm in}/k')^{k'}\), where \(u_{\rm in}=\sum_{j\in J_{\rm out}}|U^{\rm in}_j(Q)|/n\) is the in-loading of the out-rows. Bounding \(u_{\rm in}\) with high probability over \(Q\) is the second missing estimate; it is at most \(\sum_{x\in Q}u(x)\) for the label loadings \(u(x)=\sum_j|U_{x,j}|/n\), and labels of loading at least \(3(c+1)\ln n\) outside \(Q\) are excluded by the out-loading lemma, so the estimate concerns how much loading the \(N\) labels of the flat can carry when every label outside it carries at most \(3(c+1)\ln n\).

Both estimates are of one kind: a fixed family of sets (the \(X_j\), or the loaded labels) and the question of how much of it a random flat can contain; the rank lemma answers it for a single fixed set, and the sum over a family of size up to \(n^{c-1}\) is where the union bound fails. A moment bound over the flat, exploiting that \(Q\) has exactly \(N\) points as the sparse lemma did, is the natural next tool.

Main-route assessment. The first obligation is unchanged. The single-row full-class case of the window obligation is reduced to readers with more than \(n^{2/3}\) labels whose out-classes sit on \(n^{1/3}\mathrm{polylog}(n)\) rows, with two named estimates of the same kind remaining; readers with at most \(n^{2/3}\) labels switch with \(2^{c+3}\) heavy queries at every polynomial size. Parity terms remain the open core.

Process assessment. The observation of Section 1 is elementary and would have shortened the previous two cycles; the lesson, to bound the heavy queries by the labels available before analyzing rows, is recorded in the working context. No framework change is needed, and no computation was run.

18 September 2026 — Every single-row full-class reader switches at every polynomial size within the height budget: heavy labels lie in the flat, light out-loading forces a satisfied term, and the flat's light loading is small by rank

Status: working theorem with full proof (random-flat family, hole-query trees) for all mixed readers whose classes pin all rows to one label and carry a single-row light tail, on arbitrary rows; closes the residual case of the two previous entries. Spin cycle 191. Produced by Claude Code (Claude Fable 5.1 (claude-fable-5-1), low reasoning effort).

Question and stopping point. The two estimates of the residual case were to be proved by a moment bound over the flat. A simpler route closes the case: count heavy queries as labels, split labels by their loading, and observe that light-good pairs, the answers whose light survivors all lie in the flat, are few because each is charged to a light label of the flat, while a label of the flat carries little loading. The stopping point is the theorem below.

1. Notation

Classes \(\tau=(j_\tau,p_\tau,x_\tau)\) are full with single-row light tails, on arbitrary rows; \(X\) is the label set, \(L_j(z)=\{x_\tau:\ j_\tau=j,\ z\in C(p_\tau)\}\), \(U_{x,j}=\bigcup\{C(p_\tau):\ x_\tau=x,\ j_\tau=j\}\), and the loading of a label is \(u(x)=\sum_j|U_{x,j}|/n\); \(J_x\) is the set of rows hosting a class of \(x\), so \(|J_x|\le2^wu(x)\). Let \(\lambda_2=3(c+2)\ln n\), \(k''=2^{c+3}\), and \(2^w\le n^{1/3}\). A label is heavy if \(u(x)\ge\lambda_2\), light otherwise; \(H\) and \(X_L\) are the heavy and light labels. A pair \((j,z)\) is light-loaded if \(L_j(z)\cap X_L\ne\emptyset\), light-good (for \(Q\)) if \(L_j(z)\cap X_L\setminus\{z\}\subseteq Q\), and small if \(|L_j(z)\cap X_L\setminus\{z\}|

Facts used, from the loading entry and the label-set observation: a bad path (at least \(N/24\) heavy queries, no 1-leaf) has all its heavy holes in \(X\cap Q\), distinct; on it every assigned row \(j\) with label \(z_j\) has \(L_j(z_j)\setminus\{z_j\}\subseteq Q\); and a class with label outside \(Q\) whose tail row is matched consistently (to a label other than \(x_\tau\)) yields a satisfied term.

2. Theorem

Theorem. For \(N\ge N_0(c)=2^{c+11}(c+2)^2\ln^2n\) and \(n\) large, every single-row full-class reader has, with probability at least \(1-8n^{-c-1}\), fewer than \(N/24\) heavy queries on every path before any 1-leaf. Hence all such readers of a source of size \(n^c\) switch under one restriction within the height budget.

Proof. Six events, each of probability at most \(n^{-c-1}\), are excluded; on their complement a bad path is impossible. Throughout, given \(Q\), \((R',\mu')\) is a uniform bijection of the rows onto \(Q^c\) and \(N+1\) residual slots, negatively associated, and the event that a given row is matched into a given label set is increasing in that row's entries.

(E1) Heavy labels lie in \(Q\), and are few. For \(x\in H\setminus Q\), the events "row \(j\in J_x\) is matched into \(U_{x,j}\setminus(Q\cup\{x\})\)" are on distinct rows, each of probability at least \((|U_{x,j}|-N-1)/(n+1)\ge|U_{x,j}|/(2(n+1))\) since \(|U_{x,j}|\ge n2^{-w}\ge2N+2\); each yields a satisfied term, so \(\Pr[\text{none}\mid Q]\le\exp(-u(x)/3)\le n^{-c-2}\). Over at most \(n\) heavy labels, outside probability \(n^{-c-1}\) either a term is satisfied or \(H\subseteq Q\). If \(|H|\ge2^{c+3}\), then \(H\subseteq Q\) has probability at most \((N/n)^{c+4}\le n^{-c-1}\) by rank. So on a bad path, outside \(2n^{-c-1}\), the heavy holes number fewer than \(2^{c+3}\).

(E2) Large light survivor sets are never inside \(Q\). A pair with \(|L_j(z)\cap X_L\setminus\{z\}|\ge k''\) is light-good with probability at most \((N/n)^{c+4}\) (rank of a fixed set); over \(n(n+1)\) pairs this is at most \(n^{-c-1}\). Outside this event every light-good pair is small, and every assigned row of a bad path has fewer than \(k''\) light survivors.

(E3) Light out-loading is small. By the out-loading lemma applied to the light classes, \(\Pr[\text{no light out-class satisfied}\mid Q]\le\exp(-\sum_j|U^{{\rm out},L}_j(Q)\setminus Q|/(n+1))\), and \(z\notin Q\) lies in \(U^{{\rm out},L}_j(Q)\) exactly when \((j,z)\) is light-loaded and not light-good. Hence outside probability \(n^{-c-1}\), on a bad path, \(n\Lambda_L-\#\{\text{light-good pairs}\}-N(n+1)\le(c+1)(n+1)\ln n\). Every light-good pair is small (E2) and has a light survivor in \(Q\), so their number is at most \(n\,u_{\rm s}(Q)\) with \(u_{\rm s}(Q)=\sum_{x\in Q\cap X_L}u_{\rm s}(x)\); thus \(\Lambda_L\le u_{\rm s}(Q)+N+(c+2)\ln n\).

(E4) The flat's small light loading is small. Put \(\theta=1/(400ek'')\), \(X_\theta=\{x\in X_L:\ u_{\rm s}(x)\ge\theta\}\), and \(V=\sum_{x\in X_L}u_{\rm s}(x)\), so \(|X_\theta|\le V/\theta\) and \(V\le k''\Lambda_L\) (each small pair has fewer than \(k''\) light survivors). Then \(u_{\rm s}(Q)\le N\theta+\lambda_2|X_\theta\cap Q|\), as light labels have \(u_{\rm s}<\lambda_2\). Two cases. If \(V\le3Nk''\), then \(|X_\theta|\le3Nk''/\theta\le n^{2/3}\) and, by rank, \(|X_\theta\cap Q|<2^{c+3}\) outside probability \(n^{-c-1}\). If \(V>3Nk''\), then \(\Lambda_L\ge V/k''>3N\) and (E3) gives \(u_{\rm s}(Q)\ge\Lambda_L/2\ge V/(2k'')\); the labels with \(u_{\rm s}(x)\ge V/(4k''N)\) number at most \(4k''N\) and must carry at least \(V/(4k'')\) of \(u_{\rm s}(Q)\), so at least \(V/(4k''\lambda_2)\ge2^{c+3}\) of them lie in \(Q\), a rank event of probability at most \((4k''N^2/n)^{c+4}\le n^{-c-1}\). In both cases, outside \(n^{-c-1}\), \(u_{\rm s}(Q)\le N\theta+\lambda_22^{c+3}\).

(E5) Few matched rows yield light holes. Let \(G_j=\{z:\ \emptyset\ne L_j(z)\cap X_L\setminus\{z\}\subseteq Q\}\) and \(A\) the number of matched rows \(j\) with \(\mu'(j)\in G_j\); the light holes from matched rows number at most \(k''A\) by (E2). By negative association, \(\Pr[A\ge a\mid Q]\le(2\sum_j|G_j|/n)^a/a!\), and \(\sum_j|G_j|/n\le u_{\rm s}(Q)\) since each pair of \(G_j\) is small with a light survivor in \(Q\). With \(a=N/(96k'')\) and (E4), \(2e\,u_{\rm s}(Q)/a\le\tfrac{192e k''}{400e k''}+\tfrac{192e k''\lambda_22^{c+3}}{N}\le\tfrac12\) for \(N\ge N_0\), so \(\Pr[A\ge a]\le2^{-a}\le n^{-c-1}\) as \(a\ge(c+1)\log_2n\).

(E6) Few residual rows yield light holes. A residual row answered on a bad path yields light holes only if it hosts a class of a light label in \(Q\); the set of such rows is contained in \(\bigcup_{x\in Q\cap X_L}J_x\), of size at most \(N\lambda_22^w\le N\lambda_2n^{1/3}\), fixed given \(Q\) and independent of \(R'\). So the number of residual rows among them is at least \(m=2c+2\) with probability at most \(\bigl(e N\lambda_2n^{1/3}(N+1)/(nm)\bigr)^m\le n^{-c-1}\), and each such row yields fewer than \(k''\) light holes by (E2).

Outside the six events, a path without 1-leaf has fewer than \(2^{c+3}+k''N/(96k'')+(2c+1)k''

The proof uses the affine structure of \(Q\) only through the rank lemma for fixed sets (E1, E2, E4), \(|Q|=N\), and \(\Pr[x\in Q]=N/n\); the tails enter only through the loading. The constant \(N_0\) is polylogarithmic, as the budget allows.

3. Scope and what remains

This settles the window obligation for the first genuinely mixed class of readers without a size regime: full classes with single-row tails, on any rows, including the \(F^{(j)}\) family and its many-row variants. It contains the distinct-rows theorem, the bounded-loading theorem, and the label-set corollary. Two generalizations remain for all literal readers in the window: non-full pair sets, where "unmatched" is no longer "label in \(Q\)" and the comparison lemma must replace it with trigger holes taken from vertex covers of the classes' alive pairs; and multi-row tails, where loading becomes a per-class quantity and the tail comparison controls the mixed matched-residual case.

Main-route assessment. The first obligation is unchanged. On the literal frontier, single-row full-class mixed readers now switch at every polynomial size within the height budget, by one proof that organizes the earlier mechanisms by labels; the window obligation is reduced to non-full pair sets and multi-row tails. Parity terms remain the open core.

Process assessment. The moment bound announced last cycle was not needed: charging light-good pairs to light labels of the flat, whose loading is bounded, replaced it; the lesson that a random-flat estimate should be attempted first as a charging argument over the flat's \(N\) labels is recorded in the working context. No framework change is needed, and no computation was run.

18 September 2026 — Correctness review of the single-row full-class theorem: self pairs must be excluded from the light loading, the threshold for \(N\) is restated, and "assigned rows" means rows assigned before the last heavy query; the theorem stands

Status: focused correctness review with two corrections and one clarification to the theorem of the previous entry, which remains a working theorem with the corrected definitions; the general pair-set case is opened with its obstacle named. Spin cycle 192. Produced by Claude Code (Claude Fable 5.1 (claude-fable-5-1), low reasoning effort).

Question and stopping point. Before extending the theorem, its proof was reviewed once as the research protocol asks. The review found one real gap in step (E3), a constant that does not cover step (E5) as stated, and a phrase that needs a definition; all three are repaired below without changing the argument's structure. The stopping point is the corrected statement, and the first obstacle of the general pair-set case.

1. Correction: self pairs

Call \((j,z)\) a self pair if the only light survivor of \(z\) at row \(j\) is \(z\) itself: \(L_j(z)\cap X_L=\{z\}\), which happens when some class \((j,p,z)\) has \(z\in C(p)\). A self pair is light-loaded and light-good vacuously, but it has no light survivor other than \(z\), so the charge of step (E3), "every light-good pair has a light survivor in \(Q\)", fails for it; a reader with \(n\) labels on every row has up to \(n(n+1)\) self pairs, which would make (E3) vacuous. Self pairs never produce a satisfied term (the occupant of \(z\) is \(j\) itself) nor a hole (the hole \(z\) is the row's own answer), so they are irrelevant to the bad event and should be excluded from the loading. Corrected definitions: a pair is light-loaded if \(L_j(z)\cap X_L\setminus\{z\}\ne\emptyset\); \(\Lambda_L\) is the number of light-loaded pairs divided by \(n\); \(u_{\rm s}(x)=|\{(j,z)\text{ small}:\ x\in L_j(z),\ z\ne x\}|/n\); and \(V=\sum_{x\in X_L}u_{\rm s}(x)\). With these, \(z\notin Q\) lies in \(U^{{\rm out},L}_j(Q)\) exactly when \((j,z)\) is light-loaded and not light-good, every light-good light-loaded pair has a light survivor other than \(z\) in \(Q\) and is small by (E2), so the count of such pairs is at most \(n\,u_{\rm s}(Q)\), and \(V\le k''\Lambda_L\) because each small light-loaded pair has fewer than \(k''\) light survivors other than \(z\). Steps (E3), (E4) and (E5) then read exactly as written, since \(G_j\) already excluded \(z\) from the survivors. Step (E1) is unaffected: it uses \(|U_{x,j}\setminus(Q\cup\{x\})|\).

2. Correction: the threshold for \(N\)

Step (E5) needs \(192e\,k''\lambda_22^{c+3}/N\le1/50\), that is \(N\ge2^{2c+21}\cdot3e(c+2)\ln n\), which the stated \(N_0=2^{c+11}(c+2)^2\ln^2n\) does not give for \(c\ge3\) and moderate \(n\). The theorem holds with \(N_0(c)=2^{2c+24}(c+2)\ln n\), which also covers (E4) (\(N/(4\lambda_2)\ge2^{c+3}\)), the requirement \(a=N/(96k'')\ge(c+1)\log_2n\), and the final count \(2^{c+3}+N/96+(2c+1)2^{c+3}

3. Clarification: which rows are assigned

The proof uses that every assigned row \(j\) of a bad path has \(L_j(z_j)\setminus\{z_j\}\subseteq Q\). A row is "assigned" if it is matched by \(\rho'\) or answered by the path before its last heavy query. This is the correct reading: if an answer satisfies the tail of a class with a matched pair, that term is satisfied by \(\rho'\cup\pi\) and stays non-falsified, so from then on the matched-first preference always selects a matched-pair term and no further heavy query occurs; a bad path's heavy queries therefore all precede any such answer, and the rows answered after the last heavy query are not used. Likewise a term satisfied by \(\rho'\) alone prevents every heavy query on every path.

4. General pair sets: the first obstacle

For a class with an arbitrary pair set \(P_\tau\), the events "alive and unmatched" and "matched" are no longer "\(x_\tau\in Q\)" and "\(x_\tau\notin Q\)", but events on \(\mu'\) with the ratio of the comparison lemma. Two of the six exclusions transfer directly: the survivor-rank step (E2) and the residual-row step (E6) concern only holes, which remain labels in \(Q\); and triggers at sparse holes, of degree below \(D^\ast\) over all pairs of the reader, form a matching of size below \(N/48\) by the sparse lemma whatever the classes. The obstacle is in the satisfaction steps (E1) and (E3): a dense label outside \(Q\) is occupied by a row pinned to it only with probability about \(1/(96eN)\), and which classes are matched depends on \(\mu'\) at the pair rows, so the out-loading of a row is no longer a fixed set and the negative-association product over tail rows does not apply as stated. The natural first target is the class of column classes, \(P_\tau=I_\tau\times\{x_\tau\}\), where a class is matched exactly when its label is outside \(Q\) and its occupant lies in \(I_\tau\); there the occupant of each label is a single uniform row, and the loading of a label can be averaged over occupants. This is the next cycle's task.

Main-route assessment. The first obligation is unchanged. The single-row full-class theorem survives review with corrected definitions and constant; the general pair-set case is reduced to the two satisfaction steps, with column classes as the next restricted case. Parity terms remain the open core.

Process assessment. The review was worth a cycle: the self-pair gap would have propagated into the pair-set generalization; the working context's switching paragraph is consolidated in a separate commit this cycle, since it had grown to over 700 words. No framework change is needed, and no computation was run.
