18 September 2026 — Correction: the recording rule can cost every light query when rows have two roles, so the switching conclusions for mixed readers hold for role-separated readers, while the heavy-query bounds stand; the bipartite full-column theorem is the repaired target

Status: correction of the cost accounting of the recording rule, with the exact consequence for each recorded mixed-reader result; no new theorem. Found while designing the mixed-term round-trip tool. Spin cycle 193. Produced by Claude Code (Claude Fable 5.1 (claude-fable-5-1), low reasoning effort).

Question and stopping point. The plan was column classes, or the round-trip implementation of the mixed tree. Designing the decoder for the tool showed that the recording rule of the height-budget entry was accounted for incorrectly. The stopping point is the correction, the corrected scope of every affected claim, and the repaired target.

1. The gap

The decoder identifies each round's term as the first term not falsified by its current assignment, which contains the code labels of the light rows moved in later rounds. If the pinned row \(i\) of the round's term \(T\) is residual and unassigned at that round and is moved later as a light row of another term, the decoder sees \(i\) matched to a label other than \(T\)'s pinned label and skips \(T\). The recording rule kept such rows unmoved, and its cost was stated as one recorded light query per heavy round. That is wrong: the row is at risk whenever \(T\) is the round's term and ends the round unassigned, which happens when a light answer falsifies \(T\)'s tail, or when a hole query at \(T\)'s hole is answered by another row or by the empty branch. So the at-risk rows are the pinned rows of every round, up to one per round, and since every round has at least one query, every light query of a path may be recorded. A recorded light query costs a factor \(N+e\) with no gain, so in that case the extension encoding gains nothing and the bound \(A^{s_L-k}\) collapses; the height bounds for the light part of mixed trees are therefore not established for readers in which a row is pinned in one term and light in another.

The alternatives fail for the same reason: assigning the pinned row by a pigeon query first costs \(N+e\) per round with no gain; excusing the pinned row in the decoder's test makes earlier, truly falsified terms look alive; recording the term's index costs \(M\) per round. A row of two roles cannot be both moved and visible, and the number of such rows on a path is not bounded by the heavy count.

2. Corrected scope of the recorded results

Call a reader role-separated if no row is pinned in one of its terms and light in another; for single-row-tail classes this means that the pinned rows and the tail rows form disjoint sets \(A\) and \(B\). For role-separated readers pinned rows are never moved, the decoder of the adaptive-rule lemma is correct as stated, and no recording rule is needed. Accordingly:

  • Part (ii) of the adaptive-rule lemma and the recording rule of the height-budget entry hold for role-separated readers; for two-role readers the encoding of the light part is open.
  • The separate-terms corollary of the unary entry with the light part first is unaffected: the light tree involves only light terms, and the unary part needs no decoding.
  • The heavy-query bounds of the distinct-rows, bounded-loading, label-set, and single-row full-class results are unaffected: they bound the heavy queries of the canonical tree by probability alone. Their conclusion "switches within the height budget" additionally needs the light bound, hence role separation. Full classes pin every row other than the tail row, so a full-class reader with tails on more than one row is not role-separated; for these readers the results give the heavy bound only, and the switching conclusion is conditional on an encoding for two-role rows.
  • The trivial bound of the height-budget entry (heavy queries at most \(2N+1\), height \(6N+3c\)) is likewise established for role-separated readers only.

3. The repaired target: bipartite full-column readers

The natural role-separated version of full classes pins every row of a fixed set \(A\) of pinned rows, with all tails on the complementary set \(B\) of light rows, \(|A|\ge n/2\): class \(\tau=(j_\tau,p_\tau,x_\tau)\) has pairs \(A\times\{x_\tau\}\) and \(j_\tau\in B\). A class with \(x_\tau\notin Q\) is matched exactly when the occupant of \(x_\tau\) lies in \(A\), which has probability at least \(1/2-o(1)\) but is no longer certain. The proof of the single-row full-class theorem transfers with one change of exposure order: condition on \(Q\), then on \(\mu'\) restricted to \(A\) (a uniform injection into \(Q^c\)), which fixes the matched classes and the set of labels left for the light rows, and finally let the light rows map uniformly onto the remaining labels and residual slots. Given the first two, the survivor sets and the out-loading are fixed, negative association over light rows applies, and a consistent set meets the remaining labels in a hypergeometric number concentrated near \(|C(p)|/2\); the occupant events over distinct labels are negatively associated, so the out-loading over the exposure of \(A\) concentrates as well. Steps (E2), (E4), (E5), (E6) concern holes and light rows only and need no change. This is the next cycle's task, together with the round-trip tool for role-separated mixed readers, which needs no recording rule.

Main-route assessment. The first obligation is unchanged. On the literal frontier the heavy-query results stand, but the switching conclusions for mixed readers are now correctly restricted to role-separated readers, and the encoding for two-role rows is a named open problem; the bipartite full-column theorem is the repaired target. Parity terms remain the open core.

Process assessment. The gap surfaced only when the decoder had to be written as code; the lesson, to implement a decoder before stacking results on its claimed correctness, argues for building the tool next cycle rather than proving further cases first. No framework change is needed, and no computation was run.

18 September 2026 — The mixed-term tree with hole queries and its encoding pass exact round-trip tests for role-separated readers, and a constructed two-role reader fails as predicted

Status: finite check (exhaustive enumeration of the family on eight-label boards) of the decoder for the mixed canonical tree with the adaptive rule and the matched-first preference; one positive and one negative control; no new theorem. Spin cycle 194. Produced by Claude Code (Claude Fable 5.1 (claude-fable-5-1), low reasoning effort).

Question and stopping point. The correction of the previous entry came from designing a decoder; this cycle builds it. research/tools/check_mixed_term_encoding.py implements the mixed tree (terms with an optional pinned pair on a row of a set \(A\) and a light tail on rows of a set \(B\); the matched-first preference; all uncovered tail rows of the round's term queried in order; then one heavy query, the pigeon if it has at least two unkilled pinned pairs, else the hole with branches over the unassigned residual rows and the empty branch), the encoding (light rows moved to the smallest consistent free outside label that is not a pinned label, per-round star vectors marking the moved tail rows and whether a heavy answer follows, heavy answers recorded as a hole label, a row, or the empty branch), and the decoder, which recomputes the preference and the adaptive rule from the code restriction. Pinned rows are never moved, and code labels avoid pinned labels so that an alive pinned pair with a free outside hole is not hidden by a code label. The stopping point is the exhaustive verification on small boards.

1. Results

Complete enumeration of \(\Phi_e\) on \(n=8\) labels, \(N=2\), nine rows, six to eight terms, tails of at most two rows with at most \(w\in\{1,2\}\) literals, height thresholds \(h\in\{3,4\}\) (results, records). In the six role-separated runs (\(A\cap B=\emptyset\)), all 3147 rich bad paths decode to their restriction; the heavy queries per path are at most four, with the histograms recorded. Two runs with random readers whose tails may use pinned rows also showed no failure, because the random instances did not realize the failing configuration. The constructed reader with row 0 pinned in the first term (hole in \(Q\), tail on row 5) and light in the second term (pinned pair on row 1, tail on row 0) fails on 2610 of 4050 and on 2130 of 4450 rich bad paths in two runs: after the first round leaves row 0 unassigned, the second round moves it, the decoder sees the first term falsified and picks the second, and the star vector is applied to the wrong term. This is the mechanism of the two-role gap, observed.

One encoder bug found during the runs: a heavy query following a round whose term was falsified by its own tail answers belongs to the next round's term; the encoder now ends a round by the term's status rather than by the next path entry. The decoder was unchanged.

2. What this checks and what it does not

The check covers the claims of the adaptive-rule lemma (decoder-computable rule), the matched-first preference, and the hole-query branches, for role-separated readers, on boards where every restriction is enumerated; it also confirms that the failing configuration of the correction is real. It does not test the probability bounds, which need larger boards than exhaustive enumeration allows, nor readers with pinned rows of several consistent holes (window widths below \(\ell\)).

Main-route assessment. The first obligation is unchanged. The mixed tree's decoder is now verified exactly for role-separated readers, and the two-role failure is exhibited; the bipartite full-column theorem remains the repaired target for a switching statement. Parity terms remain the open core.

Process assessment. The tool took one cycle and found one encoder bug and no decoder gap beyond the recorded one; the tool now exists for later rule changes, which is the framework improvement this cycle needed. Two runs were made with an encoder that could crash on a round boundary; they were rerun after the fix into a fresh file.

18 September 2026 — The adaptive rule's distinct-holes claim fails for pigeon queries; the hole-only rule restores it, the trigger-hole theorems stand on the corrected tree, and bipartite full-column readers switch at every polynomial size within the height budget

Status: correction (part (i) of the adaptive-rule lemma refuted by an explicit reader, verified by computation) with the corrected hole-only rule, under which every recorded trigger-hole theorem holds verbatim; working theorem with full proof for bipartite full-column readers on the corrected tree, whose decoder passes exhaustive round-trip tests. Spin cycle 195. Produced by Claude Code (Claude Fable 5.1 (claude-fable-5-1), low reasoning effort).

Question and stopping point. The task was the bipartite full-column theorem, the repaired target of the two-role correction. Reviewing its heavy-query count, which like the single-row full-class theorem counts distinct trigger holes, exposed a gap in the adaptive-rule lemma: its claim that trigger holes are pairwise distinct is proved only for hole queries and is false for pigeon queries. The cycle records the counterexample, replaces the rule by the hole-only rule, checks the decoder of the corrected tree with the tool, and proves the bipartite theorem on the corrected tree.

1. The gap: pigeon queries can repeat a trigger hole

The adaptive rule queries the pigeon \(i\) of the trigger pair \((i,x)\) when \(i\) has at least two unkilled pairs. A pigeon query kills the pairs at row \(i\) but leaves the hole \(x\) free, so a later term with an alive pair \((i',x)\) at another residual row triggers \(x\) again; the lemma's proof ("a queried hole kills every pair at it") covers hole queries only. Concretely, take a full-column reader with \(k\ge2\) classes whose labels \(x_1,\dots,x_k\) lie in \(Q\), tails satisfied by \(\rho'\), and every residual row pinned, with the terms \((i,x_1)\wedge t_1\) listed first in order of \(i\). Every residual row has \(k\) unkilled pairs, so each round is a pigeon query at the next residual row, and the branch sending it to a hole outside \(\{x_1,\dots,x_k\}\) leaves every trigger alive: the path makes \(N-k+1\) pigeon queries, all triggered by \(x_1\), while \(\nu(B_{\rm t})=k\). The tool confirms it (Section 3): on \(n=16\) labels with \(N=8\) and three classes, the adaptive tree has a path with 8 heavy queries, the hole-only tree at most 3.

The consequence is not cosmetic. With \(k=2\) classes of one-literal patterns, the configuration (both labels in \(Q\), both tails satisfied) has probability of order \(N^2/n^2\), and on it the adaptive tree has a path with at least \(N-2\) heavy queries. So for \(c\ge2\) the heavy-query bounds of the distinct-rows, bounded-loading, label-set, and single-row full-class results, and the matching-number bound of the matched-first entry, are false for the adaptive tree as stated. Their proofs count distinct trigger holes, which is exactly what the adaptive rule fails to provide.

2. The corrected rule and the affected claims

Hole-only rule. At a heavy round with trigger pair \((i,x)\), \(i\in R'\), \(x\in Q\) unkilled, query the hole \(x\): branches over the uncovered residual rows moved to \(x\) and the empty branch (hole-query nodes). The tree is otherwise the canonical mixed tree with the matched-first preference.

Lemma. On every path of the hole-only tree the trigger holes are pairwise distinct, so the heavy queries number at most the hole count \(h(B_{\rm t})\) of the pairs \((i,x)\), \(i\in R'\), \(x\in Q\), whose term's tail is not falsified by \(\rho'\), in particular at most \(N\), and each heavy answer takes one of \(N+2\) values. For a role-separated reader the decoder of the light encoding identifies the round's term as in the light lemma and queries its hole, so the encoding applies with the heavy answers recorded in \(\delta\) and no rule to recompute. Proof. A queried hole is used or emptied, which kills every pair at it, and a trigger pair is unkilled. The decoder statement is part (ii) of the adaptive-rule lemma without its test. \(\square\)

Trigger rows need not be distinct: a residual row whose hole was emptied stays unassigned and may trigger another hole later, which is why the accounting through \(\nu(B_{\rm t})\) is replaced by \(h(B_{\rm t})\ge\nu(B_{\rm t})\). The height budget needs only a constant-factor bound on heavy queries, and every trigger-hole theorem bounds \(h\) directly.

Affected claims, read on the hole-only tree. The trivial count of the height budget becomes \(N\), so the heavy factor there is \(n^{N/3+o(N)}\) and the trivial height \(2N+3c+o(N)\); the obligation is unchanged. The matched-first bound becomes the hole count of the alive pairs of unmatched classes with non-falsified tails. The distinct-rows, bounded-loading, label-set, and single-row full-class theorems, with the review corrections, hold verbatim, since their proofs use the rule only through "heavy queries have distinct holes in \(X\cap Q\)". The two-role correction, the comparison lemmas, and the light lemma are unaffected. The claim index is annotated.

3. Tool verification

check_mixed_term_encoding.py gained the option --hole-only, and check_adaptive_rule_counterexample.py builds the reader of Section 1 on one explicit restriction and explores its whole tree under both rules (records). Counterexample: \(n=16\), \(N=8\), three classes, 42 terms; adaptive rule, a path with 8 heavy queries; hole-only rule, at most 3. Round trips under the hole-only rule on the four role-separated instances of the previous cycle that have rich bad paths (\(n=8\), \(N=2\), seeds 2, 3, 4, 5): 3263 rich bad paths, 0 decoding failures. The two-role example reader still fails on 2610 of 4050 paths, since the two-role gap is independent of the rule.

4. Bipartite full-column readers: setting

The rows are partitioned into pinned rows \(A\) and light rows \(B\) with \(|B|\le(n-2N-2)/2\), so \(|A\setminus R'|\ge n/3\). A class \(\tau=(j_\tau,p_\tau,x_\tau)\) has \(j_\tau\in B\), a light pattern \(p_\tau\) of at most \(w\) literals, and the pairs \(A\times\{x_\tau\}\); a reader is a set of classes with distinct tails, read by the hole-only tree. Under \(\rho'\in\Phi_0\) let \(X_A=\mu'(A\setminus R')\) be the labels occupied by pinned rows and \(\mathrm{rem}=Q^c\setminus X_A=\mu'(B\setminus R')\) those occupied by light rows. A class is matched if \(x_\tau\in X_A\), alive if \(x_\tau\in Q\) and \(A\cap R'\ne\emptyset\), and dormant if \(x_\tau\in\mathrm{rem}\); dormant classes are neither matched nor alive. Since the reader is role-separated, the encoding of Section 2 applies and the light bound is the light lemma's. Loading \(u(x)\), survivor sets \(L_j(z)\), the sets \(U_{x,j}\) and \(J_x\), and heavy (\(u(x)\ge\lambda_2=3(c+2)\ln n\)) and light labels are as in the single-row full-class entry; put \(k''=2^{c+3}\) and \(k_5=k''+(c+4)\log_2n\), call a pair \((j,z)\) small if \(|L_j(z)\cap X_L\setminus\{z\}|<k_5\), and define \(u_{\rm s}(x)\), \(V\), \(\Lambda_L\) with this notion of small, self pairs excluded as in the review.

On a bad path (at least \(N/24\) heavy queries, no 1-leaf) the heavy holes are distinct labels in \(X\cap Q\) by the lemma of Section 2, and every light row \(j\) assigned a label \(z\) before the last heavy query (by \(\rho'\) if matched, by the path if residual) has every class at \(j\) consistent with \(z\) and labelled outside \(Q\) dormant: such a class with \(x_\tau\in X_A\) is matched by a pinned row, which is not \(j\) since \(z\ne x_\tau\), with a satisfied tail, and its satisfied term prevents all further heavy queries (assigned rows). A term satisfied by \(\rho'\) alone prevents every heavy query on every path.

5. Lemma: a matching of light rows to hosted out-labels forces a satisfied term

Given \(Q\) and \(R'\), let \(G\) be the bipartite graph on the matched light rows \(B\setminus R'\) and the light labels outside \(Q\), with an edge \((j,x)\) when some class at \(j\) has label \(x\). Put \(r'_w=12\cdot2^w(c+1)\ln n\).

Lemma. If \(G\) has a matching of size \(r'_w\), then \(\Pr[\text{no term satisfied}\mid Q,R']\le n^{-c-1}\).

Proof. Fix the matching \(\{(j,x_j)\}\) and let \(F_j\) be the event that \(\mu'(j)\in U_{x_j,j}\setminus(Q\cup\{x_j\})\) and the occupant of \(x_j\) lies in \(A\). On \(F_j\) the class at \(j\) with label \(x_j\) consistent with \(\mu'(j)\) has a satisfied tail and a matched pair, so a term is satisfied. In the indicator matrix of \(\mu'\), \(F_j\) is increasing in the entries of row \(j\) and in the entries of column \(x_j\) at the rows of \(A\); for \(j\ne j'\) these coordinate sets are disjoint, since \(j,j'\in B\) are distinct rows outside \(A\) and \(x_j\ne x_{j'}\). Given \(Q,R'\), \(\mu'\) is a uniform bijection of the matched rows onto \(Q^c\), whose indicator matrix is negatively associated, so \(\Pr[\bigcap_jF_j^c]\le\prod_j(1-\Pr[F_j])\). Given \(\mu'(j)=z\ne x_j\), the occupant of \(x_j\) is uniform over the other matched rows, of which at least \(n/3\) lie in \(A\), so \(\Pr[F_j]\ge\frac{|U_{x_j,j}|-N-1}{n}\cdot\frac{n/3}{n}\ge\frac{2^{-w}}{7}\), using \(|U_{x_j,j}|\ge n2^{-w}\ge2N+2\) and \(n\ge6\). Hence \(\Pr[\bigcap_jF_j^c]\le\exp(-r'_w2^{-w}/7)=n^{-12(c+1)/7}\le n^{-c-1}\). \(\square\)

By König's theorem, if \(G\) has no matching of size \(r'_w\), it has a vertex cover \(J_0\cup X_0\) with \(|J_0|+|X_0|<r'_w\): every light class with label outside \(Q\) sits on a row of \(J_0\) or of \(B\cap R'\), or has its label in \(X_0\).

6. Theorem

Theorem. For \(2^w\le n^{1/3}\), \(N\ge N_0(c)=2^{2c+24}(c+3)^2\ln^2n\), and \(n\) large, every bipartite full-column reader has, with probability at least \(1-8n^{-c-1}\), fewer than \(N/24\) heavy queries on every path of the hole-only tree before any 1-leaf; with the light lemma for its light part, every such reader of a source of size \(n^c\) switches under one restriction within the height budget.

Proof. Events of total probability at most \(8n^{-c-1}\) are excluded; on their complement a bad path is impossible. Throughout, given \(Q\), the pair \((R',\mu')\) is a uniform bijection of the rows onto \(Q^c\) and \(N+1\) residual slots, whose indicator matrix is negatively associated, as is its restriction after conditioning on the value at one row or one column; the event that a row is matched into a given label set, and the event that a column is occupied by a row of a given set, are increasing.

(F1) Heavy labels. For a heavy label \(x\notin Q\), the event that \(x\) is dormant is increasing in the entries of column \(x\) at the rows of \(B\) and has probability at most \(|B|/(n-N)\le1/2\); over the heavy labels outside \(Q\) the columns are distinct, so \(\Pr[\text{all of }H\setminus Q\text{ dormant}\mid Q]\le2^{-|H\setminus Q|}\). For a heavy label \(x\notin Q\) that is not dormant, condition on its occupant \(i_0\in A\): the events "row \(j\in J_x\) is matched into \(U_{x,j}\setminus(Q\cup\{x\})\)" are increasing on distinct rows, each of probability at least \((|U_{x,j}|-N-1)/(n+1)\ge|U_{x,j}|/(2(n+1))\), and each yields a satisfied term, so \(\Pr[\text{no class of }x\text{ satisfied}\mid\text{occupant }i_0]\le e^{-u(x)/3}\le n^{-c-2}\). By a union bound over at most \(n\) heavy labels, outside probability \(n^{-c-1}\), every non-dormant heavy label outside \(Q\) has a satisfied class, so on a bad path all heavy labels outside \(Q\) are dormant. Split on the fixed set \(H\). If \(|H|>N+(c+1)\log_2n\), then \(|H\setminus Q|>(c+1)\log_2n\) always and the dormancy event has probability at most \(n^{-c-1}\). If \(|H|\le N+(c+1)\log_2n\), then \(\Pr[|H\cap Q|\ge2^{c+3}]\le(|H|N/n)^{c+4}\le n^{-c-1}\) by rank. In both cases, outside \(2n^{-c-1}\), a bad path has fewer than \(2^{c+3}\) heavy holes that are heavy labels.

(F2) Survivor sets. Let \((j,z)\) have \(L=L_j(z)\cap X_L\setminus\{z\}\) with \(|L|\ge k_5\), and suppose \(j\) is assigned \(z\) before the last heavy query of a bad path. Then every label of \(L\) outside \(Q\) is dormant (Section 4). For a matched row this is read after conditioning on \(\mu'(j)=z\), when the occupant of each \(x\in L\setminus Q\) is uniform over the other matched rows and the dormancy events are increasing on distinct columns at the rows of \(B\setminus\{j\}\), each of probability at most \((|B|-1)/(n-N-1)\le1/2\); for a residual row the same holds without conditioning. If \(|L|\ge N+(c+4)\log_2n\), at least \((c+4)\log_2n\) labels of \(L\) lie outside \(Q\) and their dormancy has probability at most \(n^{-c-4}\). Otherwise either \(|L\cap Q|\ge k''\), a rank event of probability at most \((|L|N/n)^{c+4}\le n^{-c-3.5}\) for large \(n\), or at least \((c+4)\log_2n\) labels of \(L\) lie outside \(Q\) and the dormancy bound applies. Over at most \(n(n+1)\) pairs, outside probability \(n^{-c-1}\), every row assigned before the last heavy query of a bad path has a small pair, hence fewer than \(k_5\) light holes.

(F3) Matching or cover. By the lemma of Section 5, outside probability \(n^{-c-1}\), on a bad path \(G\) has a cover \(J_0\cup X_0\) with \(|J_0|+|X_0|<r'_w\).

(F4) The flat's small light loading. Count the light-loaded pairs \((j,z)\), those with a light survivor other than \(z\). If all light survivors of \((j,z)\) lie in \(Q\), the pair is small outside the rank event of (F2) and has a light survivor in \(Q\), so these pairs number at most \(n\,u_{\rm s}(Q)\le nN\lambda_2\), as light labels have \(u_{\rm s}(x)\le u(x)<\lambda_2\). Otherwise some light survivor \(x\notin Q\) is the label of a light class at \(j\), which on a bad path is covered by (F3): \(j\in J_0\cup(B\cap R')\) or \(x\in X_0\); these pairs number at most \((r'_w+N+1)n+n\sum_{x\in X_0}u(x)\le(r'_w+N+1)n+r'_w\lambda_2n\). Hence \(\Lambda_L\le2(N+r'_w)\lambda_2\). Put \(\theta=1/(400ek_5)\), \(X_\theta=\{x\in X_L:\ u_{\rm s}(x)\ge\theta\}\), and \(V=\sum_{x\in X_L}u_{\rm s}(x)\le k_5\Lambda_L\), so \(|X_\theta|\le V/\theta\le800e\,k_5^2(N+r'_w)\lambda_2\le n^{2/3}\) for large \(n\), since \(r'_w\le12(c+1)n^{1/3}\ln n\) and \(N\) is polylogarithmic. By rank, \(\Pr[|X_\theta\cap Q|\ge2^{c+3}]\le(Nn^{-1/3})^{c+4}\le n^{-c-1}\), and outside this event \(u_{\rm s}(Q)\le N\theta+\lambda_22^{c+3}\).

(F5) Matched light rows. Let \(G'_j=\{z:\ (j,z)\text{ small},\ L_j(z)\cap X_L\cap Q\setminus\{z\}\ne\emptyset\}\), fixed given \(Q\), and \(A'\) the number of matched light rows with \(\mu'(j)\in G'_j\). By negative association over rows, \(\Pr[A'\ge a\mid Q]\le(2u_{\rm s}(Q))^a/a!\), since \(\sum_j|G'_j|/n\le u_{\rm s}(Q)\). With \(a=N/(96k_5)\) and (F4), \(2e\,u_{\rm s}(Q)/a\le192e\,k_5\theta+192e\,k_5\lambda_22^{c+3}/N\le0.48+0.02\) for \(N\ge N_0\), so \(\Pr[A'\ge a]\le2^{-a}\le n^{-c-1}\) as \(a\ge(c+1)\log_2n\). Every light hole from a matched row on a bad path comes from a small pair with a light survivor in \(Q\) (F2), so these holes number at most \(k_5A'<N/96\).

(F6) Residual light rows. As in step (E6) of the single-row full-class theorem, the light rows hosting a light class of a label in \(Q\) number at most \(N\lambda_22^w\le N\lambda_2n^{1/3}\), a set fixed given \(Q\) and independent of \(R'\); at least \(2c+2\) of them are residual with probability at most \(\bigl(eN\lambda_2n^{1/3}(N+1)/((2c+2)n)\bigr)^{2c+2}\le n^{-c-1}\), and each residual row assigned on a bad path gives fewer than \(k_5\) light holes by (F2).

Outside the excluded events a bad path has fewer than \(2^{c+3}+N/96+(2c+1)k_5<N/24\) distinct heavy holes, hence fewer than \(N/24\) heavy queries. \(\square\)

7. Scope

Compared with the single-row full-class theorem, the pinned rows form the fixed set \(A\) rather than all rows other than the tail row; this makes the reader role-separated, so the verified encoding gives the light bound and the conclusion is a switching theorem, not only a heavy bound. The new event is the dormancy of a label, its occupation by a light row, controlled by negative association over columns; the price is the matching dichotomy of (F3), which replaces the per-row out-loading count and costs a factor \(r'_w=O(n^{1/3}\log n)\) in the loading bound, absorbed by the rank step. Two simplifications relative to the earlier proof: the trivial bound \(u_{\rm s}(Q)\le N\lambda_2\) makes the second case of its step (E4) unnecessary, and the threshold carries \(\ln^2n\) because small pairs now allow \((c+4)\log_2n\) survivors outside \(Q\). Column classes with general pinned-row sets \(I_\tau\subseteq A\) and multi-row tails remain.

Main-route assessment. The first obligation is unchanged. In the literal window the heavy-query accounting now lives on the hole-only tree, where the recorded trigger-hole theorems are correct and the adaptive tree's matching bound is retracted; bipartite full-column readers are the first mixed class with a complete switching statement at every polynomial size within the budget on a tree whose decoder is verified. The remaining window cases are column classes with general pinned-row sets, general pair sets, multi-row tails, and the two-role encoding. Parity terms remain the open core.

Process assessment. The gap sat in a one-clause proof of a lemma that five later results used, and it surfaced only because the new proof restated what the rule provides, after which one run of the existing tool settled it; the lesson recorded in the working context is that a lemma whose proof covers one branch of its own case split is not a lemma, and that a tool built for one property should be run for every count it reports. No framework change is needed.

18 September 2026 — The hole-only rule fails for sparse pinned sets; the both-endpoints rule makes heavy rounds a matching, every trigger-hole theorem transfers, and two-tier column readers switch at every polynomial size within the height budget

Status: correction of the previous cycle's rule (the hole-only tree has \(N\) heavy queries on a unary reader with one pinned row, verified by computation) with the both-endpoints rule, whose trigger pairs form a matching, so that both the trigger-hole theorems and the matching-number bounds hold; decoder verified by exhaustive round trips; working theorem with full proof for column classes whose pinned-row sets are dense or sparse with bounded sparse degree per label. Spin cycle 196. Produced by Claude Code (Claude Fable 5.1 (claude-fable-5-1), low reasoning effort).

Question and stopping point. The task was to extend the bipartite full-column theorem to column classes with pinned-row sets \(I_\tau\subseteq A\). The first check, against the readers recorded in the alive-pair obligation as showing that distinct holes alone do not suffice, showed that the hole-only rule adopted last cycle is inadequate once a pinned row carries many labels. The cycle corrects the rule, transfers the recorded theorems, and proves the column theorem under a two-tier hypothesis that isolates the remaining case.

1. Sparse pinned sets defeat the hole-only rule

Take the unary reader \(\bigvee_x[i_0\to x]\) over all labels (tails empty). When \(i_0\in R'\), which has probability \((N+1)/(n+1)\gg n^{-c-1}\), every hole of \(Q\) carries an alive pair at \(i_0\), and the hole-only tree, which never queries \(i_0\), makes one hole query per label of \(Q\): a path with \(N\) heavy queries and no 1-leaf. The adaptive tree makes one pigeon query. So the hole-only rule gives the trigger-hole theorems, whose readers pin whole columns, but not the general window: a rule is needed under which the trigger pairs of a path are pairwise disjoint, which is what part (i) of the adaptive-rule lemma claimed and, by the previous cycle, the adaptive rule does not deliver. The tool confirms both failures (Section 3).

2. The both-endpoints rule

Rule. At a heavy round with trigger pair \((i,x)\), \(i\in R'\) unassigned, \(x\in Q\) unkilled, query the pigeon \(i\) (branches over the unused holes); on a branch \(i\mapsto y\) with \(y\ne x\), query the hole \(x\) as well (branches over the uncovered residual rows moved to \(x\), and the empty branch). On the branch \(i\mapsto x\) the round's term is satisfied and the node is a 1-leaf. The tree is otherwise the canonical mixed tree with the matched-first preference; a heavy round has two queries.

Lemma. On every path the trigger pairs of the heavy rounds are pairwise disjoint: a matching in \(B_{\rm t}\), the pairs \((i,x)\) with \(i\in R'\), \(x\in Q\) whose term's tail is not falsified by \(\rho'\). Hence the rounds number at most \(\nu(B_{\rm t})\le N\), the heavy queries at most \(2\nu(B_{\rm t})\), and each round's answers take at most \((N+e)(N+2)\) values. For a role-separated reader the decoder of the light encoding identifies the round's term as in the light lemma and reads the two answers, so the encoding applies with the heavy answers recorded in \(\delta\). Proof. After the round, \(i\) is assigned and \(x\) is used or emptied, so every pair at \(i\) or at \(x\) is killed, and a later trigger pair is unkilled. A trigger pair is the pinned pair of the round's term, whose tail is satisfied by \(\rho'\cup\pi\), hence not falsified by \(\rho'\). The decoder statement is part (ii) of the adaptive-rule lemma with the rule's test removed. \(\square\)

Transfer. Every recorded bound on heavy queries is a bound on rounds of the both-endpoints tree, with twice as many queries: the label-set observation (rounds at most \(|X\cap Q|\)), the distinct-rows and bounded-loading theorems (rounds within their stated counts), and the matched-first bound (rounds at most \(\nu(B_{\rm um})\)), restored as stated. The single-row full-class and bipartite full-column theorems keep their statements: their final counts \(2^{c+3}+N/96+(2c+1)k\) are below \(N/48\) for \(N\ge N_0\), so a bad path has fewer than \(N/48\) rounds and fewer than \(N/24\) heavy queries. The sparse lemma of the unary theorem bounds rounds directly. In the height budget, the trivial count is \(N\) rounds costing \(2r(N+e)(N+2)\) each, so the trivial height \(4N+3c+o(N)\) and the obligation, fewer than \(N/48\) rounds on paths with few light answers, are as before. The hole-only rule remains valid for the full-column theorems but is not used further.

3. Tool verification

check_mixed_term_encoding.py gained --rule {adaptive,hole,both}, and check_adaptive_rule_counterexample.py a second scenario (records). Column scenario (\(n=16\), \(N=8\), three classes): maximum heavy queries on a path 8 (adaptive), 3 (hole-only), 6 (both endpoints, three rounds). Sparse scenario (\(\bigvee_x[i_0\to x]\), \(i_0\) residual): 1 (adaptive), 8 (hole-only), 2 (both endpoints, one round). Round trips under the both-endpoints rule on the four role-separated instances with rich bad paths (\(n=8\), \(N=2\), seeds 2, 3, 4, 5): 15219 rich bad paths, 0 decoding failures; the two-role example reader fails on 1800 of 6380, as expected.

4. Two-tier column readers: setting

Rows are partitioned into pinned rows \(A\) and light rows \(B\), \(|B|\le(n-2N-2)/2\), so \(|A\setminus R'|\ge n/3\). A class \(\tau=(j_\tau,p_\tau,x_\tau,I_\tau)\) has \(j_\tau\in B\), a light pattern of at most \(w\) literals, and the pairs \(I_\tau\times\{x_\tau\}\) with \(\emptyset\ne I_\tau\subseteq A\); a reader is any set of classes, read by the both-endpoints tree. A class is dense if \(|I_\tau|\ge n/4\) and sparse otherwise; \(I^{\rm sp}_x=\bigcup\{I_\tau:\ \tau\text{ sparse},\ x_\tau=x\}\). A reader is two-tier if \(|I^{\rm sp}_x|<D^\ast=n/(400e(N+1))\) for every label \(x\). Under \(\rho'\in\Phi_0\) a class is matched if the occupant of \(x_\tau\) lies in \(I_\tau\) and alive if \(x_\tau\in Q\) and \(I_\tau\cap R'\ne\emptyset\).

Dense loading: for \(i\in A\), \(u^{\rm d}_x(i)=\sum\{|C(p_\tau)|/n:\ \tau\text{ dense},\ x_\tau=x,\ i\in I_\tau\}\), and \(u^{\rm d}(x)=\sum\{|C(p_\tau)|/n:\ \tau\text{ dense},\ x_\tau=x\}\). With \(\lambda_3=3(c+4)\ln n\) let \(I^{\rm h}_x=\{i\in A:\ u^{\rm d}_x(i)\ge\lambda_3\}\); \(x\) is heavy if \(|I^{\rm h}_x|\ge n/8\), light otherwise; \(H\) and \(X_L\) are the heavy and light labels. A light label has \(u^{\rm d}(x)<8\lambda_3\), since \((n/4)u^{\rm d}(x)\le\sum_{i\in A}u^{\rm d}_x(i)<(n/8)u^{\rm d}(x)+n\lambda_3\). Dense survivors: \(L^{\rm d}_j(z)=\{x_\tau:\ \tau\text{ dense},\ j_\tau=j,\ z\in C(p_\tau)\}\), and \(I_{j,z}(x)=\bigcup\{I_\tau:\ \tau\text{ dense},\ j_\tau=j,\ x_\tau=x,\ z\in C(p_\tau)\}\), of size at least \(n/4\) when \(x\in L^{\rm d}_j(z)\). Put \(k''=2^{c+3}\), \(k_5=k''+5(c+4)\ln n\); a pair \((j,z)\) is small if \(|L^{\rm d}_j(z)\cap X_L\setminus\{z\}|<k_5\); \(u_{\rm s}(x)\), \(V\), \(\Lambda_L\) are defined from small pairs and dense light survivors other than \(z\), as in the review, and \(J^{\rm d}_x\) is the set of rows hosting a dense class of label \(x\), \(|J^{\rm d}_x|\le2^wu^{\rm d}(x)\).

A bad path has at least \(N/48\) heavy rounds and no 1-leaf. Its rounds are classified by the trigger's class. Sparse rounds have pairwise disjoint trigger pairs in \(B^{\rm sp}=\{(i,x):\ i\in R',\ x\in Q,\ i\in I^{\rm sp}_x\}\). Dense rounds have distinct holes, each the label of a dense class with a satisfied tail at a light row assigned before the last round. Two facts: a term satisfied by \(\rho'\) prevents every round on every path; and if a light row \(j\) is assigned \(z\) before the last round, then for every \(x\in L^{\rm d}_j(z)\setminus Q\) the occupant of \(x\) lies outside \(I_{j,z}(x)\), since otherwise a dense class at \(j\) consistent with \(z\) is matched with a satisfied tail.

5. Lemma: a matching of light rows to hosted out-labels forces a satisfied term

Given \(Q,R'\), let \(G\) be the bipartite graph on the matched light rows and the light labels outside \(Q\) with an edge \((j,x)\) when some dense class at \(j\) has label \(x\), and \(r''_w=20\cdot2^w(c+1)\ln n\).

Lemma. If \(G\) has a matching of size \(r''_w\), then \(\Pr[\text{no term satisfied}\mid Q,R']\le n^{-c-1}\).

Proof. For each edge \((j,x_j)\) of the matching fix a dense class \(\tau_j\) at \(j\) with label \(x_j\), and let \(F_j\) be the event that \(\mu'(j)\in C(p_{\tau_j})\setminus(Q\cup\{x_j\})\) and the occupant of \(x_j\) lies in \(I_{\tau_j}\). On \(F_j\) the term of \(\tau_j\) at the occupant is satisfied. \(F_j\) is increasing in the entries of row \(j\) and of column \(x_j\) at the rows of \(I_{\tau_j}\subseteq A\); these coordinate sets are disjoint across the matching. Given \(\mu'(j)=z\ne x_j\), the occupant of \(x_j\) is uniform over the other matched rows, of which at least \(n/4-N-1\) lie in \(I_{\tau_j}\), so \(\Pr[F_j]\ge\frac{n2^{-w}-N-1}{n-N}\cdot\frac{n/4-N-1}{n-N-1}\ge\frac{2^{-w}}{10}\) for large \(n\). Negative association of the uniform bijection gives \(\Pr[\bigcap_jF_j^c]\le\exp(-r''_w2^{-w}/10)=n^{-2c-2}\). \(\square\)

By König's theorem, without such a matching \(G\) has a vertex cover \(J_0\cup X_0\) with \(|J_0|+|X_0|<r''_w\): every dense class with a light label outside \(Q\) sits on a row of \(J_0\) or of \(B\cap R'\), or has its label in \(X_0\).

6. Theorem

Theorem. For \(2^w\le n^{1/3}\), \(N\ge N_1(c)=2^{2c+29}(c+4)^2\ln^2n\), and \(n\) large, every two-tier column reader has, with probability at least \(1-8n^{-c-1}\), fewer than \(N/48\) heavy rounds, hence fewer than \(N/24\) heavy queries, on every path of the both-endpoints tree before any 1-leaf; with the light lemma for its light part, every such reader of a source of size \(n^c\) switches under one restriction within the height budget.

Proof. Given \(Q\), \((R',\mu')\) is a uniform bijection of the rows onto \(Q^c\) and \(N+1\) residual slots, negatively associated, also after conditioning on the value at one row or one column; \(R'\) is independent of \(Q\). The following events are excluded.

(G0) Sparse rounds. By the sparse lemma with \(k=N/192\) and degrees \(|I^{\rm sp}_x|<D^\ast\le k(n+1-k)/(2eN(N+1))\), \(\Pr[\nu(B^{\rm sp})\ge N/192]\le2^{-N/192}\le n^{-c-1}\). Outside this event a path has fewer than \(N/192\) sparse rounds.

(G1) Heavy labels. For a heavy \(x\notin Q\) the event that its occupant lies outside \(I^{\rm h}_x\) is decreasing in column \(x\) and has probability at most \(1-(n/8-N-1)/(n-N)\le8/9\); over distinct columns, \(\Pr[\text{all heavy labels outside }Q\text{ so occupied}\mid Q]\le(8/9)^{|H\setminus Q|}\). If the occupant is \(i_0\in I^{\rm h}_x\), the dense classes of \(x\) containing \(i_0\) are matched, and the events "row \(j\) is matched into \(\bigcup C(p_\tau)\setminus(Q\cup\{x\})\) over those classes at \(j\)" are increasing on distinct rows, each of probability at least half its set's density, so \(\Pr[\text{none satisfied}\mid\text{occupant }i_0]\le e^{-u^{\rm d}_x(i_0)/3}\le n^{-c-4}\); a union bound over the pairs \((x,i_0)\) costs \(2n^{-c-2}\). Outside it, on a bad path every heavy label outside \(Q\) has its occupant outside \(I^{\rm h}_x\). If \(|H|>N+9(c+1)\ln n\) this has probability at most \((8/9)^{9(c+1)\ln n}\le n^{-c-1}\); otherwise \(\Pr[|H\cap Q|\ge2^{c+3}]\le(|H|N/n)^{c+4}\le n^{-c-1}\) by rank. Dense rounds at heavy holes number fewer than \(2^{c+3}\).

(G2) Survivor sets. Let \((j,z)\) have \(L=L^{\rm d}_j(z)\cap X_L\setminus\{z\}\), \(|L|\ge k_5\), with \(j\) assigned \(z\) before the last round of a bad path. Each \(x\in L\setminus Q\) has its occupant outside \(I_{j,z}(x)\): decreasing events on distinct columns, each of probability at most \(1-(n/4-N-2)/(n-N-1)\le4/5\), read after conditioning on \(\mu'(j)=z\) when \(j\) is matched. If \(|L|\ge N+5(c+4)\ln n\), at least \(5(c+4)\ln n\) labels of \(L\) lie outside \(Q\) and the event has probability at most \((4/5)^{5(c+4)\ln n}\le n^{-c-4}\). Otherwise either \(|L\cap Q|\ge k''\), of probability at most \((|L|N/n)^{c+4}\le n^{-c-3.5}\), or again at least \(5(c+4)\ln n\) labels of \(L\) lie outside \(Q\). Over at most \(n(n+1)\) pairs this costs \(n^{-c-1}\); outside it every row assigned before the last round has a small pair and fewer than \(k_5\) dense light holes.

(G3) Matching or cover. By the lemma, outside \(n^{-c-1}\), on a bad path \(G\) has a cover \(J_0\cup X_0\) with \(|J_0|+|X_0|<r''_w\).

(G4) The flat's small light loading. A light-loaded pair (a dense light survivor other than \(z\)) either has all such survivors in \(Q\), is then small outside the rank event of (G2), and is charged to a survivor in \(Q\): at most \(n\,u_{\rm s}(Q)\le8nN\lambda_3\) pairs; or has a survivor \(x\notin Q\), whose dense class is covered on a bad path: at most \((r''_w+N+1)n+n\sum_{x\in X_0}u^{\rm d}(x)\le(r''_w+N+1)n+8\lambda_3r''_wn\) pairs. Hence \(\Lambda_L\le9(N+r''_w)\lambda_3\), \(V\le k_5\Lambda_L\), and with \(\theta=1/(800ek_5)\), \(|X_\theta|\le V/\theta\le7200e\,k_5^2(N+r''_w)\lambda_3\le n^{2/3}\) for large \(n\); by rank \(|X_\theta\cap Q|<2^{c+3}\) outside \(n^{-c-1}\), so \(u_{\rm s}(Q)\le N\theta+8\lambda_32^{c+3}\).

(G5) Matched light rows. With \(G'_j\) and \(A'\) as in the bipartite proof, \(\Pr[A'\ge a\mid Q]\le(2e\,u_{\rm s}(Q)/a)^a\), and for \(a=N/(192k_5)\), \(2e\,u_{\rm s}(Q)/a\le384e\,k_5\theta+3072e\,k_5\lambda_32^{c+3}/N\le0.48+0.02\) once \(N\ge N_1\); so \(\Pr[A'\ge a]\le2^{-a}\le n^{-c-1}\), and dense light holes from matched rows number fewer than \(k_5a=N/192\).

(G6) Residual light rows. The light rows hosting a dense class of a light label in \(Q\) number at most \(8N\lambda_32^w\le8N\lambda_3n^{1/3}\), a set fixed given \(Q\); at least \(2c+2\) of them are residual with probability at most \(\bigl(8eN\lambda_3n^{1/3}(N+1)/((2c+2)n)\bigr)^{2c+2}\le n^{-c-1}\), and each gives fewer than \(k_5\) dense light holes.

Outside the excluded events a bad path has fewer than \(N/192+2^{c+3}+N/192+(2c+1)k_5<N/48\) rounds. \(\square\)

7. Scope

The theorem contains the bipartite full-column theorem (every class dense, no sparse classes) and, for readers without tails, reproves the unary theorem's dense and sparse mechanisms on the both-endpoints tree, up to constants. What it excludes is the middle tier: labels at which sparse classes, each pinning fewer than \(n/4\) rows, together pin at least \(D^\ast=n/(400e(N+1))\) rows. There the pinned side alone gives no bound, and the tails must enter the symmetric sum: a matched light row \(j\) with label \(z\) activates the sparse classes at \(j\) consistent with \(z\), and it is the activated sparse degree at a label, not its total, that should play the role of \(D^\ast\). Since the activation events of distinct light rows are negatively associated, the expected number of \(k\)-matchings with activated tails is a sum over \(k\)-sets of labels in \(Q\) of products of activated degrees, which is the next computation. General pair sets, multi-row tails, and the two-role encoding remain.

Main-route assessment. The first obligation is unchanged. In the literal window the tree is now the both-endpoints tree, on which heavy rounds form a matching, so the trigger-hole theorems, the matching-number bounds, and the sparse lemma all apply; two-tier column readers switch at every polynomial size within the budget, and the open window cases are the middle tier of column classes, general pair sets, multi-row tails, and the two-role encoding. Parity terms remain the open core.

Process assessment. The hole-only rule was adopted last cycle without running it against the readers already recorded in the claim index as separating distinct holes from matchings, which the standing rule to search the index before naming a result would have caught; this cycle began with that check and found the failure in one tool run, so the rule needs following, not amending. No framework change is needed.

18 September 2026 — The middle tier: activated sparse degrees through a product measure, a two-stage exposure reduction for all column readers, and falsification attempts on the general column claim

Status: working lemma (activated sparse matching tail) and corollary theorem (column readers whose labels are two-tier or activation-bounded switch within the height budget); working reduction lemma for arbitrary column readers; heuristic falsification attempts recorded as evidence, not proof. Spin cycle 197. Produced by Claude Code (Claude Fable 5.1 (claude-fable-5-1), low reasoning effort).

Question and stopping point. The middle tier asks for the sparse rounds of column readers whose sparse classes pin, at some label, at least \(D^\ast=n/(400e(N+1))\) rows in total. The stopping point was either a proof that the tails restore the sparse lemma, or a precise statement of what remains. The cycle proves the tail-aware sparse lemma under an activation hypothesis, reduces the general case to a counting problem after exposing the pinned rows, and tries to falsify the general claim.

1. The general column claim

Column readers are as in the two-tier setting without the two-tier hypothesis: classes \((j_\tau,p_\tau,x_\tau,I_\tau)\), \(I_\tau\subseteq A\), \(j_\tau\in B\). Claim. For \(N\ge N_1(c)\) and large \(n\), every column reader of a source of size \(n^c\) has fewer than \(N/48\) heavy rounds on every path of the both-endpoints tree before any 1-leaf, except with probability \(O(n^{-c-1})\). Its status is conjectural; Sections 2 and 3 prove it under hypotheses on the sparse classes, Section 4 reduces it, and Section 5 fails to refute it.

2. Lemma: activated sparse degrees

For a set \(\mathcal T\) of classes, a label \(x\), and an assignment \(\zeta\) of the light rows (each row residual or at a label), let \(m_x(\zeta)=\sum_{j\in B}\bigl|\bigcup\{I_\tau:\ \tau\in\mathcal T,\ x_\tau=x,\ j_\tau=j,\ j\text{ residual or }\zeta(j)\in C(p_\tau)\}\bigr|\): the activated degree of \(x\), a union within each tail row and a sum over tail rows. Let \(B^{\mathcal T}_{\rm t}\) be the pairs \((i,x)\), \(i\in R'\), \(x\in Q\), carried by a class of \(\mathcal T\) whose tail is not falsified by \(\rho'\).

Lemma. If \(m_x(\zeta)<D^\ast\) for every label \(x\) and every \(\zeta\), then \(\Pr[\nu(B^{\mathcal T}_{\rm t})\ge N/192]\le2^{-N/192}\).

Proof. Let \(k=N/192\). A \(k\)-matching in \(B^{\mathcal T}_{\rm t}\) determines \(X\subseteq Q\) with \(|X|=k\), distinct pinned rows \(i_x\), and for each \(x\) a tail row \(j_x\) hosting a class \(\tau\in\mathcal T\) at \(x\) with \(i_x\in I_\tau\) whose tail is not falsified: \(j_x\in R'\) or \(\mu'(j_x)\in U_x\), where \(U_x\) is the union of \(C(p_\tau)\setminus Q\) over those classes. Fix \(X\), \((i_x)\), \((j_x)\). Given \(Q\), the events "\(i_x\in R'\)" are increasing on the distinct rows \(i_x\), and for each distinct tail row \(j\) the event "\(j\in R'\) or \(\mu'(j)\in\bigcap_{x:\ j_x=j}U_x\)" is increasing on row \(j\); the pinned and light rows are disjoint. Negative association gives \(\Pr\le\bigl(\tfrac{N+1}{n+1}\bigr)^k\prod_j\tfrac{N+1+|\bigcap_{x:\,j_x=j}U_x|}{n+1}=\bigl(\tfrac{N+1}{n+1}\bigr)^k\Pr_{\zeta'}[\forall x:\ j_x\text{ residual or }\zeta'(j_x)\in U_x]\), where \(\zeta'\) assigns each light row independently to a slot with probability \((N+1)/(n+1)\) and to each label with probability \(1/(n+1)\). Summing over \((i_x)\) and \((j_x)\) turns the right side into \(\bigl(\tfrac{N+1}{n+1}\bigr)^k\mathbb E_{\zeta'}\prod_{x\in X}m_x(\zeta')\le\bigl(\tfrac{N+1}{n+1}\bigr)^k(D^\ast)^k\), since a pair \((i_x,j_x)\) is counted only when \(i_x\) lies in an activated class at \((x,j_x)\). Summing over the \(\binom Nk\) sets \(X\subseteq Q\) and applying Markov, \(\Pr[\nu\ge k]\le\bigl(eN(N+1)D^\ast/(k(n+1))\bigr)^k\le2^{-k}\). \(\square\)

3. Corollary: two-tier or activation-bounded labels

Theorem. Call a label \(x\) two-tier if \(|I^{\rm sp}_x|<D^\ast\), and activation-bounded if \(m_x(\zeta)<D^\ast\) for every \(\zeta\), with \(\mathcal T\) the sparse classes. If every label is two-tier or activation-bounded, the conclusion of the two-tier theorem holds with the same constants.

Proof. Only step (G0) changes. In the lemma's count, split \(X\) into its two-tier and activation-bounded labels; for a two-tier label drop the tail event, which can only increase the probability, and count \(|I^{\rm sp}_x|\) choices of \(i_x\); the product-measure expectation then factors as \(\prod_{\text{two-tier}}|I^{\rm sp}_x|\cdot\mathbb E_{\zeta'}\prod_{\text{bounded}}m_x(\zeta')<(D^\ast)^k\). Steps (G1) to (G6) concern dense classes only. \(\square\)

This is a proper extension: a label with many sparse classes that share few tail rows, or whose patterns are pairwise inconsistent, is activation-bounded without being two-tier. It still excludes labels whose sparse classes sit on many tail rows with compatible patterns, where \(m_x\) can reach \(\Theta(n)\).

4. Reduction for arbitrary column readers: expose the pinned rows first

Lemma. Condition on stage one: \(Q\), \(R_A=R'\cap A\), and \(\mu'\) on \(A\setminus R_A\). This fixes the matched classes (occupant of \(x_\tau\) in \(I_\tau\)), the alive pairs \(B^{\rm al}=\{(i,x):\ i\in R_A,\ x\in Q,\ \exists\tau\ni i,\ x_\tau=x\}\), the remaining labels \(\mathrm{rem}\), and for each light row \(j\) the blocking set \(M_j=\bigcup\{C(p_\tau):\ \tau\text{ matched},\ j_\tau=j\}\). Given stage one, the light rows form a uniform bijection of \(B\) onto \(\mathrm{rem}\) and the remaining slots, and \[\Pr[\text{some path has }k\text{ rounds and no 1-leaf}\mid\text{stage one}]\ \le\ \sum_{M}\sum_{(\tau_x)}\prod_{j}\frac{N+1-|R_A|+\bigl|\bigcap_{x:\,j_{\tau_x}=j}C(p_{\tau_x})\cap\mathrm{rem}\setminus M_j\bigr|}{|B|},\] the sums over \(k\)-matchings \(M\) of \(B^{\rm al}\) and choices of a class \(\tau_x\ni i_x\) at each \(x\), the product over the distinct tail rows of the chosen classes.

Proof. A round's class is alive with a satisfied tail, and a matched light row whose label lies in \(M_j\) satisfies a matched class, which prevents every round; so on a bad path each chosen tail row is residual or carries a label in \(C(p_{\tau_x})\cap\mathrm{rem}\setminus M_j\), an increasing event on that row, and negative association of the light bijection gives the product. \(\square\)

The reduction makes the two decoupling devices explicit: a class's activating labels are useless to the adversary when they also activate a matched class at the same row (blocking), and the matched classes are a random subset of the reader's classes determined by stage one. Integrating over stage one, the weight of a class is its activated pinned rows times the unblocked part of its pattern, and the general claim becomes: the expected weighted number of alive \(k\)-matchings is at most \(2^{-k}\) unless stage one already yields many rows hosting matched classes, in which case the light bijection satisfies one of them with probability at least \(1-\exp(-2^{-w}J_{\rm m}/3)\), \(J_{\rm m}\) the number of such rows, by negative association over light rows once each matched pattern keeps a third of its labels in \(\mathrm{rem}\) (hypergeometric concentration over the exposure of \(A\), union bound over at most \(n^c\) classes).

5. Falsification attempts

Three families were checked against the claim by computing expected rounds and satisfied terms; none refutes it. (a) Private labels. Each pinned row \(i\) carries its own label set \(X_i\) of size \(m\) with private tails: rounds are a binomial over residual rows with success \(mN/n\), so \(\Pr[\text{rounds}\ge N/48]\le(24emN/n)^{N/48}\), while no satisfied term has probability about \(e^{-m2^{-w}/4}\); the product is below \(n^{-c-1}\) for every \(m\). (b) Shared labels. Rows in groups of size \(g\) sharing a label set of size \(m\): rounds need \(N/48\) groups whose sets meet \(Q\), probability about \((mN/n)^{N/48}\) by rank unless \(m\ge n/(2N)\), and no satisfied term has probability about \(2^{-m(1-2^{-w})}\) per group; again negligible. (c) One hosting row. All classes on one light row with one pattern and sparse pinned sets of size \(D^\ast\) at every label: activation is all-or-nothing, and when it happens the reader is a unary reader of edge mass \(nD^\ast\), satisfied except with probability \(\exp(-D^\ast)\). The common structure is that rounds need activated edge mass of order \(n^2/N\) or a rank coincidence, and the same mass forces a satisfied term through the matched classes; only dormancy (labels occupied by light rows) and blocking can separate the two, and both are random from the reader's side. This is heuristic evidence for the claim, not a proof.

Main-route assessment. The first obligation is unchanged. In the window, the column claim is now stated in general, proved for two-tier or activation-bounded labels, and reduced for arbitrary column readers to a weighted matching count after exposing the pinned rows, with the satisfaction side handled by negative association over light rows; the remaining work is the integration over stage one, which is a comparison between alive and matched classes at the level of \(k\)-matchings. General pair sets, multi-row tails, and the two-role encoding remain. Parity terms remain the open core.

Process assessment. The cycle began by stating the general claim and attacking it before refining hypotheses, as the task-selection rule asks; the falsification attempts cost little and shaped the reduction, while the hypothesis extension of Section 3 is minor and is the last case-style step to be taken before the general integration. No framework change is needed, and no computation was run.

18 September 2026 — Activated union degrees after exposing the light rows, and a short proof that column readers whose light rows host few labels switch within the height budget

Status: working lemma (activated union degrees, conditioned on the light rows) and working theorem with full proof (row-spread column readers), with no density hypothesis and a polylogarithmic threshold; the remaining column case is named. Spin cycle 198. Produced by Claude Code (Claude Fable 5.1 (claude-fable-5-1), low reasoning effort).

Question and stopping point. The task was to integrate the two-stage reduction over the pinned-row exposure. Reversing the exposure order, light rows first, gives a sharper sparse count in which a label's activated pinned rows are counted once across all tail rows; the dichotomy on the number of labels with a large activated union then closes the general column claim for readers whose light rows host few labels, and isolates the obstruction for the rest.

1. Lemma: activated union degrees

Column readers are as in the general claim. Let \(\zeta\) be the light assignment (the residual light rows and the labels of the matched ones), and for a label \(x\) let \(U_x(\zeta)=\bigcup\{I_\tau:\ x_\tau=x,\ j_\tau\in R'\text{ or }\zeta(j_\tau)\in C(p_\tau)\}\) over all classes. Call \(x\) activation-sparse if \(|U_x(\zeta)|<D_2^\ast=n/(800e(N+1))\) for every \(\zeta\), and let \(X_{\rm mid}\) be the other labels, a set fixed by the reader. Given \(Q\) and \(\zeta\), the residual pinned rows \(R_A\) form a uniform subset of \(A\) of size at most \(N+1\), and every trigger pair of a path lies in \(B^{\rm act}=\{(i,x):\ x\in Q,\ i\in R_A\cap U_x(\zeta)\}\), the pairs of a path forming a matching.

Lemma. \(\Pr[\nu(B^{\rm act}\text{ restricted to activation-sparse labels})\ge N/192]\le2^{-N/192}\).

Proof. Given \(Q\) and \(\zeta\), a \(k\)-matching, \(k=N/192\), consists of \(k\) labels \(X\subseteq Q\) and distinct rows \(i_x\in U_x(\zeta)\) all lying in \(R_A\); the last event has probability at most \(\bigl((N+1)/(|A|-k)\bigr)^k\le(2(N+1)/n)^k\), since \(|A|\ge n/2+N+2\). The expected number of \(k\)-matchings is therefore at most \(\binom Nk(D_2^\ast)^k(2(N+1)/n)^k\le\bigl(2eN(N+1)D_2^\ast/(kn)\bigr)^k=(0.48)^k\), and Markov's inequality finishes. \(\square\)

The lemma contains the sparse lemma and, up to the constant, the product-measure lemma, whose activated degree sums over tail rows where this one takes a union.

2. Theorem: row-spread column readers

A column reader is row-spread if every light row hosts classes of fewer than \(n^{1/3}\) distinct labels.

Theorem. For \(N\ge2^{c+11}(c+1)\log_2n\), \(2^w\le n^{1/3}/(2^{15}e(N+1)(c+1)\ln n)\), and \(n\) large, every row-spread column reader has, with probability at least \(1-4n^{-c-1}\), fewer than \(N/48\) heavy rounds on every path of the both-endpoints tree before any 1-leaf; with the light lemma for its light part, every such reader of a source of size \(n^c\) switches under one restriction within the height budget.

Proof. Rounds at activation-sparse labels number fewer than \(N/192\) outside probability \(2^{-N/192}\le n^{-c-1}\), by the lemma. Rounds at labels of \(X_{\rm mid}\) have distinct holes in \(X_{\rm mid}\cap Q\). Split on the reader.

Few middle labels, \(|X_{\rm mid}|\le n^{2/3}\): by rank, \(\Pr[|X_{\rm mid}\cap Q|\ge2^{c+3}]\le(|X_{\rm mid}|N/n)^{c+4}\le n^{-c-1}\), so a path has fewer than \(N/192+2^{c+3}<N/48\) rounds.

Many middle labels, \(|X_{\rm mid}|>n^{2/3}\): every \(x\in X_{\rm mid}\) has \(|I_x|\ge D_2^\ast\) for \(I_x=\bigcup_{x_\tau=x}I_\tau\). Given \(Q\), the events "the occupant of \(x\) lies in \(I_x\)", \(x\in X_{\rm mid}\setminus Q\), are increasing on distinct columns, each of probability \(|I_x|/(n+1)\ge1/(900e(N+1))\), so their number \(M\) is negatively associated with mean at least \(n^{2/3}/(1000e(N+1))\) and, by the Chernoff bound for negatively associated indicators, \(M\ge n^{2/3}/(2000e(N+1))\) outside probability \(\exp(-n^{2/3}/(8000e(N+1)))\). Each such label has a class \(\tau_x\) containing its occupant, whose pinned pair is satisfied by \(\rho'\); the tail rows of these classes form a set \(J'\) with \(|J'|\ge M/n^{1/3}\) by row-spreadness, of which at least \(|J'|-N-1\) are matched. Expose the pinned rows: the remaining labels \(\mathrm{rem}\) form a uniform subset of \(Q^c\) of size \(|B\setminus R'|\ge|J'|-N-1\), so by hypergeometric concentration and a union bound over at most \(n^c\) patterns, outside probability \(n^{-c-2}\) every pattern \(p\) of the reader has \(|C(p)\cap\mathrm{rem}|\ge2^{-w}|\mathrm{rem}|/4\). Given the pinned rows, the light rows form a uniform bijection onto \(\mathrm{rem}\) and the remaining slots, and the events "\(\mu'(j)\in C(p_{\tau_x})\cap\mathrm{rem}\)" for the matched rows \(j\in J'\) are increasing on distinct rows and each satisfies a term; negative association gives \(\Pr[\text{no term satisfied}]\le\exp(-(|J'|-N-1)2^{-w}/8)\le n^{-c-1}\) under the bound on \(2^w\). A term satisfied by \(\rho'\) prevents every round, so outside probability \(3n^{-c-1}\) no path has a round at all.

In both cases a bad path is impossible outside probability \(4n^{-c-1}\). \(\square\)

3. Scope and the remaining column case

The theorem needs no dense classes, no loading, and no survivor sets: the light-rows-first exposure makes the sparse count exact enough that only the number of labels with a large activated union matters, and many such labels force many matched classes, which under row-spreadness sit on many rows and are satisfied by the light bijection. Its threshold for \(N\) is polylogarithmic with a single logarithm, against \(\ln^2n\) for the loading proofs; its restriction on \(2^w\) is the light lemma's range up to polylogarithmic factors. It is incomparable with the two-tier and full-column theorems, whose readers may host all labels on one row. What remains of the general column claim is exactly a light row hosting at least \(n^{1/3}\) labels among more than \(n^{2/3}\) middle labels: with one pattern per row the host has edge mass at least \(n^{1/3}D_2^\ast\) and is matched, hence satisfied when activated; with many patterns per row the matched patterns are a random subset of the row's patterns, which blocks the alive ones (a label activating many alive patterns while avoiding every matched pattern is a rare event), and this random-subset blocking is the argument still to be written.

Main-route assessment. The first obligation is unchanged. In the window, the general column claim now holds for row-spread readers by a short proof, alongside the earlier theorems for readers hosting all labels on one row with full or dense columns; the open column case is a row hosting many labels with many patterns, and after it general pair sets, multi-row tails, and the two-role encoding. Parity terms remain the open core.

Process assessment. Reversing the exposure order, suggested by the falsification attempts of the previous cycle, replaced six loading steps by one count; the lesson recorded in the working context is to try both exposure orders before optimizing constants within one. No framework change is needed, and no computation was run.

18 September 2026 — Hosts, not labels: every single-row-tail reader whose light rows carry few patterns switches within the height budget; correction of the rank step for label sets of size \(n^{2/3}\)

Status: working theorem with full proof (role-separated single-row-tail readers with any pinned pairs and at most \(H_{\max}\) patterns per light row, hence every width up to \(\ell/(2\log_2(2\ell+1))\)), containing the role-separated column theorems; correction of four earlier rank steps. Spin cycle 199. Produced by Claude Code (Claude Fable 5.1 (claude-fable-5-1), reasoning effort xhigh (user setting)).

Verification gate. The proofs of the activated union lemma, the both-endpoints rule, the row-spread theorem, the sparse lemma, and the hole-query lemma were re-read; the recorded counterexample readers of the alive-pair obligation, the adaptive-rule gap, and the two-role correction were checked against the conclusion; no rule or encoding changed, so no tool run; a fresh-context reviewer found gaps in steps (H1), (H3), (H4) and the scope of the first draft, all resolved below, and traced the (H3) error to three earlier entries, corrected in Section 3.

Question and stopping point. The task was the last column case, a light row hosting many labels with many patterns. Rewriting the row-spread proof in terms of hosts, the pairs (light row, pattern), shows that labels per row never mattered: what a row's hosts share is the row's label, so a host with a matched pair blocks the row, and the light hosts obey the union-degree count.

1. Hosts

A reader consists of terms \([i\to x]\wedge[j\in p]\) with \(i\in A\), \(j\in B\), \(|B|\le(n-2N-2)/2\), and \(p\) a pattern of at most \(w\) literals on the bits of row \(j\); this is the setting of the general column claim, a class being the terms with one tail and one label. It is read by the both-endpoints tree with the matched-first preference. A host is a pair \(h=(j,p)\); \(P_h\) is the set of pinned pairs \((i,x)\) of the terms with tail \((j,p)\), \(m_h=|P_h|\) its mass, and \(I_{h,x}=\{i:\ (i,x)\in P_h\}\). Given the light assignment \(\zeta\), a host is activated if \(j\in R'\) or \(\zeta(j)\in C(p)\), and \(U_x(\zeta)=\bigcup_{h\text{ activated}}I_{h,x}\). A host is heavy if \(m_h\ge2N(n+1)\) and light otherwise; \(U^{\rm L}_x=\bigcup_{h\text{ light}}I_{h,x}\), \(\Omega_{\rm L}=\sum_x|U^{\rm L}_x|\), and \(H\) is the largest number of hosts on one light row. Put \(D_2^\ast=n/(800e(N+1))\), \(J_0=32\cdot2^w(c+1)\ln n+N+1\), \(\Omega_0=4N(n+1)J_0H\), and \(H_{\max}=n^{2/3}/(3300eN(N+1)J_0)\).

Two facts about a bad path (at least \(N/48\) rounds, no 1-leaf). Its trigger pairs form a matching of pairs \((i,x)\in P_h\) with \(x\in Q\), \(i\in R'\), and \(h\) activated, so they lie in the graph of the activated union lemma. And a host with a matched pair, \(\mu'(i)=x\) for some \((i,x)\in P_h\), contributes no trigger pair: at a matched row its term is satisfied by \(\rho'\), which prevents every round; at a residual row the matched-first preference queries that term's row before any round, an answer in \(C(p)\) is a 1-leaf, and any other answer falsifies every term of the host.

2. Theorem

Theorem. For \(N\ge2^{3c+10}(c+1)\log_2n\), \(2^w\le n^{1/3}\), \(H\le H_{\max}\), and \(n\) large, every such reader of a source of size \(n^c\) has, with probability at least \(1-3n^{-c-1}\), fewer than \(N/48\) heavy rounds on every path before any 1-leaf; with the light lemma for its light part, it switches under one restriction within the height budget. In particular this holds for every single-row-tail reader with \((2\ell+1)^w\le H_{\max}\), for instance \(w\le\ell/(2\log_2(2\ell+1))\).

Proof. (H1) Heavy hosts have a matched pair. Given \(Q\), for the labels \(x\notin Q\) of \(P_h\) the events "the occupant of \(x\) lies outside \(I_{h,x}\)" are decreasing on distinct columns, each of probability \(1-|I_{h,x}|/(n+1)\), while labels in \(Q\) have no occupant and carry mass at most \(N(n+1)\le m_h/2\). So a heavy host has no matched pair with probability at most \(e^{-m_h/(2(n+1))}\le e^{-N}\), and over at most \(n^c\) hosts this costs \(n^{-c-3}\). Outside this event the trigger pairs of a bad path come from light hosts, so the activated union may be read over light hosts, where \(U_x(\zeta)\subseteq U^{\rm L}_x\).

(H2) Light labels. By the activated union lemma applied to the light hosts, the rounds at labels with \(|U^{\rm L}_x|<D_2^\ast\) number fewer than \(N/192\) outside probability \(2^{-N/192}\le n^{-c-1}\).

(H3) Small union mass, \(\Omega_{\rm L}<\Omega_0\): the labels with \(|U^{\rm L}_x|\ge D_2^\ast\) form a set fixed by the reader with fewer than \(\Omega_0/D_2^\ast\le n^{2/3}\) elements, so by the rank lemma with \(d=3c+4\), \(\Pr[\text{at least }2^{3c+4}\text{ of them lie in }Q]\le(n^{2/3}N/n)^{3c+5}=N^{3c+5}n^{-(3c+5)/3}\le n^{-c-1}\) for large \(n\). A bad path then has fewer than \(N/192+2^{3c+4}<N/48\) rounds.

(H4) Large union mass, \(\Omega_{\rm L}\ge\Omega_0\): for a set \(J\) of fewer than \(J_0\) light rows, the light hosts on rows outside \(J\) have, over the labels outside \(Q\), \(\sum_{x\notin Q}|\bigcup_hI_{h,x}|\ge\Omega_{\rm L}-2N(n+1)J_0H-N(n+1)\ge2N(n+1)J_0H-N(n+1)\), so by the product over columns none of them has a matched pair with probability at most \(e^{-NJ_0H}\); over at most \(n^{J_0}\) sets \(J\) this costs less than \(n^{-c-1}\). Outside it, a set \(J^\ast\) of at least \(J_0\) light rows carries a light host with a matched pair. Expose the pinned rows: \(\mathrm{rem}\) is a uniform subset of \(Q^c\) of size \(|B|-s_B\ge|B|-N-1\ge32\cdot2^w(c+1)\ln n\), where \(s_B\le N+1\) is the number of slots left for \(B\), so by hypergeometric concentration and a union bound over at most \(n^c\) patterns, outside probability \(n^{-c-2}\) every pattern has \(|C(p)\cap\mathrm{rem}|\ge2^{-w}|\mathrm{rem}|/4\). Given the pinned rows, the light rows form a uniform bijection onto \(\mathrm{rem}\) and the slots; the events "\(\mu'(j)\in C(p)\cap\mathrm{rem}\)" for \(j\in J^\ast\) and its matched host \((j,p)\) are increasing on distinct rows, each of probability at least \(2^{-w}|\mathrm{rem}|/(4|B|)\ge2^{-w}(J_0-N-1)/(4J_0)\) since \(|B|\ge|J^\ast|\ge J_0\), and each satisfies a term; negative association gives \(\Pr[\text{no term satisfied}]\le\exp(-2^{-w}(J_0-N-1)/4)=n^{-8c-8}\). A term satisfied by \(\rho'\) prevents every round.

The cases are exclusive and fixed by the reader; the excluded events total at most \(3n^{-c-1}\). The final clause: a light row carries at most \(\sum_{t\le w}\binom{\ell}{t}2^t\le(2\ell+1)^w\) patterns, and for \(w\le\ell/(2\log_2(2\ell+1))\) this is at most \(n^{1/2}\le H_{\max}\), since then \(J_0=n^{o(1)}\). \(\square\)

3. Correction: the rank step for label sets of size \(n^{2/3}\)

The independent-points form of the rank lemma gives \(\Pr[|X\cap Q|\ge2^d]\le(|X|N/n)^{d+1}\). For \(|X|\le n^{2/3}\) this is \((Nn^{-1/3})^{d+1}\), which is below \(n^{-c-1}\) only when \((d+1)/3>c+1\), that is \(d\ge3c+3\); for \(|X|\le n^{1/3}{\rm polylog}(n)\) it suffices that \(2(d+1)/3>c+1\), that is \(d\ge2c+2\). Four recorded steps used \(d=c+3\) with larger sets, which fails for every \(c\ge1\); the first draft of (H3) repeated it. Corrected readings, with statements otherwise unchanged: (i) the corollary of the label-set observation holds with \(2^{3c+4}\) heavy rounds in place of \(2^{c+3}\); (ii) step (F4) of the bipartite full-column theorem and step (G4) of the two-tier theorem have \(|X_\theta|\le n^{1/3}{\rm polylog}(n)\), so they give \(|X_\theta\cap Q|<2^{2c+2}\) and \(u_{\rm s}(Q)\le N\theta+\lambda2^{2c+2}\), which raises the thresholds to \(N_0=2^{3c+24}(c+4)^2\ln^2n\) and \(N_1=2^{3c+28}(c+4)^2\ln^2n\) (also for the activation-bounded corollary) and leaves the final counts unchanged; (iii) the few-middle-labels case of the row-spread theorem holds with \(2^{3c+4}\) and the threshold \(N\ge2^{3c+10}(c+1)\log_2n\). The single-row full-class, bounded-loading, and distinct-rows theorems apply the lemma to fixed sets contained in \(Q\) or to sets of polylogarithmic size and are unaffected.

4. Scope

The theorem contains the role-separated versions of the single-row full-class theorem and the bipartite full-column, two-tier, and row-spread theorems on the both-endpoints tree whenever their readers have at most \(H_{\max}\) patterns per light row, with a threshold for \(N\) of one logarithm and no loading, survivor, or density step, and it settles the general column claim for all widths up to \(\ell/(2\log_2(2\ell+1))\). What remains in the single-row-tail window is a light row carrying more than \(H_{\max}\) patterns, which requires \(w\) above roughly \(2\ell/(3\log_2(2\ell))\): there the light hosts on one row are too many for the union bound of (H4), and the random-subset blocking argument, the matched hosts of a row being a random subset of its hosts that blocks the alive ones, is still the way to close it. Multi-row tails are the other open direction: the structure applies with hosts spanning several rows, and (H4) must then handle hosts with overlapping row sets.

Main-route assessment. The first obligation is unchanged. In the literal window, all single-row-tail readers of narrow patterns (width up to \(\ell/(2\log_2(2\ell+1))\)) with arbitrary pinned pairs now switch at every polynomial size within the height budget, on a tree whose decoder is verified; open are wide patterns crowded on one row, multi-row tails, and the two-role encoding. Parity terms remain the open core.

Process assessment. This was the first cycle under the verification gate: the fresh-context reviewer found a rank-step error that four cycles had repeated and two further gaps in the draft, all fixable without changing the statement, while re-reading the dependencies produced the host formulation that removed the column hypothesis; the gate cost one review round and is kept. No framework change beyond the gate is needed, and no computation was run.
